chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: The Trojans, after a seven years' voyage, set sail for Italy, but are overtaken by a dreadful storm, which Aeolus raises at the request of Juno. The tempest sinks one ship and scatters the rest. Neptune drives off the winds and calms the sea. Aeneas, with his own ship and six more, arrives safe at an African port. Venus complains to Jupiter of her son's misfortunes. Jupiter comforts her, and sends Mercury to secure him a kind reception among the Carthaginians. Aeneas, going out to discover the country, meets his mother in the shape of a huntress, who conveys him in a cloud to Carthage, where he sees his friends whom he thought lost, and receives a kind welcome from the queen. Dido, by a device of Venus, begins to feel a passion for him, and, after some conversation, asks to hear the history of his adventures since the siege of Troy, which becomes the subject of the two following books.

I sing of arms and of the man who, forced by fate and by the unrelenting hatred of haughty Juno, was expelled and exiled from the Trojan shore. He endured long labors both by sea and land, and fought a doubtful war before he won the realm of Latium and built the destined town. He restored his banished gods to their sacred rites, and established a secure succession in his line, from which came the race of Alban fathers and the long glories of majestic Rome. O Muse, tell me the causes and the crimes! What goddess was provoked, and what kindled her hatred? For what offense did the Queen of Heaven begin to persecute so brave and just a man, entangling his anxious life in endless cares, exposing him to want, and hurrying him into wars? Can heavenly minds harbor such high resentment, or exercise their spite in human suffering?

Far opposite the mouth of the Tiber, an ancient town was seated by the sea—a Tyrian colony, its people hardened for war and devoted to trade. Its name was Carthage, and Juno loved it more than her own Argos or the Samian shore. Here she kept her chariot; and here, if Heaven favored her, she planned to set the seat of imperial power. Yet she had heard an ancient rumor circulating among the gods, that in times to come the Trojan race would ruin her Carthage and throw down her towers, and that this race, not content with that, would lay the yoke of sovereign rule upon the necks of all nations. She brooded on this, and feared it was fated. Nor could she forget the recent war she had waged for conquered Greece against the Trojan state. Besides, long-standing causes were working in her mind, and secret seeds of envy remained: deep in her heart lay the verdict of partial Paris, her own beauty disdained, the grace bestowed on ravished Ganymede, the glories of Electra, and her own wronged bed. Each was a cause in itself, and all together kindled vengeance in her haughty mind. For these reasons, far distant from the coast of Latium, she drove the remnants of the Trojan host, and for seven long years the unhappy wandering company were tossed by storms and scattered through the seas. So much time, so much toil, was required to found the Roman name—so vast a frame demanded such long labor.

The Trojan fleet, with sails and oars, had scarcely left behind the fair shores of Sicily, entering the watery realm with cheerful shouts and cutting foamy furrows in the main, when, still laboring under endless discontent, the Queen of Heaven gave vent to her fury:

"Am I then defeated? Must I yield?" she said. "Must the Trojans reign in Italy? So fate wills it, and Jove adds his force; nor can my power divert their happy course. Could angry Pallas, with vengeful spleen, burn the Grecian fleet and drown its men? For the fault of one offender, she presumed to hurl the very bolts of Jove: with whirlwinds from below she tossed the ship, and laid bare the bosom of the deep. Then, as an eagle grips trembling prey, she seized the wretch—still hissing with her father's flame—and with a burning wound transfixed him, and bound him naked on a rock. But I, who walk in majestic state above, the majesty of heaven, the sister-wife of Jove, have for year after year employed my force in vain against the thin remains of ruined Troy! What nations now will pray to Juno's power, or lay offerings upon my slighted altars?"

So raged the goddess; and, filled with fury, she sought the restless regions of the storms, where, in a spacious cave of living stone, the tyrant Aeolus, from his airy throne, curbs the struggling winds with imperial power and binds the sounding tempests in dark prisons. This way and that the impatient captives strain, and, pressing for release, they rend the mountains. High in his hall the undaunted monarch stands, shakes his scepter, and commands their rage. Did he not do so, their unresisted sway would sweep the world before them; earth, air, and seas would roll through empty space, and heaven itself would flee before the driving blast. In fear of this, the Father of the Gods confined their fury to those dark abodes, locked them safe within, weighed down by the loads of mountains, and imposed a king with arbitrary power to loose their fetters or restrain their force. To him the suppliant queen addressed her prayers, and expressed her suit in these terms:

"O Aeolus, to you the King of Heaven has given the power of tempests and of winds; your force alone can restrain their fury, and smooth the waves or swell the troubled main. A race of wandering slaves, hateful to me, are cutting across the Tuscan sea with a prosperous passage; they steer their course for fruitful Italy, and intend to build new temples there to their vanquished gods. Raise all your winds; cover the skies with night; sink or disperse my fatal enemies. Twice seven charming daughters of the sea wait upon me and bear my train; the fairest, Deiopea, shall be yours, and shall make you the father of a happy line."

To this the god replied: "It is yours, O queen, to will, and my duty to fulfill the work. These airy kingdoms, and this wide command, are all the gifts of your bountiful hand. Yours is the favor of my sovereign, and I sit as your guest at the celestial feast of the gods. Raise tempests at your pleasure or subdue them; dispose of the empire that I hold from you."

He spoke, and hurled his quivering spear against the mountain's side, with all the strength of a god. The raging winds rushed through the hollow wound, danced aloft in air, and skimmed along the ground. Then, settling on the sea, they swept the surges, raised liquid mountains, and laid bare the deep. South, East, and West roared in mixed confusion, and rolled the foaming billows to the shore. The cables cracked; the sailors' fearful cries rose up; black night covered the skies, and heaven itself was ravished from their sight. Loud peals of thunder rolled from the poles; flashes of fire renewed the momentary light. The face of things bore a frightful aspect, and present death appeared in many forms. Struck with unusual terror, the Trojan chief, with lifted hands and eyes, invoked help, and cried: "Three and four times happy those who died before their parents' eyes beneath the walls of Ilium! Tydides, bravest of the Grecian host, why could I not have been slain by that mighty arm, and lie by noble Hector on the plain, or by great Sarpedon, in those bloody fields where Simois rolls the bodies and the shields of heroes, whose dismembered hands still clutch the dart and the pointed spear!"

While the pious prince lamented his fate, fierce Boreas drove against his flying sails and tore the sheets; the raging billows rose, and lifted the tossing vessels to the skies. The shivering oars could not sustain the blow; the galley gave way at the side and turned her prow, while those astern, descending down the steep, saw the boiling deep through yawning waves. Three ships were carried off by the southern blast, and dashed with fury on the hidden shoals—rocks which the Ausonian sailors knew: when they rose above the flood and showed their broad backs, they called them the Altars. Three more ships fierce Eurus, in his angry mood, dashed on the shallows of the shifting sand, and left them stranded in mid-ocean. Orontes' ship, that bore the Lycian crew—a horrid sight, even in the hero's view—was overwhelmed from stem to stern; the trembling pilot, torn from his rudder, was hurled headlong; three times the ship was tossed around, then broke apart at once, and was lost in the deep. Here and there above the waves were seen weapons, pictures, precious goods, and floating men. Even the stoutest vessel gave way to the storm, and sucked in the rushing sea through loosened planks. Ilioneus was her captain; and old Alethes, faithful Achates, and young bold Abas suffered no less. Their ships, with gaping seams, let in the flood of brine.

Meanwhile imperial Neptune heard the sound of raging billows breaking on the ground. Displeased, and fearing for his watery reign, he raised his awful head above the sea, serene in majesty, and rolled his eyes over the space of earth, seas, and skies. He saw the Trojan fleet scattered and distressed, oppressed by stormy winds and wintry sky. Well the god knew his sister's envy, and what her aims and her schemes pursued. He summoned Eurus and the western blast, cast an angry glance on both, and then rebuked them thus: "Audacious winds! From where comes this bold attempt, this rebel insolence? Is it for you to ravage seas and land, unauthorized by my supreme command? To raise such mountains on the troubled sea? Whom I—but first it is fitting to restrain the waves; and then you shall be taught obedience to my rule. Hence! Carry my royal mandate to your lord. The realms of ocean and the fields of air are mine, not his. By fatal lot the liquid empire and the trident of the sea fell to me. His power is confined to hollow caverns. There let him reign, the jailer of the winds, summoning his breathing subjects with hoarse commands, and boasting and blustering in his empty hall." He spoke; and as he spoke, he smoothed the sea, dispelled the darkness, and restored the day. Cymothoe and Triton, and the sea-green train of lovely nymphs, the daughters of the main, cleared the vessels from the rocks with their hands. The god himself, with his ready trident, opened the deep, spread out the shifting sands, and heaved the ships off the shoals. Wherever he guided his finny coursers and rode in triumph, the waves grew smooth and the sea subsided. As when a riot rises among an ignoble crowd, their motions are mad, and their tongues are loud; stones and firebrands fly in rattling volleys, and every rustic weapon that fury can supply; but if some grave and pious man appears, they hush their noise and lend a listening ear; he soothes their angry mood with sober words, and quenches their inborn desire for blood—so, when the Father of the Flood appeared, and raised his sovereign trident over the seas, their fury fell. He skimmed the liquid plains, high on his chariot, and with loosened reins he moved along majestic, maintaining awful peace. The weary Trojans plied their shattered oars toward the nearest land, and reached the Libyan shores.

Within a long recess there lies a bay. An island shields it from the rolling sea, and forms a harbor where ships can ride in safety. Broken by the jutting land on either side, the briny waters glide in in two streams. Between two rows of rocks a sylvan scene appears above, with groves forever green; a grotto is formed beneath, with mossy seats, to rest the Nereids and keep out the heat. Down through the crannies of the living walls, crystal streams descend in murmuring falls. No hawsers are needed here to bind the vessels, nor any toothed anchors; for they fear no storms. Seven ships met within this happy harbor, the thin remainder of the scattered fleet. The Trojans, worn with toils and spent with woes, leaped onto the welcome land, and sought their longed-for rest.

First, good Achates, with repeated strokes of clashing flints, struck their hidden fire. A short flame caught; a bed of withered leaves received the dying sparks as they fell. Kindled into life, they rose in fiery fumes and, fed with stronger fuel, mounted to the skies. The Trojans, dripping wet, either stood around the cheerful blaze or lay along the ground. Some dried their grain, spoiled with brine, ground it between stones, and prepared to dine. Aeneas climbed the mountain's airy brow and took a prospect of the seas below, hoping to spy Capys from there, or Antheus, or to see the streamers of Caicus flying. No vessels were in view; but on the plain three stately stags, with branching heads, led a lordly train; the more ignoble herd followed their stately steps, grazing slowly along. He halted; and while they fed in security below, he took the quiver and the trusty bow that Achates was used to carry. First he laid the leaders low, and then pierced the rest; nor did he cease from his arrows until seven mighty bodies stained the shaded plain with their blood. For the seven ships he made an equal share, and returned to the port in triumph from the hunt. He broached the jars of generous wine—Acestes' gift, when the fleet left his Trinacrian shores—and prepared for the feast, sharing the wine equally with the venison. While he dealt it round, the pious chief allayed the common grief with cheerful words: "Endure, and conquer! Jove will soon dispose our past and present sufferings to future good. With me you have survived the rocks of Scylla, and defied the inhuman Cyclops and his den. What greater ills can you endure after that? Take courage again and put away care; an hour will come when it will be a pleasure to recall your past sorrows, as blessings sent by Fate. Through various hazards and events we move to Latium and the realms foreordained by Jove. There we are called (that is the promise of the skies), where Trojan kingdoms may rise once again. Endure the hardships of your present state; live, and keep yourselves for a better fate."

These were the words he spoke, but he did not speak them from his heart; his outward smiles concealed his inward pain. The jolly crew, forgetful of the past, shared the quarry and hurried their plentiful dinner. Some stripped off the skin; some divided up the spoil; limbs, still trembling, boiled in the cauldrons; some broiled the steaming entrails over the fire. Stretched at ease on the grassy turf, they dined, restoring their strength with meat and cheering their souls with wine. Their hunger thus appeased, their thoughts turned to the doubtful fortune of their absent friends. Alternate hopes and fears possessed their minds, whether to count them dead or still distressed. Above the rest, Aeneas mourned the fate of brave Orontes, and the uncertain state of Gyas, Lycus, and Amycus. The day, but not their sorrows, ended thus.

When almighty Jove, from on high, surveyed the earth, the air, the shores, and the navigable seas, he at length fixed his eyes on the Libyan realms. As he pondered thus on human miseries, Venus saw him, and with a downcast look, not free from tears, addressed her heavenly sire:

"O King of Gods and Men, whose awful hand scatters thunder on the seas and land, and disposes all things with absolute command! How could my pious son incense your power? Or what, alas, was vanished Troy's offense? Our hope of Italy is not only lost, tossed on various seas by various tempests, but we are shut out from every shore and barred from every coast. You once promised a divine progeny of Romans rising from the Trojan line, who in time to come should hold the world in awe, and give law to land and ocean. How is your decree reversed, which eased my care when Troy was ruined in that cruel war? Then I could balance fates against fates; but now, when Fortune still pursues her former blow, what can I hope? What worse can still come? What end has your will decreed to these labors? Antenor was able to pass safely from the midst of Grecian hosts, and pierce the Illyrian coasts, where Timavus rages as it rolls down from the heights and empties through nine channels. At length he founded the happy seat of Padua, and gave his Trojans a secure retreat; there he established their arms, renewed their name, and now rules in peace, crowned with fame. But we, descended from your sacred line, entitled to your heaven and your divine rites, are banished from earth; and, because of the wrath of one, removed from Latium and the promised throne. Are these our scepters? Are these our due rewards? And is this how Jove keeps his plighted word?"
To her the Father of the immortal race, smiling with that serene and indulgent face with which he drives the clouds and clears the skies, first gave a holy kiss, and then replied:

"Daughter, dismiss your fears. The fates of your descendants stand fixed and unchanged, as you desire. You shall behold the Lavinian walls you wish for; and when Aeneas, ripe for heaven, is called by fate, you shall bear him up, sublime, to me. No counsel has reversed my firm decree. And lest new fears disturb your happy state, know that I have searched the mystic rolls of Fate. Your son (nor is the appointed season far off) shall wage successful war in Italy, tame fierce nations in the bloody field, impose sovereign laws, and build cities, until, every foe subdued, the sun has run its annual race three times through the signs. This is his appointed time. Then Ascanius, now called Iulus, shall begin his reign. He shall wear the crown for thirty rolling years, and then shall transfer the seat from Lavinium, and with hard labor shall build Alba Longa. The throne shall be filled by his successors for three hundred more years, and then Ilia the fair shall be seen, a priestess and a queen, who, filled with the seed of Mars, shall in due time bring forth twin boys at a single birth. A tawny wolf shall suckle the royal babes. Then Romulus shall gain his grandfather's throne, shall found towers of war, shall call the people Romans, and the city Rome. To them I assign no bounds of empire, nor term of years to their immortal line. Even haughty Juno, who now turmoils earth, seas, and heaven, and Jove himself, with endless broils, shall be reconciled at last, and join her friendly power to cherish and advance the Trojan line. The subject world shall acknowledge Rome's dominion, and lying prostrate shall adore the nation of the toga. An age is ripening in revolving fate when Troy shall overturn the Grecian state, and her conquering sons shall call for sweet revenge, to crush the people who conspired at her fall. Then Caesar shall arise from the Julian stock, whose empire shall be bounded only by ocean, and whose fame only by the skies; whom, laden with eastern spoils, our heaven, the just reward of human toils, shall securely receive with divine rites, and incense shall rise before his sacred shrine. Then dire debate and impious war shall cease, and the stern age shall be softened into peace. Then banished Faith shall return once more, and Vestal fires shall burn in hallowed temples; and Remus with Quirinus shall sustain the righteous laws, and restrain fraud and force. Janus himself shall stand before his shrine and guard the dreadful gates, with bolts and iron bars: within remains Fury, imprisoned, bound in brazen chains; high on a trophy of useless weapons he sits, and threatens the world with vain alarms."

He spoke, and sent Cyllenius with command to open the ports and the Punic land to the Trojan guests, lest the queen, ignorant of fate, should force them from her town and state. Down from the steep of heaven Cyllenius flew, cleaving the yielding skies with all his wings. Soon the god descended upon the Libyan shore, performed his message, and displayed his rod. The surly murmurs of the people ceased; and, as the Fates required, they offered peace. The queen herself suspended the rigid laws, pitied the Trojans, and protected their cause.

Meanwhile Aeneas lay in the shadows of night. Care seized his soul, and sleep forsook his eyes. But when the sun restored the cheerful day, he rose to survey the coast and country, anxious and eager to discover more. It looked a wild and uncultivated shore; but whether mankind or beasts alone possessed this new-found region was still unknown. Beneath a ledge of rocks he hid his fleet. Tall trees surrounded the mountain's shady sides; the overhanging brow above provided a safe retreat. Armed with two pointed darts, he left his friends, and true Achates attended on his steps. Behold, in the deep recesses of the wood, his goddess mother stood before his eyes—a huntress in dress and bearing, clothed as a maid, but her air proclaimed a queen. Her knees were bare, and knots tied up her garments; her hair was loose, and played upon the wind; her hand supported a bow, and her quiver hung behind. She seemed a virgin of the Spartan blood: in such attire Harpalyce bestrode her Thracian courser, outstripping the rapid flood. "Ho, strangers," she said, "have you lately seen one of my sisters, dressed as I am, who crossed the lawn, or strayed in the forest? A painted quiver at her back she bore; she wore a spotted lynx's hide, and at full cry pursued the tusky boar."

So spoke Venus; and her son replied: "None of your sisters have we heard or seen, O virgin, or by whatever other name you bear above that style—O more than mortal fair! Your voice and appearance betray celestial birth. If, as you seem, you are the sister of the day, or at least one of chaste Diana's train, do not let a humble suppliant plead in vain. Tell a stranger, long tossed in tempests, what land we tread, and who rules this coast. Then wretched mortals shall call upon your name, and fall as offered victims at your altars." "I dare not," she replied, "assume the name of goddess, or claim celestial honors. Tyrian virgins bear bows and quivers, and wear purple buskins over their ankles. Know, gentle youth, that you are in the land of Libya, a people rude in peace and rough in war. The rising city you see from afar is Carthage, a Tyrian colony. Phoenician Dido rules the growing state; she fled from Tyre to escape her brother's hate. Great were her wrongs, her story full of fate, which I will briefly tell. Sichaeus, famous for his wealth and brother to the Punic throne, possessed fair Dido's bed; and both hearts were wounded at once with an equal dart. Her father gave her, a spotless maid; Pygmalion then held the Tyrian scepter—a man who despised both divine and human laws. Then strife arose, and cursed gold was its cause. The monarch, blinded by the desire for wealth, stealthily attacked his brother with steel, made him bleed before the sacred altar, and long concealed the cruel deed from her. He daily coined some tale, some new pretense, to soothe his sister and delude her mind. At length, in the dead of night, the ghost of her unhappy husband appeared. The specter stared, and with erected eyes bared his bloody breast; he told her of the cruel altars and his fate, revealed the dire secret of his house, and warned the widow to flee, with her household gods, to remote abodes. Finally, to support her on so long a journey, he showed her where his hidden treasure lay. Admonished thus, and seized with mortal fear, the queen provided companions for her flight. They met, and all agreed to leave the state—those who hated the tyrant, or feared his hate. They seized a fleet that was already rigged and ready, and Pygmalion's treasure was not left behind. The vessels, heavily laden, put out to sea with prosperous winds; a woman led the way. I do not know whether driven by stress of weather, or whether their fatal course was disposed by Heaven; at last they landed where from afar your eyes may now see the towers of new Carthage rising. There they bought a piece of ground, which they called Byrsa, from the bull's hide with which they first enclosed and walled it. But where are you from? What country claims your birth? What do you seek, strangers, on our Libyan earth?"

To her, with tears streaming from his eyes, and deeply sighing, her son replied: "O nymph, could you bear to hear, or I to relate, the tedious annals of our fate! If I should run through such a train of woes, the day would end sooner than the tale. From ancient Troy, expelled by force, we come, if by chance you have heard the Trojan name. Tossed by various tempests on various seas, we have at last landed on your Libyan coast. I am called the good Aeneas—a name, while Fortune favored me, not unknown to fame. With pious care I rescued my household gods, companions of my sufferings, from our enemies. My course was bent for fruitful Italy; and I am descended from the King of Heaven. With twice ten sail I crossed the Phrygian sea; Fate and my mother the goddess led the way. Scarcely seven, the thin remainders of my fleet preserved from storms, have met within your harbor. Distressed myself, an exile, and unknown, shut out from Europe, and cast forth from Asia, I wander thus alone in Libyan deserts."

His tender parent could bear no more; but, interposing, she sought to soothe his care. "Whoever you are, you are not unbeloved by Heaven, since your ships are driven upon our friendly shore. Take courage; commit the rest to the gods, and lay your just request before the queen. Now take this earnest of further success: your scattered fleet is gathered again upon the shore; the winds are changed, and your friends are free from danger—or else I renounce my skill in augury. Behold twelve swans moving in beautiful order, which the bird of Jove, pursuing them through the clouds, had driven along. Now, united in a fair team, they skim the ground, and seek the quiet stream. As they, rejoicing at their return, clap their wings, and ride the circuit of the skies in rings—so too your ships and every friend already hold the port, or are descending to it with swift sails. No more advice is needed. Pursue the path before you, and the town in view."

Having said this, she turned, and revealed her radiant neck and her disheveled hair, which, flowing from her shoulders, reached the ground. Ambrosial scents spread wide around her; her sweeping gown descended in long folds, and by her graceful walk the Queen of Love was known. The prince pursued the departing deity with words like these: "Ah! Where do you fly? Unkind and cruel! To deceive your son in borrowed shapes, and shun his embrace! Never to bless my sight, but always unknown, and still to speak in accents not your own!" So he complained to the goddess; but he took the path and obeyed her commands. They marched hidden from view, for Venus kindly shrouded their persons in mists and enveloped them in clouds, so that, unseen, no one might stay their passage or force them to tell the reasons for their coming. This done, the goddess flew sublime to visit Paphos and her native climes, where garlands, ever green and ever fair, are offered with vows and solemn prayer. A hundred altars smoke in her temple; a thousand bleeding hearts invoke her power.

They climbed the next rise, and, looking down, now viewed the town at a nearer distance. The prince gazed in wonder at the stately towers, which had lately been huts and rude shepherds' bowers, at the gates and streets, and heard from every side the noise and busy concourse of the marketplace. The toiling Tyrians called to one another to ply their labor. Some extended the wall; some were building the citadel; the brawny throng either dug, or pushed unwieldy stones along. Some chose a spot of ground for their dwellings, which they first marked out and then surrounded with ditches. Some ordained laws; some attended the election of holy senators, chosen by voice. Here some designed a mole; there others laid deep foundations for a theater, and hewed mighty columns from marble quarries for scenery and future display. Their toil and their busy pains were like those of bees in flowery plains, when, winter past and summer scarcely begun, they are called forth to labor in the sun. Some lead their young abroad; some condense their liquid store; some dispense it into the cells; some stand ready at the gate to receive the golden burden, and relieve their returning friends; all combine with united force to drive the lazy drones from the laborious hive. Stung with envy, they watch each other's deeds; the fragrant work proceeds with diligence. "Three times happy you, whose walls already rise!" said Aeneas, and with lifted eyes he gazed upon their lofty towers. Then, entering at the gate (marvelous to relate), concealed in clouds, he mixed unnoticed among the busy throng, was borne along by the tide, and passed along unseen.

In the very center of the town stood a venerable wood, thick with trees. The Tyrians, landing near this holy ground and digging here, had found a prosperous omen: from beneath the earth they drew out a horse's head, which foreshadowed their growth and future fortune. Juno, the foundress, had given them this fated sign of a fruitful soil and a brave people. Here Sidonian Dido built and consecrated Juno's temple with solemn state, enriched with gifts and with a golden shrine; but the goddess made the place still more divine. On brazen steps the marble threshold rose, and brazen plates enclosed the cedar beams. The rafters were crowned with brazen coverings, and the lofty doors sounded on brazen hinges. What Aeneas first beheld in this place revived his courage and drove away his fear. For while, awaiting the queen, he raised his wondering eyes and gazed around the temple, admiring the fortune of the rising town, the competing artists, and the fame of their art, he saw, in order painted on the wall, all that had befallen unhappy Troy: the wars that fame had blown around the world, every scene true to life, every leader known. There he sees Agamemnon, and here Priam, and fierce Achilles, who defies them both. He stopped, and weeping, said: "O friend! Even here monuments of Trojan suffering appear! Our known disasters fill even foreign lands: see there, where old unhappy Priam stands! Even the mute walls relate the warrior's fame, and Trojan griefs stir Tyrian pity!" He said, and his tears found a ready passage, as he devoured with his eyes the scenes so well depicted, and fed his mind with an empty picture. For there he saw the fainting Greeks yielding, and there the trembling Trojans quitting the field, pursued by fierce Achilles across the plain as he drove his high chariot over the slain. Next came the tents of Rhesus, and his grief was renewed, their white sails betraying them to nightly view, and wakeful Diomede, whose cruel sword slew the sentries and did not spare their slumbering lord; then he took the fiery steeds before they tasted the food of Troy or drank from the river Xanthus. Elsewhere he saw where Troilus defied Achilles, and tried unequal combat; then, where the boy, disarmed, with loosened reins, was hurried over the plain by his horses, hung by the neck and hair, and dragged around, the hostile spear still sticking in his wound, inscribing the dusty ground with tracks of blood. Meanwhile the Trojan matrons, oppressed with woe, went in long procession to the temple of Pallas, hoping to reconcile their heavenly enemy. They wept, beat their breasts, tore their hair, and bore richly embroidered vests as offerings; but the stern goddess stood unmoved by prayer. Three times Achilles dragged Hector's corpse around the Trojan walls, whom he had slain in combat. Here Priam was suing; and there, for sums of gold, the lifeless body of his son was being sold. So sad an object, and so well expressed, drew sighs and groans from the grieving hero's breast, to see the figure of his lifeless friend, and his old father stretching out his helpless hand. He saw himself also amid the Grecian train, mingled in the bloody battle on the plain; and he knew swarthy Memnon in his armor, his pompous ensigns, and his Indian crew. There was Penthesilea, leading an Amazonian race to war with haughty grace; in their right hands they wielded a pointed dart, and their left sustained the lunar shield for defense. She threw a golden belt across her breast, and alone among the press she provoked a thousand foes, daring to oppose her maiden arms to manly force.

While the Trojan prince thus employed his eyes, fixed upon the walls with wonder and surprise, the beautiful Dido, with a numerous retinue and pomp of guards, ascended the sacred temple. Such, on the banks of Eurotas or on the heights of Cynthus, Diana appears; and so she charms the sight, when in the dance the graceful goddess leads the choir of nymphs and towers above their heads. Known by her quiver and her lofty mien, she walks majestic, and looks their queen; Latona sees her shine above the rest, and fills her silent heart with secret joy. Such was Dido—with such becoming state she walks serenely great amidst the crowd. She presses their labor forward for her future realm, and proceeds with a gracious glance; then mounts the throne, high placed before the shrine. The swarming people gather in crowds around her. She takes petitions, dispenses laws, hears and determines every private case, divides the tasks in equal portions, and where unequal, decides them by lot. By chance Aeneas turned his eyes another way, and unexpectedly saw his friends—Antheus, grave Sergestus, strong Cloanthus, and behind them a mighty Trojan throng, whom the tempest had lately tossed on the waves and scattered widely on another shore. The prince, unseen, stood astonished with wonder, and longed to join their hands with joyful haste; but, doubtful of the event he wished, he waited, and surveyed his friends from within the hollow cloud, impatient till they told their present state, and where they had left their ships, and what their fate was, and why they came, and what their request; for these had been sent, commissioned by the rest, to ask permission to land their sickly men, and to gain admission to the gracious queen. Entering with cries, they filled the holy fane; then thus, with lowly voice, Ilioneus began:

"O Queen, indulged by the favor of the gods to found an empire in these new abodes, to build a town, and to restrain with statutes the wild inhabitants beneath your reign, we wretched Trojans, tossed from every shore, from sea to sea, implore your clemency. Forbid the fires to deface our shipping! Receive the unhappy fugitives with grace, and spare the remnant of a pious race! We come not with any design of wasteful plunder, to drive off the country or carry off the shepherds. Our strength is not such, nor is such our desire; the vanquished dare not aspire to such thoughts. There is a land, of old named Hesperia, with a fruitful soil and a bold people; the Oenotrians once held it, but it is now commonly called Italia, from their leader's name. Our voyage was bent toward that sweet region, when winds and every warring element disturbed our course, and, far from sight of land, cast our torn vessels on the shifting sand. The sea came on; the south wind, with a mighty roar, dispersed and dashed the rest upon the rocky shore. The few you see escaped the storm, and fear, unless you intervene, a shipwreck even here. What men, what monsters, what inhuman race, what laws, what barbarous customs of this place, shut up a desert shore against drowning men, and drive us to the cruel seas again? If our hard fortune draws no compassion from you, nor any hospitable rights or human laws, the gods are just, and will avenge our cause. Aeneas was our prince: a juster lord, or a nobler warrior, never drew a sword; observant of right, and religious in his word. If he still lives and breathes this vital air, we, his friends, shall not despair of safety; nor shall you, great queen, repent these offices, which he will repay in kind, and perhaps augment. We are not in want of cities, nor of the coasts of Sicily, where King Acestes boasts of his Trojan lineage. Permit our ships a shelter on your shores, refitted from your woods with planks and oars, that, if our prince is safe, we may renew our destined course and pursue Italy. But if, O best of men, the Fates decree that you are swallowed in the Libyan sea, and if our young Iulus is no more, dismiss our fleet from your friendly shore, that we may return to good Acestes, and mourn our common losses with our friends." So spoke Ilioneus; and the Trojan crew renewed his request with cries and clamor.

The modest queen pondered the speech for a while, with downcast eyes, then briefly replied: "Trojans, dismiss your fears. My cruel fate, and the doubts of an unsettled state, force me to guard my coast from foreign foes. Who has not heard of the story of your sufferings, the name and fortune of your native place, the fame and valor of the Phrygian race? We Tyrians are not so devoid of sense, nor so remote from the influence of Phoebus. Whether your course is bent for the Latian shores, or, driven by tempests from your first intent, you seek the government of good Acestes, your men shall be received, your fleet repaired, and sent on with convoy ships for your guard. Or, if you would stay and join your friendly power to raise and defend the Tyrian towers, my wealth, my city, and I myself are yours. Would to Heaven that the same storm you felt might bring your wandering king onto Carthaginian coasts! My people shall, by my command, explore the ports and creeks of every winding shore, and towns and wilds and shady woods, in quest of so renowned and so desired a guest."

The Trojan hero stood with his spirits raised, and longed to break forth from his surrounding cloud. Achates perceived it, and urged him on: "From where comes this long delay, O goddess-born? What more could you desire, with your welcome assured, your fleet safe, and your friends secure? Only one is missing, and we saw him overcome by the storm and swallowed in the sea. Orontes paid the forfeit with his fate; the rest accords with what your mother said." Scarcely had he spoken when the cloud gave way, the mists flew upward and dissolved into day.

The Trojan chief appeared in open sight, august in visage, and serenely bright. His mother goddess, with her divine hands, had formed his curling locks, made his temples shine, given his rolling eyes a sparkling grace, and breathed a youthful vigor on his face. He looked like polished ivory, beautiful to behold, or like Parian marble set in gold. Thus, radiant, he broke from the encircling cloud; and thus, with manly modesty, he spoke:

"He whom you seek am I—tossed by tempests, and saved from shipwreck on your Libyan coast. I present before your throne, gracious queen, a prince who owes his life to you alone. Fair majesty, the refuge and redress of those whom fate pursues and wants oppress, you, who employ your pious offices to save the remnants of abandoned Troy—receive the shipwrecked on your friendly shore, relieve the poor with hospitable rites, take into your town a wandering company, and entertain strangers in your palace. What thanks can wretched fugitives return, who, scattered through the world, mourn in exile? The gods, if gods are inclined to goodness, and if acts of mercy touch their heavenly minds, and, more than all the gods, your generous heart, conscious of its worth, shall requite its own desert! This age is happy in you, and so is this earth, and parents more than mortal gave you birth. While rolling rivers shall run into seas, and the radiant sun shall course around the vault of heaven, while trees shall shade the mountain tops, your honor, name, and praise shall never die. Whatever abode my fortune has assigned me, your image shall be present to my mind." Having said this, he turned with pious haste and joyfully embraced his waiting friends. With his right hand he honored Ilioneus, and with his left Serestus; then pressed Cloanthus and noble Gyas to his breast; and so by turns he greeted the rest.

The Tyrian queen stood fixed upon his face, pleased with his movements, entranced by his grace. She admired his fortunes, but admired the man more. Then, recollecting herself, she began: "What fate, O goddess-born, what angry powers have cast you shipwrecked on our barren shores? Are you the great Aeneas, known to fame, who claim your lineage from celestial seed?

Are you that same Aeneas whom fair Venus bore to famed Anchises on the Idaean shore? It calls to my mind, though I was then a child, when Teucer came, exiled from Salamis, and sought my father's aid to be restored. My father Belus then invaded Cyprus with fire and sword, made the region bare, and finished the successful war as conqueror. From him I learned of the Trojan siege, the Grecian chiefs, and your illustrious blood. Your enemy himself praised the Dardan valor, and traced his own ancestry from the Trojans. Enter, my noble guest, and you shall find, if not a costly welcome, yet a kind one. For I myself, like you, have been in distress, until Heaven afforded me this place of rest; like you, an alien in an unknown land, I have learned to pity woes so like my own." She spoke, and led her guest to the palace; then offered incense and proclaimed a feast. Nor yet less careful for his absent friends, she sent twice ten fat oxen to the ships; besides a hundred boars, and a hundred lambs, with bleating cries, attending their milky dams; and jars of generous wine and spacious bowls she gave, to cheer the drooping souls of the sailors. Now purple hangings clothed the palace walls, and splendid halls served up sumptuous feasts. They dined on richly wrought Tyrian carpets; the sideboards shone with loads of massive plate, and antique vases all embossed with gold (the gold itself less valuable than the workmanship), of curious work, where on the sides were seen the battles and figures of illustrious men, from their first founder to the present queen.

Good Aeneas, whose fatherly care could no longer bear the absence of Iulus, sent Achates in haste to the ships, to bring a glad report of what had passed, and, laden with precious gifts, to bring the boy, snatched from the ruins of unhappy Troy: a robe of tissue stiff with golden wire; an upper vest, once Helen's rich attire, brought from Argos by that famous adulteress when she came to ruin Troy and set the world ablaze, wrought with golden flowers and winding foliage, a present from her mother Leda; the scepter that Priam's eldest daughter bore, her oriental necklace, and the crown she wore, of double texture, glorious to behold, one band set with gems, and one with gold. Instructed thus, the wise Achates went, and showed his duty by his diligence.

But Venus, anxious for her son's affairs, tried new counsels and prepared new designs: that Cupid should assume the shape and face of sweet Ascanius, and his sprightly grace; that he should bring the presents in her nephew's stead, and shed the gentle poison into Eliza's veins. For she feared the double-tongued Tyrians greatly, and knew the town was under Juno's care. These thoughts broke her golden slumbers in the night, and, so alarmed, she spoke thus to winged Love: "My son, my strength, whose mighty power alone controls the Thunderer on his awful throne, to you your much-afflicted mother flies, and relies on your help and your faith. You know, my son, how Jove's vengeful wife attempts your brother's life by force and fraud, and you have often mourned with me his sufferings. Dido now detains him with blandishments; but I suspect the town where Juno reigns. For this reason it is needful to forestall her craft, and fire the proud Phoenician's heart with love—a love so violent, so strong, so certain, that neither age can change it nor art can cure it. How this may be done, hear now my mind. Ascanius is planned by his father to come from the port, laden with presents, to gratify the queen and win the court. I mean to plunge the boy in a pleasing sleep, and, having carried him off, to keep him in the Idalian bowers, or on lofty Cythera, so that the sweet deceit may pass unseen, and no one prevent the trick. You take his form and shape. I beg the grace for only one night's revolving space: yourself a boy, assume a boy's dissembled face; so that when, in the fervor of the feast, the Tyrian queen hugs and caresses you on her breast, and, with sweet kisses, clasps you in her arms, you may infuse your venom into her veins." The God of Love obeyed, and set aside his bow and quiver and his feathered pride; he walked as Iulus in his mother's sight, and took delight in the sweet resemblance.

The goddess then flew to young Ascanius, and sealed his eyes in a pleasing slumber. Lulled in her lap, amid a train of Loves, she gently bore him to her blissful groves, then crowned his head with a wreath of myrtle, and laid him softly on a flowery bed. Cupid meanwhile assumed his form and face, and followed Achates at a shorter pace, bringing the gifts. The queen was already seated amidst the Trojan lords, in shining state, high on a golden bed; her princely guest sat next to her side, and the rest in order. Then baskets were heaped high with bread; attendants supplied water for their hands, and when they had washed, dried them with silken towels. Next, fifty handmaids in long order bore the censers, and adored the gods with fumes. Then twice as many youths and maidens joined to place the dishes and to serve the wine. The Tyrian train, admitted to the feast, approached and rested on the painted couches. All gazed in wonder at the Trojan gifts, but gazed with greater amazement at the beautiful boy—his rosy-colored cheeks, his radiant eyes, his movements, voice, and shape, and all the god's disguise. Nor did the vest and divine veil pass without praise, woven through with wandering foliage and rich flowers. But far above the rest, the royal lady (already doomed to love's disastrous flame), with insatiable eyes and tumultuous joy, beheld the presents, and admired the boy. The guileful god hung long about the hero, with children's play and false embraces; then sought the queen, and she took him into her arms with greedy pleasure, and devoured his charms. Unhappy Dido little thought what guest, or how dire a god, she drew so near her breast. But he, not forgetful of his mother's prayer, worked in the pliant bosom of the fair, molding her heart anew, and blotting out her former care. The dead is given up to the living love; and Aeneas enters wholly into her mind.

Now, when the rage of hunger was appeased, the meat removed, and every guest was pleased, the golden bowls were crowned with sparkling wine, and cheerful cries resounded through the palace. From gilded roofs hung lamps displayed nocturnal beams that rivaled the day. The queen commanded that a golden bowl, shining with divine gems, should be crowned with wine—the bowl which Belus and all the Tyrian line had used. Then, when silence had been proclaimed through the hall, she spoke: "O hospitable Jove, we invoke your sacred name and power with solemn rites; bless this auspicious hour for both nations! So may the Trojan and the Tyrian line be joined in lasting concord from this day. You, Bacchus, god of joys and friendly cheer, and you, gracious Juno, both be present here! And you, my lords of Tyre, address your vows to Heaven with mine, to ratify the peace." Then she took the goblet crowned with nectar (sprinkling the first libations on the ground), and raised it to her mouth with sober grace. Then, after sipping, she offered it to the next in place. It was Bitias whom she called, a thirsty soul; he took the challenge, embraced the bowl, and with pleasure swallowed the gold, nor did he cease to draw until he saw the bottom of the cup. The goblet went around; Iopas brought his golden lyre, and sang what ancient Atlas had taught him: the various labors of the wandering moon, and whence the eclipses of the sun proceed; the origin of men and beasts; and whence the rains arise, and fires dispense their warmth; and how the fixed and wandering stars dispose their influence; what shakes the solid earth; what cause delays the summer nights and shortens winter days. The Tyrians praised the song with peals of shouts, and those peals were echoed by the Trojan throng. The unhappy queen prolonged the night with talk, and drank large drafts of love with vast delight. She inquired much of Priam, and more of Hector; then asked what arms the swarthy Memnon wore, and what troops he had landed on the Trojan shore; the steeds of Diomede varied the discourse, and fierce Achilles, with his matchless force. At length, as fate and her ill stars required, she desired to hear the whole series of the war. "Relate fully, my godlike guest," she said, "the Grecian stratagems, the town betrayed, the fatal issue of so long a war, your flight, your wanderings, and your woes. For, since your men have been distressed on every sea and every coast, and your navy tossed, seven times the sun has seen either tropic, the winter has been banished, and the spring renewed."

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: Aeneas recounts how the city of Troy was taken, after a ten years' siege, by the treachery of Sinon and the stratagem of the wooden horse. He declares his fixed resolution not to survive the ruin of his country, and the various adventures he encountered in its defense. At last, having been advised earlier by Hector's ghost, and now by the appearance of his mother Venus, he is persuaded to leave the town and establish his household gods in another country. To do this, he carries off his father on his shoulders, leads his little son by the hand, and his wife follows behind. When he arrives at the place appointed for the general rendezvous, he finds a great gathering of people, but he misses his wife, whose ghost afterwards appears to him and tells him the land destined for him.

All were attentive to the godlike man, when from his lofty couch he began to speak: “Great queen, what you ask me to relate renews the sorrowful memory of our fate: an empire torn up from its old foundations, and every woe the Trojans suffered; a peopled city reduced to a desert; all that I saw, and part of which I was. Not even the hardest of our enemies could hear it, nor could stern Ulysses tell it, without a tear. And now the last watch of the wasting night, and the setting stars, invite us to rest. But since you take such interest in our sorrow, and wish to know Troy's disastrous end, I will hold back my tears and briefly tell what befell us on that last and fatal night.

“Compelled by destiny and in despair, the Greeks grew weary of the long war, and with Minerva's help they built a structure which looked like a horse of monstrous height. The sides were planked with pine; they pretended it was made as an offering for their safe return, and this was the vow they paid. So they pretended, but in the hollow side they hid chosen soldiers. They loaded the dread machine with arms within, and stuffed its dark belly with men of iron. In sight of Troy lies Tenedos, an island once famous for wealth while Fortune smiled on Priam's empire, but now a treacherous bay where ships lay exposed to wind and weather. There their fleet was concealed. We thought they had hoisted sail for Greece, and we were relieved of our fears. The Trojans, cooped up within their walls for so long, unbarred their gates and poured out in a throng, like swarming bees, and with delight they surveyed the deserted camp where the Greeks had lain. They pointed out the quarters of the various chiefs: here Phoenix made his abode, here Achilles; here the battles joined, there the navy rode at anchor. Some stared in wonder at the pile, the pile that Pallas had raised to ruin Troy. Thymoetes was first—whether bribed or because Trojan destiny required it—to urge that the ramparts be broken down to lodge the monstrous fabric in the town. But Capys, and the rest of sounder mind, wanted the fatal gift thrown into the flames, or cast into the sea, or at least bored open so its hidden frauds might be explored. The giddy crowd, swayed by their whims, made much noise but said nothing, and split into factions. Then Laocoön, followed by a numerous crowd, came running from the citadel and cried out from a distance: ‘O wretched countrymen! What madness is this? What worse than madness has possessed your brains? Do you think the Greeks have left your coasts? Are Ulysses' tricks no better known than this? Either this hollow fabric encloses our secret foes within its blind recess, or it is an engine raised above the town to overlook the walls and then to batter them down. Something is surely planned, by fraud or force. Trust not their presents, and do not admit the horse.' Having said this, he hurled his forceful spear against the steed, which, hissing as it flew, pierced through the yielding planks of jointed wood and stood trembling in the hollow belly. The pierced sides returned a rattling sound, and the groans of the Greeks enclosed within came issuing through the wound. And had Heaven not decreed Troy's fall, or had men not been fated to be blind, enough was said and done to inspire a better mind. Then our lances would have pierced the treacherous wood, and the Trojan towers and Priam's empire would still stand. Meanwhile, with shouts, Trojan shepherds brought a captive Greek in chains before the king—one taken so that he might take; one who had given himself up as prey, to impose on their belief and betray Troy; fixed on his purpose, determined either to die undaunted or to deceive us. Around the captive, tides of Trojans flowed; all pressed to see, and some insulted the foe. Now hear how well the Greeks disguised their tricks; behold a nation compressed into one man. Trembling the wretch stood, unarmed and bound; he stared and rolled his haggard eyes around, and then said: ‘Alas! What land remains, what sea is open to receive unhappy me? What fate awaits a wretched fugitive, scorned by my foes, abandoned by my friends?' He said this, and sighed, and cast a rueful eye: our pity was kindled, and our passions died. We urged the youth to defend himself, and to tell us freely what he was and where he came from, what news he could bring. We longed to know what to believe from a captive foe.

“His fear at last dismissed, he said: ‘Whatever my fate decrees, my words shall be sincere: I neither can nor dare disown my birth. Greece is my country, Sinon is my name. Though plunged by Fortune's power into misery, it is not in Fortune's power to make me lie. If the name of Palamedes has reached you—not unknown to fame—who suffered from the malice of the times, accused and sentenced for imaginary crimes because he sought to prevent these fatal wars, whose death the wretched Greeks too late lament—I, then a boy, was committed to his care by my father, who was poor and had no other means. He was my kinsman and his companion in the war. While Fortune favored him, while his counsel ruled the court, I too made some figure there; my name was not obscure, nor was I without my share of fame. But when Ulysses, with his deceitful arts, made his impression on the people's hearts and forged a treason in my patron's name—I speak of things too widely known by fame—my kinsman fell. Then I, without support, mourned his loss in private and left the court. Mad as I was, I could not bear his fate with silent grief, but loudly blamed the state and cursed the direful author of my woes. Word of it got back; and from this my ruin rose. I swore that if indulgent Heaven would once more land me safely on my native shore, I would avenge his death doubly. This stirred the murderer's hate; soon the effects of malice from so proud a man followed. Ambiguous rumors he spread through the camp, and sought by treachery to take my devoted head. He invented new crimes; he left no stone unturned to make my guilt appear and to hide his own, until at last he forced Calchas to speak. But why—why do I dwell on that anxious thought? If it is your aim to take just revenge upon my nation, and to be a Greek is to be your enemy, you already know my name and country: quench your thirst for blood and strike the blow! My death will please both the kingly brothers, and will set the insatiable man of Ithaca at ease.' This fair unfinished tale, these broken starts, raised expectations in our longing hearts, unknowing as we were in Grecian arts. With his former trembling once again renewed, with feigned fear, the villain went on:

“‘Long had the Greeks (tired with fruitless care and wearied by an unsuccessful war) resolved to raise the siege and leave the town. And had the gods permitted, they would have gone. But often the wintry seas and southern winds had stopped their passage home and changed their minds. Omens and prodigies amazed their souls; but above all when this stupendous pile was raised. Then flaming meteors were seen hanging in the air, and thunders rattled through a clear sky. Dismayed, and fearing some dire event, they sent Eurypylus to inquire their fate. From the gods he brought back this dreadful answer:

“‘O Greeks, when you first sought the Trojan shores, your passage was bought with a virgin's blood: so too must your safe return be bought, and Grecian blood must once more atone to the sea.' The rumor spread among the people; all feared, and each believed himself to be the one. Ulysses took advantage of their fear, called Calchas forth, and produced him in open sight. Then he bade him name the wretch ordained by fate to be the public victim, who would redeem the state. Already some sensed the dire event, and saw what sacrifice Ulysses intended. For twice five days the good old seer withstood the intended treachery, and would not pronounce a victim's name. But at last, tired out by the endless clamor and pursuit of the man of Ithaca, he was silent no longer, and, as had been agreed, he pronounced that I was destined by the wrathful gods to die. All praised the sentence, pleased that the storm should fall on one alone, whose doom had threatened them all. The dismal day arrived; the priests prepared their leavened cakes, and the fillets for my hair. But I obeyed nature's law, and—I must confess—I broke my bonds and fled the fatal blow. I lay hidden all night in a weedy lake, secure of safety when they sailed away. But now what hope remains for me—to see my friends, my native soil, again? My tender infants, my careful father, whom they will demand to death on my account? They will carry out their first design upon them, and take the forfeit of their heads for mine. O, if pity can move mortal minds, if there is faith below or gods above, if innocence and truth can claim any reward, you Trojans, turn away from this injured wretch his ruin.'

“False tears stirred true pity. The king commanded his fetters loosed, his hands unbound. Then he added these friendly words: ‘Dismiss your fears; forget the Greeks; be one of us as you were one of them. But tell me truly: was it for force or cunning, or for some religious purpose, that you raised this pile?' Thus spoke the king. He, full of fraudful arts, told his well-invented tale for truth: ‘O lamps of heaven!' he said, lifting high his now-free hands, ‘O venerable sky! Inviolable powers, adored with dread! O fatal fillets that once bound this head! O sacred altars from whose flames I fled! Be all of you my witnesses; and grant that without a crime I may betray the ungrateful Greeks, reveal the secrets of their guilty state, and justly punish whom I justly hate! But you, O king, keep the faith you gave, if I, to save myself, save your empire. The Greeks' hopes and all their attempts were founded only on Minerva's aid. But from the time when impious Diomedes and false Ulysses, that inventive head, dragged her fatal image from her temple, killing the sleeping guardians of the citadel, and polluted her virgin statue with their bloody hands, and profaned her holy bands—from then on the tide of their fortune left the shore, and ebbed much faster than it had flowed before. Their courage failed as their hopes decayed; and Pallas, now unfriendly, refused her aid. Nor did the goddess leave her altered mind in doubt. When first her fatal image touched the ground, she cast her glaring eyes sternly around, so that they sparkled as they rolled, and seemed to threaten. Her heavenly limbs ran with a briny sweat. Three times she leaped from the ground, was seen to wield her brandished lance, and shake her horrid shield. Then Calchas told our host to flee and to hope for no conquest from the tedious war, until they had first sailed for Greece. There they must with prayers beseech her injured power, and bring back better omens. And now their navy plows the watery main; yet soon expect it on your shores again, with Pallas pleased, as Calchas has ordained. But first, to reconcile the blue-eyed maid for her stolen statue and her tower betrayed, we have—warned by the seer—raised and dedicated to her offended name this wondrous frame. It is so lofty lest it pass through your forbidden gates and intercept our better fates. For, once admitted there, our hopes are lost; and Troy may then boast a new Palladium. For so religion and the gods ordain, that if you violate Minerva's gift with impious hands, your town shall burn in flames (may that omen, O gods, turn upon Greece instead!). But if with your assisting hands it climbs the Trojan walls and stands within the city, then Troy shall burn Argos and Mycenae, and the reverse of fate shall fall upon us.'

“With such deceits he won their easy hearts, which were too prone to credit his perfidious arts. What Diomedes could not do, nor Thetis' greater son, nor a thousand ships, nor ten years' siege—false tears and fawning words won the city.

“A greater omen, and of worse portent, tormented our unwary minds with fear, contributing to the dire event. Laocoön, chosen by lot that year to be Neptune's priest, was making solemn sacrifice of a bull, when, dreadful to behold, we saw from the sea two serpents, side by side, parting the waters and sweeping smoothly along the swelling tide. They raised their flaming crests above the waves; their bellies seemed to burn the seas below; their speckled tails steered their course, and on the sounding shore the flying billows were driven. Now they held the strand, now the plain; their ardent eyes were filled with bloody streaks; their nimble tongues they brandished as they came, and licked their hissing jaws, which sputtered flame. We fled, amazed. They took their destined way and made straight for Laocoön and his children. First they wound around his tender boys, and with sharpened fangs ground their limbs and bodies. The wretched father, running to their aid with pious but vain haste, they next invaded. Twice their winding coils rolled about his waist; twice they folded about his gasping throat. The priest, thus doubly choked, was overtopped by their crests, as they rode in triumph over his head. With both hands he labored at the knots; his holy fillets were stained by their blue venom; his roaring filled the flitting air around him. So, when an ox receives a glancing wound, he breaks his bonds, flies from the fatal altar, and breaks the yielding skies with his loud bellowing. Their task performed, the serpents left their prey and made their way to the tower of Pallas. There they couched at her feet, protected by her great shield and extended spear. Amazement seized us all; the general cry proclaimed that Laocoön had justly been doomed to die, for his hand had withstood the will of Pallas, and had dared to violate the sacred wood. All voted to admit the steed, that vows might be paid and incense offered to the offended maid. A spacious breach was made; the town lay bare. Some prepared hoisting levers, some the wheels, which were fastened to the horse's feet; the rest hauled the unwieldy beast along with cables. Each called on his fellow for help; at last the fatal fabric mounted the walls, big with destruction. Boys crowned with chaplets, and choirs of virgins, sang and danced around it. Thus raised aloft, and then descending down, it passed in over our heads and threatened the town. O sacred city, built by hands divine! O valiant heroes of the Trojan line! Four times it struck: as often the clashing sound of arms was heard, and inward groans rebounded. Yet, mad with zeal, and blinded by our fate, we hauled along the horse in solemn state, and placed the dire portent within the tower. Cassandra cried out, and cursed the unhappy hour; she foretold our fate; but by the gods' decree, all heard her, and none believed the prophecy. We adorned the temples with branches, and in jollity we wasted the day ordained to be our last. Meanwhile the rapid heavens rolled down the light, and night rushed upon the shaded ocean. Our men, feeling secure, kept no guards nor sentries, but easy sleep compelled their weary limbs. The Greeks had embarked their naval forces from Tenedos, and sought our well-known shores, safe under cover of the silent night, and guided by the imperial galley's light. Then Sinon, favored by the partial gods, unlocked the horse and opened its dark abode, restoring to vital air our hidden foes, who joyfully rose from their long confinement. Bold Tysander, and Sthenelus their guide, and dire Ulysses slid down the cable. Then Thoas, Athamas, and Pyrrhus hastened; nor was the Podalirian hero the last, nor injured Menelaus, nor the famed Epeus, who had framed the fatal engine. A nameless crowd followed; they joined forces to invade the town, which was oppressed with sleep and wine. The few they found awake first met their fate; then they unbarred the gates to their comrades.

“It was in the dead of night, when sleep repairs our bodies worn with toil and our minds with care, when Hector's ghost appeared before my sight. He seemed a bloody shroud, and bathed in tears; such as he was when, slain by Pelides, Thessalian horses dragged him over the plain. His feet were swollen, as when the thongs had been thrust through the pierced holes; his body was black with dust; unlike that Hector who had returned from the toils of war, triumphant, in Aeacian spoils, or who had made the fainting Greeks retreat, and had launched Phrygian fire against their navy. His hair and beard stood stiff with his gore; and all the wounds he had borne for his country streamed afresh, and ran with new crimson. I wept to see the visionary man, and, while my trance continued, I began to speak: ‘O light of the Trojans, and support of Troy, your father's champion, your country's joy! O, long expected by your friends! From where have you returned so late for our defense? Do we see you at last, wearied as we are with the length of our toils, with the toils of war? After so many funerals of your own, are you restored to your declining town? But tell me: what wounds are these? What new disgrace deforms the manly features of your face?'

“To this the ghost gave no reply, but answered the purpose for which he had come, and, groaning from the bottom of his breast, he expressed this warning in these mournful words: ‘O goddess-born! Escape by timely flight the flames and horrors of this fatal night. The foes already hold the walls; Troy nods from on high, and totters to her fall. Enough has been paid to Priam's royal name, more than enough to duty and to fame. If my father's throne could have been defended by any mortal hand, it had been defended by mine alone. Now Troy commends to you her future state, and gives you her gods as companions of your fate. Expect, from their assistance, walls which, after long wandering, you shall at last erect.' He said this, and brought me, from their blessed abodes, the venerable statues of the gods, with ancient Vesta from the sacred choir, the wreaths and relics of the immortal fire.

“Now peals of shouts came thundering from afar—cries, threats, and loud laments, and mingled war. The noise approached, though our palace stood apart from the streets, encompassed by a wood. Louder and yet louder I heard the alarms of human cries distinct, and the clash of arms. Fear broke my sleep; I stayed no longer, but mounted the terrace, and from there surveyed the town, listening to what the frightful sounds conveyed. So, when a flood of fire is driven by wind, it rolls crackling and mows down the standing corn; or when deluges descend upon the plains, they sweep over the yellow ear, and destroy the labor of oxen and the peasant's gains; they uproot the forest oaks, and carry away flocks, folds, and trees, and undistinguished prey. The shepherd climbs the cliff and sees from afar the wasteful ravage of the watery war. Then Hector's warning was manifestly confirmed, and Grecian frauds appeared in open light. The palace of Deiphobus rose in smoky flames, and caught fire from its neighbors. Ucalegon's house burned next; the seas were bright with a splendor not their own, and shone with Trojan light. New clamors and new clangors now arose, the sound of trumpets mingled with battle cries. Seized with frenzy, I ran to meet the alarms, resolved on death, resolved to die in arms; but first to gather friends, with them to oppose, if fortune favored, and to drive back the foes. I was spurred on by my own courage, fired by my country, and inspired by a sense of honor and revenge.

“Pantheus, Apollo's priest, a sacred name, had escaped the Grecian swords and passed through the flames. Loaded with relics, he fled to my doors, and led his tender grandson by the hand. ‘What hope is there, O Pantheus? Where can we run? Where make a stand? And what may still be done?' Hardly had I said this when Pantheus, with a groan, replied: ‘Troy is no more, and Ilium was a town! The fatal day, the appointed hour, has come, when wrathful Jove's irrevocable doom transfers the Trojan state to Grecian hands. The fire consumes the town, the foe commands; and armed hosts, an unexpected force, break from the bowels of the fatal horse. Within the gates proud Sinon is flinging the flames; and foes press in from outside—a thousand others, whom I fear to name, more than ever came from Argos or Mycenae. They have divided their parties to several posts; some block the narrow streets, some scour the wide. They kill the bold and surprise the unwary; whoever fights finds death, and death finds him who flees. The wardens of the gate can scarcely maintain the unequal combat, and resist in vain.'

“I heard him; and Heaven, which inspires well-born souls, prompted me through lifted swords and rising fires to run where clashing arms and clamor called, and to rush undaunted to defend the walls. Ripheus and Iphitus engaged at my side, one renowned for valor, the other for age. Dymas and Hypanis, knowing my motion and bearing by moonlight, drew to my party, along with young Coroebus, who had been led by love to win renown and the bed of fair Cassandra, and had lately brought his troops to Priam's aid—warned in vain by the prophetic maid. When I saw them resolved to fall in arms, and that one spirit animated all, I said: ‘Brave souls! But brave, alas, in vain: come, finish what our cruel fates ordain. You see the desperate state of our affairs, and heaven's protecting powers are deaf to our prayers. The passive gods behold the Greeks defile their temples, and abandon their own abodes to the spoiler. We, a feeble few, conspire to save a sinking town, engulfed in fire. Then let us fall, but fall amidst our foes: despair of life shows the means of living.' So bold a speech encouraged their desire for death, and added fuel to their fire.

“As hungry wolves, with raging appetite, scour through the fields, not fearing the stormy night—their whelps at home await the promised food, and long to wet their dry jaws in blood—so we rushed forth at once, resolved to die, resolved in death to try the last extremes. We left the narrow lanes behind, and dared the unequal combat in the public square. Night was our friend; our leader was despair. What tongue can tell the slaughter of that night? What eyes can weep its sorrows and affright? An ancient and imperial city fell; the streets were filled with frequent funerals; houses and holy temples floated in blood, and hostile nations made a common flood. Not only Trojans fell; but in their turn the vanquished triumphed, and the victors mourned. Our men took new courage from despair and night; the fortune was confused, the fight was confused. All parts resounded with tumult, plaints, and fears; and grisly Death appeared in sundry shapes. Androgeos fell among us with his band; he thought we were Greeks newly come to land. ‘From where,' he said, ‘my friends, this long delay? You loiter while the spoils are being borne away. Our ships are laden with Trojan store, and you, like truants, have come too late ashore.' He said this, but soon corrected his mistake, realizing from our doubtful answers. Amazed, he would have shunned the unequal fight; but we, being more numerous, intercepted his flight. As when some peasant in a bushy brake unwarily treads on a snake, and starts aside astonished, when he sees its rising crest, blue neck, and rolling eyes—so Androgeos, surprised, fled from our arms. In vain; for we surrounded him and his, possessed with fear and unfamiliar with the ground, and found them an easy conquest. Thus Fortune smiled on our first endeavor. Then Coroebus, beguiled by youthful hopes, swollen with success and a daring mind, fatally designed this new invention. ‘My friends,' he said, ‘since Fortune shows the way, it is fitting to obey the auspicious guide. Why has she bestowed these Grecian arms on us, but for their destruction and the Trojans' good? Then let us change shields, and bear their devices: let fraud supply the want of force in war. They furnish us the arms.' Having said this, he dressed himself in dead Androgeos' spoils—his upper vest, his painted buckler, and his plumy crest. Likewise Ripheus, Dymas, all the Trojan train, laid down their own attire, and stripped the slain. Mingled with the Greeks, we went on with ill foreboding, flattering ourselves with hopes of glutting our greedy rage. Unknown, we assaulted whomever we blindly met, and strewed the street with Grecian corpses. Thus, while we defeated their straggling parties, some retreated to the shore and safer ships; and some, oppressed with a more ignoble fear, climbed back into the hollow horse, and panted in secret there.

“But, ah! What use of valor can be made, when heaven's propitious powers refuse their aid? Behold the royal prophetess, the fair Cassandra, dragged by her disheveled hair, whom neither Minerva's shrine nor sacred bands could protect from sacrilegious hands. She cast her eyes on heaven, she sighed, she cried (that was all she could do); her tender arms were bound. So sad a sight Coroebus could not bear; but, fired with rage, distracted with despair, he flew among the barbarous ravishers. We followed our leader's rash example. But storms of stones poured down from the proud temple's height, and fell upon our battered helmets. We received this fatal blow from our own friends, who thought we were Greeks, as we seemed in show. They aimed from above at the mistaken crests; and ours lay beneath the ponderous ruin. Then, moved with anger and disdain to see their troops dispersed and the royal virgin freed, the Greeks rallied and united their powers. They charged us with fury, and renewed the fight. The brother kings joined their force with Ajax, and with the whole squadron of Thessalian horse.

“Thus, when the rival winds try their quarrel, contending for the kingdom of the sky—south, east, and west, borne on airy coursers—the whirlwind gathers, and the woods are torn; then Nereus strikes the deep, the billows rise, and, mixed with ooze and sand, pollute the skies. The troops we had at first scattered reappeared from various quarters, and closed in behind us. They first observed, and betrayed to the rest, our different speech, and surveyed our borrowed arms. Oppressed with odds, we fell. Coroebus fell first, at Pallas' altar, pierced by Peneleus. Then Ripheus followed, in the unequal fight, the most just of his word, most observant of the right—but Heaven judged otherwise. Dymas met the same fate, with Hypanis, mistaken by their friends. Nor did your miter, Pantheus, nor the bands of awful Phoebus, save you from impious hands. You Trojan flames, bear witness to what I performed and what I suffered there; I avoided no sword in the fatal strife, exposed to death, prodigal of life. Bear witness, you heavens: I live not by my own fault; I strove to earn the death I sought. But, when I could not fight and would have died, I was borne off to a distance by the growing tide. Old Iphitus and I were hurried from there, with Pelias wounded and defenseless. New clamors rang from the besieged palace; we ran to die, or to relieve the king. So hot was the assault, so high the tumult rose, as our men defended and the Greeks attacked, that it seemed as if all the Dardan and Argive race had been crammed into that narrow space; or as if all the rest of Ilium were void of fear, and tumult, war, and slaughter were only there. Their shields cast in a tortoise formation, the foes, advancing in safety, rose to the turrets. Some mounted scaling ladders; others, bolder, climbed upward by posts and pillars. With their left hand they gripped their bucklers in the ascent, while with their right they seized the battlement. From their demolished towers the Trojans threw huge heaps of stones, which, falling, crushed the foe; and heavy beams and rafters from the sides (such arms their last necessity provides), and gilded roofs, came tumbling down from on high, the marks of state and ancient royalty. The guards below, fixed in the pass, attended the charge undaunted, and defended the gate. Renewed in courage, with recovered breath, a second time we ran to tempt our death, to clear the palace of the foe, to relieve the weary who still fought, and to avenge the dead.

“A postern door, still unobserved and free, joined by the length of a blind gallery to the king's closet, afforded us a way well known to Hector's wife while Priam held the throne, through which she had unseen brought Astyanax to cheer his grandsire and his grandsire's queen. Through this we passed, and mounted the tower, from which the Trojans were making defense with unavailing arms. From this the trembling king had often spied the Grecian camp, and seen their navy ride at anchor. With our swords we hewed beams from its lofty height, then wrenching with our hands, renewed the assault; and where the rafters met on the columns, we pushed them headlong with our arms and feet. The lightning does not fly swifter than the fall, nor thunder louder than the ruined wall. Down at once went the top; the Greeks beneath were piecemeal torn, or pounded into death. Yet more came to take their place, and more were sent to death; we ceased not from above, nor did they relent below. Before the gate stood Pyrrhus, threatening loud, conspicuous in the crowd with glittering arms. So shines, renewed in youth, the crested snake, who slept the winter in a thorny brake, and, casting off his slough when spring returns, now looks aloft, and burns with new glory; restored by poisonous herbs, his ardent sides reflect the sun; and, raised on spires, he rides high over the grass, hissing he rolls along, and now and then brandishes his forky tongue. Proud Periphas, and fierce Automedon, his father's charioteer, ran together to force the gate; the Scyrian infantry rushed on in crowds, and freed the barred passage. Entering the court, they rent the skies with shouts, and flaming firebrands rose to the roofs.
