He himself, among the foremost, dealt his blows, and with his axe bestowed repeated strokes on the strong doors; then all their shoulders plied the beam until, from the posts, the brazen hinges flew. He hewed apace; the double bars at length yielded to his axe and unresisted strength. A mighty breach was made: the concealed rooms appeared, and the palace was revealed; the halls of audience and of public state, and where the lonely queen had sat in secret. Armed soldiers were now seen by trembling maids, with scarcely a door, and scarcely a space, between. The house was filled with loud laments and cries, and the shrieks of women rent the vaulted skies. The fearful matrons ran from place to place, and kissed the thresholds, and embraced the posts. The fatal work inhuman Pyrrhus plied, and all his father sparkled in his eyes; nor bars, nor fighting guards, could sustain his force: the bars were broken, and the guards were slain. In rushed the Greeks, and filled all the apartments; the few defenders they found, they killed. Not so fiercely does the foaming flood roar, when it finds its rapid course withstood, bearing down the dams with unresisted sway, and sweeping cattle and cottages away. These eyes beheld him when he marched between the brother kings. I saw the unhappy queen, the hundred wives, and old Priam, where he stood to stain his hallowed altar with his son's blood. The fifty nuptial beds—such hopes he had, so large a promise of progeny—the posts of plated gold, and hung with spoils, fell as the reward of the proud victor's toils. Wherever the raging fire had left a space, the Greeks entered and possessed the place.

“Perhaps you may inquire Priam's fate. When he saw his regal town on fire, his ruined palace, and his entering foes—on every side inevitable woes—he put on his disused armor upon his aged limbs, decayed like them; a late and useless aid. His feeble shoulders could scarcely sustain the weight; loaded, not armed, he crept along in pain, despairing of success, ambitious to be slain. Uncovered, but by heaven, there stood in view an altar; near the hearth an old laurel tree grew, whose boughs encompassed the household gods and shaded the holy ground. Here Hecuba, with all her helpless train of dames, had sought shelter, but sought in vain. Driven like a flock of doves along the sky, they hugged the images, and fled to their altars. When the Queen beheld her trembling lord, and saw a heavy sword hanging by his side, ‘What rage,' she cried, ‘has seized my husband's mind? What arms are these, and for what use designed? These times require other aids! Were Hector here, even Hector would now appear in vain, like Priam. With us you shall find one common shelter, or you shall be joined with us in one common fate.' She said this, and, embracing the poor old man with a last salute, placed him by the laurel. Behold! Polites, one of Priam's sons, pursued by Pyrrhus, came running for safety. Amazed and hurt, he fled through swords and foes, through empty courts and open galleries. Pyrrhus, urging him with his lance, pursued him, and often reached him, and renewed his thrusts. The youth, transfixed, with lamentable cries expired before his wretched parent's eyes. When Priam saw him gasping at his feet, the fear of death gave place to nature's law; and, shaking more with anger than with age, ‘The gods,' he said, ‘requite your brutal rage! As surely they will, barbarian, surely they must, if there are gods in heaven, and if the gods are just—you who take an insolent delight in wrongs; who have infected a father's sight with a son's death. Not he, whom lying fame and you conspire to call your father, not he, your vaunted sire, so used my wretched age. He feared the gods, he heard the laws of nature and of nations. He cheered my sorrows; and, for sums of gold, he sold the bloodless body of my Hector; he pitied the woes a parent suffered, and sent me back in safety from his tent.'
“Having said this, his feeble hand threw a javelin, which, fluttering, seemed to loiter as it flew; just, and but barely, it reached its mark, and faintly tinkled on the brazen shield.

“Then Pyrrhus said: ‘Go from me, then, to fate, and relate to my father my foul deeds. Now die!' With that he dragged the trembling sire, slipping through clotted blood and holy mire (the mingled paste his murdered son had made), hauled him from beneath the violated shade, and laid the royal victim on the sacred pile. His right hand held his bloody falchion bare; his left he twisted in his hoary hair; then, with a speeding thrust, he found his heart: the lukewarm blood came rushing through the wound, and bloody streams stained the sacred ground. Thus Priam fell, and shared one common fate with Troy in ashes, and his ruined state—he, who the scepter of all Asia had swayed, whom monarchs had obeyed like domestic slaves. On the bleak shore now lies the abandoned king, a headless carcass, and a nameless thing.

“Then, not before, I felt my curdled blood congeal with fear, my hair stood up with horror. My father's image filled my pious mind, lest equal years might find equal fortune. Again I thought on my forsaken wife, and trembled for my son's abandoned life. I looked about, but found myself alone, deserted at my hour of need! My friends were gone. Some, spent with toil, some oppressed with despair, had leaped headlong from the heights; the flames consumed the rest. Thus, wandering on my way without a guide, I spied graceless Helen in the porch of Vesta's temple. There she lurked alone, sitting muffled, and, as much as she could, unknown. But by the flames that cast their blaze around, I recognized that common bane of Greece and Troy. For now that Ilium burned, she dreaded the Trojan sword; and more dreaded the vengeance of her injured lord; even those gods she had taken refuge with abhorred her. Trembling with rage, I regarded the strumpet, resolved to give her guilt its due reward: ‘Shall she sail triumphant before the wind, and leave unhappy Troy behind her in flames? Shall she see again her kingdom and her friends, attended in state with a captive crew, while unavenged the good old Priam falls, and Grecian fires consume the Trojan walls? For this were the Phrygian fields and the Xanthian flood swollen with bodies and drunk with blood? True, a soldier can gain small honor, and can boast no conquest, from killing a woman: yet the deed shall not pass without applause, the vengeance being taken in so just a cause. The punished crime shall set my soul at ease, and appease the murmuring ghosts of my friends.' Thus while I raved, a gleam of pleasing light spread over the place; and, shining heavenly bright, my mother stood revealed before my sight. Never did her eyes appear so radiant; not her own star confessed so clear a light. Great in her charms, as when she looks upon the gods above, and breathes herself into their love. She held my hand, to break the destined blow; then from her rosy lips began to speak: ‘My son, from where comes this madness, this neglect of my commands, and of those whom I protect? Why this unmanly rage? Recall to mind whom you forsake, what pledges you leave behind. Look whether your helpless father yet survives, or if Ascanius or Creüsa lives. Around your house the greedy Greeks are roving; and these would have perished in the nightly war, but for my presence and protecting care. Not Helen's face, nor Paris, is at fault; but this destruction was brought by the gods. Now cast your eyes around, while I dissolve the mists and films that wrap mortal eyes; I will purge the dross from your sight, and make you see the shape of each avenging deity. Enlightened thus, fulfill my just commands, and do not fear obedience to your mother's will. Where that disordered heap of ruin lies—stones rent from stones, where clouds of dust arise—amid that smother Neptune holds his place, drives his mace below the wall's foundations, and heaves the building from its solid base. Look, where, in arms, imperial Juno stands, full in the Scaean gate, with loud commands, urging on shore the tardy Grecian bands. See! Pallas, proud of her snaky buckler, bestrides the tower, refulgent through the cloud. See! Jove supplies new courage to the foe, and arms the partial deities against the town. Haste from here, my son; end this fruitless labor. Haste, where your trembling spouse and sire await you. Haste; and a mother's care shall befriend your passage.' She said, and swiftly vanished from my sight, obscure in clouds and gloomy shades of night. I looked, I listened: I heard dreadful sounds; and the dire forms of hostile gods appeared. I saw Troy sunk in flames, nor could I prevent it; and Ilium rent from its old foundations, rent like a mountain ash, which had dared the winds, and stood the sturdy strokes of laboring hinds. About its roots the cruel axe resounds; the stumps are pierced with oft-repeated wounds: the war is felt on high; the nodding crown now threatens a fall, and throws down its leafy honors. At last, though late, it yielded to their united force, and mourned with mortal groans its approaching fate. The roots could no longer sustain its upper load, and down it fell, and spread a ruin across the plain.

“Descending from there, I escaped through foes and fire; before the goddess, foes and flames retired. Arrived at home, I found that he for whose sake—or most for his—I had undertaken such toils, the good Anchises, whom by timely flight I had purposed to secure on Ida's height, refused the journey. He was resolved to die, and to add his own funeral to Troy's fate, rather than endure exile and old age. ‘Go, you whose blood runs warm in every vein. Had Heaven decreed that I should enjoy life, Heaven would have decreed to save unhappy Troy. It is enough—if not too much—for one man to have seen Ilium overthrown twice. Hasten to save the poor remaining crew, and say a long goodbye to this useless corpse. These weak old hands suffice to stop my breath; at least the pitying foes will aid my death, to take my spoils, and leave my body bare. As for my sepulcher, let Heaven take care. It is long since I, loathed by the gods for my celestial wife, have dragged a lingering life; since every hour and moment I expire, blasted from heaven by Jove's avenging fire.' This he repeated often, and stood fixed to die. Myself, my wife, my son, my family, entreat, pray, beg, and raise a doleful cry: ‘What, will he still persist, resolved on death, and involve his whole house in his ruin?' He still persisted to maintain his reasons; our prayers, our tears, our loud laments, were in vain.

“Urged on by despair, I went once again to try the fortunes of arms, resolved to die in the fight: ‘What hope remains, but what my death must give? Can I, without so dear a father, live? You call it prudence, what I call baseness: could such a word fall from such a parent? If Fortune pleases, and so the gods ordain, that nothing shall remain of ruined Troy, and if you conspire with Fortune to be slain, the way to death is wide, the approaches near: for soon relentless Pyrrhus will appear, reeking with Priam's blood—the wretch who slew the son, inhumanly, in the father's view, and then dragged the sire himself to the dire altar. O goddess mother, give me back to Fate; your gift was undesired, and came too late! Did you, for this, unhappy me convey through foes and fires, to see my house a prey? Shall I behold my father, wife, and son weltering in blood, each folded in the others' arms? Haste! Gird on my sword, though spent and overcome: it is the last summons to receive our doom. I hear you, Fate; and I obey your call! Not unavenged shall the foe see my fall. Restore me to the yet unfinished fight: my death is wanting to conclude the night.' Armed once again, my glittering sword I wielded, while my other hand sustained my weighty shield, and I rushed forth to seek the abandoned field. I went; but sad Creüsa blocked my way, and lay across the threshold in my passage, and embraced my knees. When I would have gone, she showed me my feeble sire and tender son: ‘If death is your design,' she said, ‘at least take us along to share your destiny. But if any further hopes remain in arms, maintain this place, these pledges of your love. To whom do you abandon your father's life, your son's, and mine, your now forgotten wife!' While she thus filled the house with clamorous cries, our hearing was diverted by our eyes: for while I held my son, in the short space between our kisses and our last embrace, a lambent flame arose—strange to relate—from young Iülus' head, and gently spread around his brows, and fed upon his temples. Amazed, we prepared with running water to quench the sacred fire, and slake his hair. But old Anchises, versed in omens, raised his hands to heaven, and preferred this request: ‘If any vows, almighty Jove, can bend your will; if piety can commend our prayers, confirm the glad presage which you are pleased to send.' Hardly had he said this, when on our left we heard a peal of rattling thunder roll in the air. A streaming lamp shot along the sky, which seemed to fly on winged lightning. It moved from over the roof, and, trailing, vanished in the Idaean grove. It swept a path in heaven, and shone as a guide, then died in a steaming stench of sulphur.

“The good old man with suppliant hands implored the gods' protection, and adored their star. ‘Now, now,' he said, ‘my son, no more delay! I yield, I follow where Heaven shows the way. Keep, O my country gods, our dwelling place, and guard this remnant of the Trojan race, this tender child! These omens are your own, and you can yet restore the ruined town. At least accomplish what your signs foreshow; I stand resigned, and am prepared to go.'

“He said. The crackling flames appeared on high, and driving sparks danced along the sky. The rising winds conspired with Vulcan's rage, and a flood of fire rolled near our palace. ‘Haste, my dear father—it is no time to wait—and load my shoulders with a willing freight. Whatever befalls, your life shall be my care; we shall share one death, or one deliverance. My hand shall lead our little son; and you, my faithful consort, shall follow in our steps. Next, you, my servants, heed my strict commands: outside the walls there stands a ruined temple, once hallowed to Ceres; a cypress tree nearby shoots up its venerable head on high, kept holy by long religion. There bend your steps, and let us meet in divided parties. Our country gods, the relics, and the bands, take, father, in your guiltless hands: it would be impious for me to bear holy things, red as I am with slaughter, fresh from war, until I cleanse in some living stream the guilt of dire debate and blood spilled in battle.' So, arranging all that prudence could provide, I clothed my shoulders with a lion's hide and yellow spoils; then on my bending back I took the welcome load of my dear father; while Ascanius hung on my better hand, and tripped along with unequal paces. Creüsa kept behind; by choice we strayed through every dark and every devious way. I, who just before had been so bold and dauntless, who bore the Grecian darts and the shock of lances, was now seized with fear at every shadow—not for myself, but for the charge I bore. At last, arrived near the ruined gate, I felt secure, and deemed all the danger past, when we heard a frightful noise of trampling feet. My father, looking through the shadows, cried out in fear: ‘Haste, haste, my son, the foes are near; I see their swords and shining armor.' Some hostile god, for some unknown offense, had surely bereft my mind of better sense. For while I took my flight through winding ways, and sought the shelter of the gloomy night, alas, I lost Creüsa. It is hard to tell whether she fell by her fatal destiny, or had sat down weary, or wandered off in fright; but she was lost forever to my sight. I did not know, nor even reflect on it, until I met my friends at Ceres' now deserted seat. We met: not one was missing; only she deceived her friends, her son, and wretched me.

“What mad expressions did my tongue not refuse! Whom did I not accuse, of gods or men! This was the fatal blow, which pained me more than all I had felt from ruined Troy before. Stung with my loss, raving with despair, abandoning my now forgotten care, bereft of counsel, comfort, and of hope, I left my sire, my son, my country gods. In shining armor I sheathed my limbs once again, not feeling wounds, not fearing death. Then headlong I ran to the burning walls, and sought the danger I had been forced to shun. I retraced my former tracks; through the night I explored each passage and every street I had crossed before. All things were full of horror and affright, and dreadful even was the silence of the night. Then to my father's house I returned, with some small glimpse of hope to find her there. Instead of her, I met the cruel Greeks: the house was filled with foes, and beset with flames. Driven on the wings of the winds, whole sheets of fire were transported through the air, to aspire to the roofs. From there I went to Priam's palace, and searched the citadel and the deserted court. Then, unobserved, I passed by Juno's shrine: a guard of Greeks had possessed the porch. There Phoenix and Ulysses watched the prey, and brought all the wealth of Troy there—the spoils which they had caught from ransacked houses, golden bowls caught from burning altars, the tables of the gods, purple vests, the people's treasure, and the pomp of priests. A rank of wretched youths, with pinioned hands, and captive matrons, stood in long order. Then, with ungoverned madness, I proclaimed through all the silent street Creüsa's name. ‘Creüsa!' I called; at last she heard, and suddenly appeared through the shades of night. She appeared, no more Creüsa, nor my wife, but a pale specter, larger than in life. Aghast, astonished, and struck dumb with fear, I stood; my stiffened hair rose like bristles. Then the ghost began to soothe my grief: ‘No tears, no cries, can give relief to the dead. Desist, my much-loved lord, from indulging your pain; you bear no more than what the gods ordain. My fates permit me not to fly from here; nor he, the great controller of the sky. Long wandering ways the powers decree for you; hard labors on land, and a length of sea. Then, after many painful years are past, you shall be cast on Latium's happy shore, where gentle Tiber from his bed beholds the flowery meadows and the feeding folds. There shall your toils end; and there your fates provide a quiet kingdom, and a royal bride: there Fortune shall restore the Trojan line, and you shall weep no more for lost Creüsa. Fear not that I shall watch, with servile shame, the imperious looks of some proud Grecian dame; or, stooping to the victor's lust, disgrace my goddess mother, or my royal race. And now, farewell! The parent of the gods restrains my fleeting soul in her abodes: I trust our common issue to your care.' She said, and gliding, passed unseen in air. I strove to speak; but horror tied my tongue; three times about her neck I flung my arms, and three times deceived, I hung on empty embraces. Light as an empty dream at break of day, or as a blast of wind, she rushed away.

“Thus having passed the night in fruitless pain, I returned again to my longing friends, amazed to see how their number had grown—men and matrons, young and old, mingled together, a wretched exiled crew brought together, appointed with arms, and laden with treasure, resolved and willing, under my command, to run all hazards of both sea and land. The Morning began, from Ida, to display her rosy cheeks; and Phosphor led the day. Before the gates the Greeks had taken their post, and all pretense of late relief was lost. I yielded to Fate, unwillingly retired, and, loaded, carried my sire up the hill.”

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: Aeneas continues his narration. He gives an account of the fleet with which he sailed, and the success of his first voyage to Thrace. From there he directs his course to Delos, and asks the oracle what place the gods had appointed for his habitation. By a mistake of the oracle's answer, he settles in Crete. His household gods give him the true sense of the oracle in a dream. He follows their advice, and makes the best of his way for Italy. He is cast on several shores, and meets with very surprising adventures, until at length he lands on Sicily, where his father Anchises dies. This is the place from which he was sailing when the tempest rose and threw him upon the Carthaginian coast.

When Heaven had overturned the Trojan state and Priam's throne by too severe a fate; when ruined Troy became the Greeks' prey, and Ilium's lofty towers lay in ashes; warned by celestial omens, we retreated, to seek a happier seat in foreign lands. Near old Antandros, at the foot of Ida, we cut the timber of the sacred groves, and built our fleet, still uncertain what place the gods had assigned for our repose. Friends flocked in daily; and scarcely had the kindly spring begun to clothe the ground and the birds to sing, when old Anchises summoned us all to sea. The crew obeyed my father and the Fates. With sighs and tears I left my native shore, and the empty fields where Ilium had stood before. My sire, my son, our lesser and greater gods, all set sail at once, and cleaved the briny floods.

"Opposite our coast appears a spacious land, which fierce Lycurgus once commanded—Thracia was its name; its people were bold in war, their fields vast, and tillage was their care. It was a hospitable realm while Fate was kind, joined with Troy in friendship and religion. I landed, and then, with unlucky omens, I adored their gods and drew a line along the shore. I laid the deep foundations of a wall, and called the city Aenos, from my own name. Vows were paid to Dionaean Venus, and to all the powers that aid rising labors; a bull was laid upon Jove's imperial altar. Not far away, a rising hillock stood in view; sharp myrtles and cornels grew on its sides. There, while I went to crop the sylvan scenes and shade our altar with their leafy green, I pulled up a plant—with horror I relate a prodigy so strange and so full of fate. The rooted fibers rose, and from the wound black drops of blood distilled upon the ground. Mute and amazed, my hair stood with terror; fear shrank my sinews, and congealed my blood. Recovering once more, I tried another plant: that other also gushed with the same sanguine dye. Then, fearing I was guilty of some unknown offense, with prayers and vows I sought to atone to the Dryads, to all the sisters of the woods, and most to the God of Arms, who rules the Thracian coast, asking that they, or he, would avert these omens, release our fears, and grant better signs. Cleared, as I thought, and at length fully resolved to learn the cause, I tugged with all my strength; I braced my knees against the ground; once more the violated myrtle ran with gore. Scarcely do I dare to tell the sequel. From the womb of the wounded earth, and from the caverns of the tomb, a groan as of a troubled ghost renewed my fright, and then these dreadful words ensued: 'Why do you rend my buried body thus? Spare the corpse of your unhappy friend! Spare to pollute your pious hands with blood. The tears do not distil from the wounded wood; but every drop this living tree contains is kindred blood, and ran in Trojan veins. O fly from this inhospitable shore, warned by my fate; for I am Polydore! Here loads of lances, steeped in my blood, again shoot upward, renewed by my blood.'

"My faltering tongue and shivering limbs declared my horror, and my hair rose up like bristles. When Troy was hard pressed by Grecian arms, old Priam, fearful of the war's outcome, had sent this hapless Polydore to Thracia. Loaded with gold, he sent his darling far from noise and tumults and destructive war, committed to the faithless tyrant's care. The tyrant, when he saw Troy's power decline, forsook the weaker side to join the stronger, broke every bond of nature and of truth, and murdered the royal youth for his wealth. O sacred hunger of pernicious gold! What bonds of faith can impious lucre hold? Now, when my soul had shaken off her fears, I called my father and the Trojan peers; I related the prodigies of Heaven, asked what he commanded, and begged their advice. All voted to leave that execrable shore, polluted with the blood of Polydore. But before we sailed, we prepared his funeral rites, and then raised a tomb and altars to his ghost. The matrons walked in mournful procession around it, crowned with baleful cypress and blue fillets, with eyes downcast and hair unbound. Then we poured bowls of tepid milk and blood, and thrice invoked the soul of Polydore.
"Now, when the raging storms no longer reigned, but southern gales invited us to the main, we launched our vessels with a prosperous wind, and left the cities and the shores behind.

"An island appears in the Aegean main, which Neptune and watery Doris claim as theirs. It once floated, until Phoebus fixed its sides to rooted earth, and now it braves the tides. Here, borne by friendly winds, we came ashore, and with needful ease restored our weary limbs, and adored the Sun's temple and his town.

"Anius, the priest and king, crowned with laurel, his hoary locks bound with purple fillets, who saw my sire ascend the Delian shore, came forth with eager haste to meet his friend; he invited him to his palace, and in sign of their ancient love they joined their plighted hands. Then I went to the temple of the god, and thus before the shrine presented my vows: 'Grant, O Thymbraean, grant a resting place to the sad relics of the Trojan race—a secure seat, a region of their own, a lasting empire, and a happier town. Where shall we fix ourselves? Where shall our labors end? Whom shall we follow, and what fate attend? Let not my prayers find a doubtful answer, but unveil your mind in clear auguries.' Scarcely had I said this when he shook the holy ground, the laurels, and the lofty hills around; and from the tripod rushed a bellowing sound. We fell prostrate, and acknowledged the present god, who gave this answer from his dark abode: 'Undaunted youths, go, seek the mother earth from which your ancestors derive their birth. The soil that sent you forth shall again embrace her ancient race in her old bosom. Through the wide world the Aeneian house shall reign, and children's children shall sustain the crown.' Thus Phoebus disclosed our future fates: a mighty tumult, mixed with joy, arose.

"All were concerned to know what place the god had assigned, and where he had determined our abode. My father, long revolving in his mind the race and lineage of the Trojan kind, answered their demands thus: 'Hear, you princes, your pleasing fortune, and dispel your fears. The fruitful island of Crete, well known to fame, sacred of old to Jove's imperial name, lies in the midst of the ocean, with wide command, and on its plains stand a hundred cities. Another Ida rises there; from there we derive our Trojan ancestry. From there, as is commonly reported by certain fame, old Teucer came to the Rhoetean shores; there he fixed himself, and chose it as the seat of empire, before Ilium and the Trojan towers arose. In humble vales they built their soft abodes, until Cybele, the mother of the gods, charmed the Idaean woods with tinkling cymbals; she taught secret rites and ceremonies, and brought the savage lions beneath the yoke. Let us go and explore the land Heaven appoints; let us appease the winds, and seek the Cnossian shore. If Jove assists the passage of our fleet, the third propitious dawn shall discover Crete.' Having said this, he laid sacrifices on the smoking altars, and paid them to the gods: a bull, the due oblation to Neptune; another bull he slew to bright Apollo; a milk-white ewe to please the western winds, and a coal-black one to calm the stormy seas. Before this, a flying rumor had been spread that fierce Idomeneus had fled from Crete, expelled and exiled; that the coast was free from foreign or domestic enemies.

"We left the Delian ports and put to sea. We made our way by Naxos, famed for its vintages; then we passed green Donysa, and sailed in sight of Paros, white with marble quarries. We passed the scattered islands of the Cyclades, which, scarcely distinguishable, seem to stud the seas. The shouts of sailors redoubled near the shores; they stretched their canvas, and plied their oars. 'All hands aloft! For Crete! For Crete!' they cried, and swiftly flew through the foamy billows. At length we bore full upon the promised land, and descended with joy upon the Cretan shore. With eager haste I framed a rising town, which I named Pergamus, from the Trojan one. The name itself was gratifying; I exhorted them to found their houses and erect a fort. Our ships were hauled upon the yellow strand; the youth began to till the labored land; and I myself promoted new marriages, gave laws, and distributed dwellings by lot—when rising vapors choked the wholesome air, and blasts of noisome winds corrupted the year; devouring caterpillars burned the trees; the grass was parched, and the corn was blighted; nor did the beasts escape—for Sirius, from on high, infected the sky with pestilential heat. Some of my men fell dead; the rest were fevered. Again my father bade me seek the shore of sacred Delos, and implore the god, to learn what end we might expect to our woes, and to what land we should direct our weary course.

"It was night, when every creature, free from cares, shares the common gift of balmy slumber. The statues of my gods (for such they seemed), those gods whom I had rescued from flaming Troy, stood before me, majestically bright, full in the beams of Phoebe's entering light. Then they spoke, and eased my troubled mind: 'What you are going to the Delian god to find, he tells you here, and sends us to relate. We are those powers, companions of your fate, who were brought from the burning town by you, who followed your fortune, and worked for your safety. As we have attended your steps through seas and lands, so shall our care befriend your glorious race. The fates ordain an ample realm for you, a town that shall reign over the conquered world. You must build mighty walls for mighty nations; do not let your weary mind yield to these labors. But change your seat: for neither the Delian god nor we have given you Crete as your abode. There is a land, called Hesperia of old; its soil is fruitful, and its natives bold. The Oenotrians once held it; by later fame it is now called Italia, from their leader's name. There Jasius and Dardanus were born; from there we came, and to there we must return. Rise, and greet your sire with these glad tidings. Search Italy; for Jove denies you Crete.'

"Astonished at their voices and their sight (for they were no dreams, but visions of the night: I saw, I recognized their faces, and descried, in perfect view, their hair tied with fillets), I started up from my couch; a clammy sweat sat upon all my limbs and shivering body. I lifted my hands to heaven with pious haste, and cast sacred incense in the flames. Thus, having done the gods their perfect honors, I ran more cheerfully to my good old sire, and told him the pleasing news. In a little space he found his error concerning the double race: not, as he had before believed, descended from Crete; no more deluded by the doubtful meaning. Then he said: 'O son, so turmoiled in Trojan fate! Cassandra related such things as these. This day revives in my mind what she foretold of Troy renewed in Italy and the Latian lands. But who then would have thought that Phrygian gods should be brought to Latium? Or who believed what mad Cassandra taught? Now let us go where Phoebus leads the way.'

"He spoke, and with glad consent we obeyed; we forsook the seat, and, leaving a few behind, we spread our sails before the willing wind. Now our galleys moved out of sight of land, with only seas around and skies above, when a burst of rain descended over our heads, and night with sable clouds enveloped the main. The ruffling winds raised the foamy billows; the scattered fleet was forced on different courses. The face of heaven was ravished from our eyes, and the roaring thunder flew in redoubled peals. Cast from our course, we wandered in the dark, with no stars to guide us, no point of land to mark. Even Palinurus could find no distinction between night and day; such darkness reigned around. For three starless nights the doubtful fleet strayed, without distinction, and for three sunless days. The fourth renewed the light, and from our shrouds we viewed a rising land, like distant clouds; the mountain tops confirmed the pleasing sight, and curling smoke ascending from their height. The canvas fell; the sailors plied their oars; from the rude strokes the whirling waters flew. At length I landed on the Strophades, safe from the danger of the stormy seas. These islands are surrounded by the Ionian main—the dire abode where the foul Harpies reign, forced by the winged warriors to return to their old homes and leave their costly fare. No more fierce monsters did offended Heaven ever send from hell's abyss for human punishment: with virgin faces, but obscene wombs, foul paunches, still unclean with their filth, with claws for hands, and faces forever lean.

"We landed at the port, and soon beheld fat herds of oxen grazing the flowery field, and wanton goats straying without a keeper. With weapons we invaded the welcome prey, then called the gods as partners of our feast, and Jove himself as the chief invited guest. We spread the tables on the greensward ground; we fed with hunger, and the bowls went round. When from the mountain tops, with hideous cry and clattering wings, the hungry Harpies flew; they snatched the meat, defiling all they found, and, departing, left a loathsome stench behind. Close by a hollow rock we sat again, dressed the dinner anew, and refitted the beds, secure from sight beneath a pleasing shade, where tufted trees made a natural arbor. Again the holy fires burned on the altars; and once again the ravenous birds returned, either from the dark recesses where they lie, or from another quarter of the sky. With filthy claws they repeated their odious meal, and mixed their loathsome ordure with our meat. I then bade my friends prepare for vengeance, and wage war with the hellish nation. As I commanded, they prepared for the fight, and hid their glittering weapons in the grass. Then, when we heard their clattering wings along the crooked shore, and saw the foes appear, Misenus sounded a charge; we took up the alarm, and armed our strong hands with swords and bucklers. In this new kind of combat, all employed their utmost force to destroy the monsters. In vain: the fated skin was proof against wounds, and the shining sword rebounded from their plumes. At length, rebuffed, they left their mangled prey, and displayed their stretched pinions to the skies. Yet one remained, the messenger of Fate: Celaeno sat high on a craggy cliff, and thus related her dismal errand: 'What! Not content with our oxen slain, do you dare to maintain an impious war with Heaven, and drive the Harpies from their native reign? Heed, therefore, what I say; and keep in mind what Jove decrees, what Phoebus has designed, and what I, the queen of the Furies, relate from them both. You seek the Italian shores, foredoomed by fate; you are granted to find the Italian shores, and a safe passage to the port assigned. But know that before you build your promised walls, my curses shall be severely fulfilled: fierce famine shall be your lot for this misdeed, reduced to grinding the plates on which you feed.' She said this, and flew to the neighboring forest. Our courage failed us, and our fears renewed. Hopeless of winning by war, we fell to prayers, and humbly called upon the offended Harpies, and whether they were gods or obscene birds, we preferred our vows for pardon and for peace. But old Anchises, offering sacrifice, and lifting up his hands and eyes to heaven, adored the greater gods: 'Avert these omens,' he said, 'render this prophecy vain, and free a pious people from the impending curse!'

"Having said this, he bade us put to sea. We loosed our hawsers from shore, obeyed, and soon pursued the watery way with swelling sails. In the midst of our course, Zacynthian woods appeared; next we steered by rocky Neritos; we flew from the detested shore of Ithaca, and cursed the land that bore dire Ulysses. At length Leucate's cloudy top appeared, and the temple of the Sun, which sailors fear. Resolved to breathe a while from our past labor, we cast our crooked anchors from the prow, and hastened joyfully to the little city. Here, safe beyond our hopes, we paid our vows to Jove, the guide and patron of our way. We followed the customs of our country, and renewed Trojan games on the Actian shore. Our youth anointed their naked limbs with oil, and exercised the noble toil of wrestlers, pleased to have sailed so long before the wind, and to have left so many Grecian towns behind. The sun had now fulfilled his annual course, and Boreas displayed his force on the seas. I fixed upon the temple's lofty door the brazen shield that vanquished Abas had borne; the verse beneath speaks my name and action: 'These arms Aeneas took from conquering Greeks.' Then I gave the command to weigh anchor; the seamen plied their sweeping oars; the smoking billows flew. The sight of lofty Phaeacia we soon lost, and skimmed along the rocky coast of Epirus.

"Then we bent our course to Chaonia's port, and, landed, we ascended the heights of Buthrotus. Here wondrous things were loudly noised by fame: how Helenus had revived the Trojan name, and reigned in Greece; that Priam's captive son had succeeded Pyrrhus in his bed and throne, and that fair Andromache, restored by fate, was once more happy in a Trojan mate. I left my galleys riding in the port, and longed to see the new Dardanian court. By chance the mournful queen, before the gate, was then solemnizing her former husband's fate. She had crowned green altars, raised of turf, with gifts; sacred priests stood around in order, and thrice sounded the name of hapless Hector. The grove itself resembled Ida's wood; and Simois seemed the well-dissembled flood. But when, at a nearer distance, she beheld my shining armor and my Trojan shield, astonished at the sight, the vital heat forsook her limbs; her veins no longer beat. She fainted, she fell, and, scarcely recovering her strength, at length with a faltering tongue she spoke:

"'Are you alive, O goddess-born?' she said. 'Or if a ghost, then where is Hector's shade?' At this she let loose a loud and frightful cry. With broken words I made this brief reply: 'All that remains of me appears in sight. I live, if living means to loathe the light. No phantom; but I drag a wretched life, my fate resembling that of Hector's wife. What have you suffered since you lost your lord? By what strange blessing are you now restored? Are you still Hector's? Or has Hector fled, and his remembrance been lost in Pyrrhus' bed?' With downcast eyes, in a lowly tone, after a modest pause she thus began:

"'O only happy maid of Priam's race, whom death delivered from the foes' embrace! Ordered to die on Achilles' tomb, not forced, like us, to hard captivity, or to lie in a haughty master's arms. We unhappy ones were borne in Grecian ships, endured the victor's lust, sustained the scorn: thus I submitted to the lawless pride of Pyrrhus, more a handmaid than a bride. Cloyed with possession, he forsook my bed, and sought to wed Helen's lovely daughter; then he resigned me to Trojan Helenus, and joined his two slaves in equal marriage; until young Orestes, pierced with deep despair, and longing to redeem his promised fair, slew the ravisher before Apollo's altar. By Pyrrhus' death we regained the kingdom; at least one half remained with Helenus. He calls our portion Chaonia, from Chaon, and names the rising walls Pergamus. But what fates have landed you on our coast? What gods have sent you, or what storms have tossed you here? Does young Ascanius enjoy life and health, saved from the ruins of unhappy Troy? O tell me how he bears his mother's loss, what hopes are promised from his blooming years, how much of Hector appears in his face?' She spoke, and mingled her speech with mournful cries; fruitless tears came trickling from her eyes.

"At length her lord descended upon the plain, in pomp, attended by a numerous train. He received his friends, and led them to the city, shedding tears of joy amid his welcome. Proceeding on, I saw another Troy—or rather, in less compass, Troy's epitome. A rivulet ran by the name of Xanthus, and I embraced the Scaean gate again. My friends were entertained in porticoes; feasts and pleasures reigned throughout the city. Tables filled the spacious hall around, and golden bowls were crowned with sparkling wine. We passed two days in mirth, till friendly gales, blown from the south, filled our swelling sails. Then to the royal seer I thus began: 'O you who know, beyond the reach of man, the laws of heaven, and what the stars decree; whom Phoebus taught unerring prophecy, from his own tripod and his holy tree; who are skilled in the winged inhabitants of the air, and in what auspices their notes and flights declare—O tell me; for all religious rites portend a happy voyage and a prosperous end, and every power and omen of the sky directs my course toward destined Italy; but dire Celaeno alone, from the gods, fatally forebodes a dismal famine. O tell me what dangers I must first shun, what toils I must vanquish, and what course to take.'

"The prophet first, with sacrifice, adored the greater gods; then implored their pardon. He unbound the fillet from his holy head; next he led my trembling steps to Phoebus, full of religious doubts and awful dread. Then, possessed by his god, before the shrine, these words proceeded from his divine mouth: 'O goddess-born (for Heaven's appointed will foreshows your voyage with greater auspices of good than ill, and directs your course; your fates conspire, and Jove himself protects you), of many things I shall explain a few—to teach you to shun the dangers of the main, and how at length to gain the promised shore. The rest the fates hide from Helenus, and Juno's angry power forbids me to tell. First, then: that happy shore, that seems so near, will fly far from your deluded wishes; long tracts of sea divide your hopes from Italy. You must cruise along the Sicilian shores, and stem the currents with your struggling oars; then steer your navy round the Italian coast, and after this veer to Circe's island. Last, before your new foundations rise, you must pass the Stygian lake and view the nether skies. Now mark the signs of future ease and rest, and bear them safely treasured in your breast. When, in the shady shelter of a wood, and near the margin of a gentle flood, you behold a sow upon the ground, encompassed by thirty sucking young, the dam and offspring white as falling snow—these shall bestow their name upon your city, and there shall end your labors and your woe. And do not let the threatened famine fright your mind, for Phoebus will assist, and Fate will find the way. Do not let your course be bent toward that ill coast which faces the Epirian continent from afar; those parts are all possessed by Grecian foes; the savage Locrians infest the shores here; there fierce Idomeneus builds his city, and guards the Salentine fields with arms; and on the mountain's brow stands Petilia, which Philoctetes commands with his troops. Even when your fleet is landed on the shore, and priests adore the gods with holy vows, envelop your eyes with a purple veil, lest hostile faces blast the sacrifice. Commend these rites and customs to the rest, that they may descend to your pious race.

'When, having departed, the wind that waits to bear you for Sicily brings you to the straits where proud Pelorus opens a wider way, tack to the larboard, and stand off to sea; veer starboard from sea and land. The Italian shore and fair Sicily's coast were once one, before an earthquake caused the rift: the roaring tides broke a passage that now divides land from land; and where the lands drew back, the rushing ocean rides between. Distinguished by the straits, on either hand now stand rising cities in long order, and fruitful fields: so much can time invade the moldering work that beauteous Nature made. Far on the right, foul Scylla hides her dogs; Charybdis roars on the left, and sucks down the tides in her greedy whirlpool, then spouts them from below; the waves, driven by fury, mount up and wash the face of heaven. But Scylla, from her den, with open jaws, draws the sinking vessel into her eddy, then dashes it on the rocks. A human face and virgin bosom hide the disgrace of her tail; her obscene parts descend below the waves, enclosed by dogs, and end in a dolphin. It is safer, then, to bear aloof to sea, and to coast Pachynus, though with more delay, than once to view misshapen Scylla near, and hear the loud yell of watery wolves.

"'Besides, if faith be due to Helenus, and if prophetic Phoebus tells me true, do not forget this precept from your friend, which therefore I must repeat more than once: above all else, adore the name of great Juno; pay vows to Juno; implore Juno's aid. Let gifts be designed for the mighty queen, and soften her haughty mind with prayers. Thus at length your passage shall be free, and you shall safely descend on Italy. When you arrive at Cumae, and view the flood of black Avernus and the sounding wood, you shall find the mad prophetic Sibyl, dark in a cave, reclining on a rock. She sings the fates, and in her frantic fits commits the notes and names, inscribed, to leaves. What she commits to leaves she lays in order, and displays them before the cavern's entrance. Unmoved they lie; but if a blast of wind from outside, or vapors from behind, issue in, the leaves are borne aloft in the liquid air, and she resumes her musing care no more, nor gathers up the scattered verse from the rocks, nor sets in order what the winds disperse. Thus, many not succeeding, most upbraid the madness of the visionary maid, and leave the mystic shade with loud curses.

"'Do not think it a loss of time to stay a while, though your companions chide your long delay; though the seas summon you, though pleasing gales invite your course and stretch your swelling sails: but beg the sacred priestess to relate your fate with willing words, not to write it. She will show you the fierce Italian people, and all your wars, and all your future woe, and what you may avoid, and what must undergo. She shall direct your course, instruct your mind, and teach you how to find the happy shores. This is what Heaven allows me to relate. Now part in peace; pursue your better fate, and raise the Trojan state by strength of arms.'

"When the priest had declared this with friendly voice, he gave me leave to go, and prepared rich gifts. Bounteous of treasure, he supplied my want with heavy gold, and polished ivory; then he put Dodonaean cauldrons on board, and stored every ship with sums of silver. He sent me a trusty coat of mail, thrice chained with gold, for use and ornament; and the helm of Pyrrhus added to the rest, which flourished with a plume and waving crest. Nor was my sire forgotten, nor my friends; and he sent large reinforcements to my navy: men, horses, captains, arms, and warlike stores; he supplied new pilots and new sweeping oars. Meanwhile my sire commanded us to hoist our sails, lest we should lose the first auspicious gales.

"The prophet blessed the parting crew, and last, with words like these, embraced his ancient friend: 'Old happy man, the care of the gods above, whom heavenly Venus honored with her love, and twice preserved your life when Troy was lost, behold from afar the wished Ausonian coast. Land there; but take a larger compass round, for that nearer shore is all forbidden ground. The shore that Phoebus has designed for you lies at farther distance, concealed from view. Go happy from here, and seek your new abodes, blessed in a son, and favored by the gods; for I am prolonging your stay with useless words, when the southern gales have summoned you away.'

"Nor less did the queen deplore our parting, nor was she less bounteous than her Trojan lord. She brought a noble present for my son: a robe with flowers wrought on golden tissue, a Phrygian vest; and she loaded him besides with gifts of precious texture and Asian splendor. 'Accept,' she said, 'these monuments of love, which in my youth I wove with happier hands. Regard these trifles for the giver's sake; it is the last present Hector's wife can make. You call my lost Astyanax to mind; I find his features and his form in you. His eyes sparkled with the same lively flame; such were his motions; such was all his frame; and, ah! had Heaven so pleased, his years would have been the same.'

"With tears I took my last farewell, and said: 'Your fortune, happy pair, is already made, and leaves you no further wish. My different state, avoiding one, incurs another fate. The gods allow you a quiet seat: you have no shores to search, no seas to plow, nor fields of flying Italy to chase (deluding visions, and a vain embrace!). You see another Simois, and enjoy, by the labor of your hands, another Troy, with better auspice than her ancient towers, and less exposed to the Greek powers. If ever the gods, whom I adore with vows, conduct my steps to Tiber's happy shore; if ever I ascend the Latian throne, and build a city I may call my own; as both of us derive our birth from Troy, so let our kindred lines live in concord, and both strive in acts of equal friendship. Our fortunes, good or bad, shall be the same: the double Troy shall differ only in name; and what we now begin may never end, but descend far to late posterity.'

"We bore our course near the Ceraunian rocks, the shortest passage to the Italian shore. Now the sun had withdrawn his radiant light, and the hills were hidden in dusky shades of night. We landed, and on the bosom of the ground found a safe retreat and a bare lodging. Close by the shore we lay; the sailors kept their watches, and the rest slept securely. The night, proceeding with silent pace, stood at her noon, and viewed with equal face her steepy rise and her declining race. Then wakeful Palinurus rose, to spy the face of heaven and the nocturnal sky; and listened to try every breath of air; observed the stars, and noted their sliding course—the Pleiades, Hyades, and their watery force; and was careful to behold both the Bears, and bright Orion, armed with burnished gold. Then, when he saw no threatening tempest near, but a sure promise of a settled sky, he gave the sign to weigh. We broke our sleep, forsook the pleasing shore, and plowed the deep.

"And now the rising morn, with rosy light, adorned the skies, and put the stars to flight, when from afar, like bluish mists, we descried the hills, and then the plains, of Italy. Achates first pronounced the joyful sound; then 'Italy!' the cheerful crew rebounded. My sire Anchises crowned a cup with wine, and, offering it, thus implored the divine powers: 'You gods who preside over lands and seas, and you who appease the raging winds and waves, breathe a prosperous wind on our swelling sails, and smooth our passage to the port assigned!' The gentle gales renewed their flagging force, and now the happy harbor was in view. Minerva's temple then saluted our sight, placed, as a landmark, on the mountain's height. We furled our sails, and turned our prows to shore; the curling waters roared round the galleys. The land lies open to the raging east; then, bending like a bow, it is compressed by rocks, which shut out the storms; the winds and waves complain, and vent their malice on the cliffs in vain. The port lies hidden within; on either side two towering rocks divide the narrow mouth. The temple we had viewed aloft before flew to a distance, and seemed to shun the shore. Scarcely landed, the first omens I beheld were four white steeds that cropped the flowery field. 'War, war is threatened from this foreign ground,' my father cried, 'where warlike steeds are found. Yet, since they submit when reclaimed to chariots, and bend to stubborn yokes, and champ the bit, peace may succeed to war.' We bent our way toward Pallas, and ascended the sacred hill; there, prostrate, we prayed to the fierce Virago, whose temple was the landmark of our way. Each of us veiled his head with a Phrygian mantle, and all obeyed Helenus' commands, paying pious rites to Grecian Juno. These dues performed, we stretched our sails, and stood to sea, forsaking that suspected land.

"From here the bay of Tarentum appears in view, renowned for Hercules, if fame be true. Just opposite, Lacinian Juno stands; then the Caulonian towers, and the Scylacian strands, feared for shipwrecks. From there we spied Mount Aetna, known by the smoky flames that cloud the sky. Far off we heard the waves invade the rocks with surly sound, and the rocks returning groans. The billows broke upon the sounding strand, and rolled the rising tide, impure with sand. Then thus Anchises, old in experience: 'It is that Charybdis which the seer foretold, and those the promised rocks! Bear off to sea!' The frightened mariners obeyed in haste. First Palinurus veered to the larboard; then all the fleet steered by his example. We rode aloft to heaven on ridgy waves, then descended as they divided, as into hell; and three times our galleys struck the stony ground, and three times the hollow rocks returned the sound, and three times we saw the stars, that stood bedewed around. The flagging winds forsook us with the sun, and we ran, weary, onto Cyclopian shores. The port, capacious and secure from wind, is joined to the foot of thundering Aetna. By turns she rolls a pitchy cloud on high; by turns hot embers fly from her entrails, and flakes of mounting flames that lick the sky. Often massive rocks are thrown from her bowels, and, shivered by the force, come tumbling down in pieces. Often liquid lakes of burning sulphur flow, fed from the fiery springs that boil below. Enceladus, they say, transfixed by Jove, came tumbling down from above with blasted limbs; and where he fell, the avenging father drew this flaming hill, and threw it over his body. As often as he turns his weary sides, he shakes the solid island, and smoke hides the heavens. In shady woods we passed the tedious night, where bellowing sounds and groans affrighted our souls, of which no cause was offered to our sight; for not one star was kindled in the sky, nor could the moon supply her borrowed light, for misty clouds enveloped the firmament, the stars were muffled, and the moon was pent.

"Scarcely had the rising sun revealed the day, scarcely had his heat dispelled the pearly dews, when from the woods there darted out before our sight something between a mortal and a sprite—so thin, so ghastly lean, and so wan, so bare of flesh, that he scarcely resembled a man. This creature, all tattered, seemed from afar to implore our pious aid, and pointed to the shore. We looked behind him, and then viewed his shaggy beard; his clothes were tagged with thorns, and filth besmeared his limbs. The rest of him, in bearing, in dress, and in face, appeared a Greek, and such indeed he was. He cast a frightful glance on us from afar, and, soon knowing us for Trojans and foes, stood still, and paused; then all at once began to stretch his limbs, and trembled as he ran. As soon as he came near, he fell upon his knees, and thus called for pity with tears and sighs: 'Now, by the powers above, and by what we share of Nature's common gift, this vital air, O Trojans, take me from here! I beg no more; but bear me far from this unhappy shore. It is true, I am a Greek, and further I admit I was among those who besieged your imperial town. If for such demerits my death be due, I sue no more for this abandoned life; only let my tears obtain this favor, to throw me headlong into the rapid main: since my crime demands nothing more than death, I die content to die by human hands.' He said, and on his knees embraced mine. I bade him boldly tell his past fortune, his present state, his lineage, and his name, the occasion of his fears, and whence he came. Good Anchises raised him with his hand; thus encouraged, he answered our demand: 'I came from Ithaca, my native soil, to Troy; and Achaemenides is my name. My poor father sent me with Ulysses (O had I stayed, content with poverty!). But my countrymen, fearful for themselves, left me forsaken in the Cyclops' den. The cave, though large, was dark; the dismal floor was paved with mangled limbs and putrid gore. Our monstrous host, of more than human size, raises his head, and stares into the skies; bellowing is his voice, and horrid is his hue. You gods, remove this plague from mortal view! The joints of slaughtered wretches are his food; and for his wine he quaffs the streaming blood. These eyes beheld it, when with his spacious hand he seized two captives of our Grecian band; stretched on his back, he dashed their broken bodies against the stones, and their crackling bones; the purple pavement swam with spouting blood, while the dire glutton ground the trembling limbs.

"'Ulysses did not bear their fate unrevenged, nor was he thoughtless of his own unhappy state; for when the giant, gorged with flesh and drunk with human wine, lay fast asleep, supine, snoring aloud, and belching from his maw his undigested foam and raw morsels—we prayed; we cast lots, and then surrounded the monstrous body stretched along the ground. Each, as he could approach him, lent a hand to bore his eyeball with a flaming brand. His eye lay beneath his frowning forehead, for only one supplied that vast frame—but that a globe so large that it filled his front, like the sun's disk, or like a Grecian shield. The stroke succeeded, and the pupil bent downward: this was our vengeance for our slaughtered friends. But haste, unhappy wretches, haste to fly! Cut your cables, and rely on your oars! Such as Polypheme, and as vast, a hundred more are borne by this hated island: like him, they shut their woolly sheep in caves; like him, they keep their herds on mountain tops; like him, with mighty strides, they stalk from steep to steep. And now three moons have renewed their sharpened horns, since thus, in woods and wilds, obscure from view, I drag out my loathsome days with mortal fright, and lodge by night in deserted caverns. Often from the rocks I see a dreadful prospect of the huge Cyclops, like a walking tree. From afar I hear his thundering voice resound, and trampling feet that shake the solid ground. Cornels and wild berries of the wood, and roots and herbs, have been my meager food. While I cast my longing eyes all around, I at last saw your happy ships appear. On these I fixed my hopes; to these I ran. It is all I ask, to shun this cruel race; you yourselves may bestow whatever other death you please.'

"Scarcely had he said this when, on the mountain's brow, we saw the giant shepherd stalking before his following flock, and leading them to the shore—a monstrous bulk, deformed, deprived of sight; his staff a trunk of pine, to guide his steps aright. His ponderous whistle descended from his neck; his woolly charge attended their pensive lord. This was the only solace his hard fortune sent. As soon as he reached the shore and touched the waves, he laved the guttering blood from his bored-out eye. He gnashed his teeth, and groaned; he strode through the seas, and scarcely did the topmost billows touch his sides.

"Seized with a sudden fear, we ran to sea, cut the cables, and departed in silent haste; we took the well-deserving stranger aboard, and, buckling to the work, our oars divided the main. The giant hearkened to the dashing sound; but when he found our vessels out of reach, he strode onward, and essayed in vain the Ionian deep, and dared wade no further. With that he roared aloud: the dreadful cry shook earth, air, and seas; the billows fled before the bellowing noise to distant Italy. Neighboring Aetna trembled all around; the winding caverns echoed to the sound. His brother Cyclopes heard the yelling roar, and, rushing down the mountains, crowded the shore. From afar we saw their stern distorted looks, and their one-eyed glances, which vainly threatened war—a dreadful council, with their heads on high (the misty clouds flew about their foreheads), not yielding to the towering tree of Jove, or to the tallest cypress of Diana's grove. New pangs of mortal fear assailed our minds; we tugged at every oar, and hoisted every sail, and took advantage of the friendly gale. Forewarned by Helenus, we strove to shun Charybdis' gulf, nor did we dare to run toward Scylla. An equal fate appeared on either side. We, tacking to the left, were free from fears; for from Pelorus' point the north wind arose, and drove us back where swift Pantagias flows. We passed his rocky mouth, and made our way by Thapsus, and by Megara's winding bay. This passage Achaemenides had shown, tracing the course which he had run before.

"Right opposite Plemmyrium's watery strand, there lies an island once called the Ortygian land. Alpheus, as old fame reports, has found a secret passage under ground from Greece, led by love for beauteous Arethusa; and mingling here, they roll in the same sacred bed. As Helenus enjoined, we next adored Diana's name, protectress of the shore. With prosperous gales we passed the quiet sounds of still Elorus, and his fruitful bounds. Then, doubling Cape Pachynus, we surveyed the rocky shore extended to the sea. From afar we saw the town of Camarina, and its fenny lake, undrained by fate's decree. In sight of the Geloan fields we passed, and the large walls where mighty Gela once stood. Then Agragas, crowned with lofty summits, long renowned for its race of warlike steeds. We passed Selinus, and the palmy land, and widely shunned the Lilybaean strand, unsafe for secret rocks and shifting sand. At length the weary fleet arrived on shore, which Drepanum's unhappy port received. Here, after endless labors, often tossed by raging storms, and driven on every coast, I lost my dear, dear father, worn out by age—the ease of my cares, the solace of my pain, saved through a thousand toils, but saved in vain. The prophet who had revealed my future woes yet concealed this, the greatest and the worst; and dire Celaeno, whose foreboding skill denounced all else, was silent as to this ill. This was my last labor. Some friendly god from there conveyed us to your blessed abode."
Thus, to the listening queen, the royal guest recounted his wandering course and all his toils; and here concluding, he retired to rest.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: Dido reveals to her sister her passion for Aeneas, and her thoughts of marrying him. She prepares a hunting match for his entertainment. Juno, with Venus' consent, raises a storm, which separates the hunters and drives Aeneas and Dido into the same cave, where their marriage is supposed to be completed. Jupiter dispatches Mercury to Aeneas, to warn him away from Carthage. Aeneas secretly prepares for his voyage. Dido finds out his intention, and, to put a stop to it, uses her own and her sister's entreaties, and displays all the variety of passions that attend a neglected lover. When nothing could prevail upon him, she contrives her own death, with which this book concludes.

But anxious cares had already seized the queen. She fed an unseen flame within her veins. The hero's valor, his deeds, and his birth inspired her soul with love, and fanned the secret fire. His words, his looks, imprinted in her heart, deepened her passion, and increased the smart. Now, when the purple morn had chased away the dewy shadows and restored the day, she sought out her sister first with early care, and thus in mournful accents eased her thought:

"My dearest Anna, what new dreams affright my laboring soul! What visions of the night disturb my quiet, and distract my breast with strange ideas of our Trojan guest! His worth, his actions, and majestic air declare him a man descended from the gods. Fear always argues a degenerate kind; his birth is well asserted by his mind. Then, what he suffered when he was betrayed by Fate! What brave attempts he made for falling Troy! Such were his looks, so gracefully he spoke, that, were I not resolved against the yoke of hapless marriage, never to be cursed with a second love—so fatal was my first—I might yield to this one error again. For, since Sichaeus was untimely slain, only this one man is able to subvert the fixed foundations of my stubborn heart. And, to confess my frailty to my shame, I find something within me, if not the same, too like the sparks of my former flame. But first let yawning earth rend a passage, and let me descend through the dark abyss; first let avenging Jove, with flames from on high, drive this body down to the nether sky, condemned to lie with ghosts in endless night, before I break the plighted faith I gave! No! He who had my vows shall have them still; for whom I loved on earth, I worship in the grave."

She said; the tears ran gushing from her eyes, and stopped her speech. Her sister replied thus: "O dearer to me than the vital air I breathe, will you bequeath your blooming years to grief, condemned to waste your lonely life in woes, without the joys of mother or of wife? Do you think these tears, this pompous train of woe, are known or valued by the ghosts below? I grant that, while your sorrows were still fresh, it well became a woman and a queen to neglect the vows of Tyrian princes, to scorn Hyarbas and reject his love, together with all the Libyan lords of mighty name. But will you fight against a pleasing flame? This little spot of land which Heaven bestows is hemmed on every side with warlike foes: Gaetulian cities are spread around here, and fierce Numidians bound your frontiers there; here lies a barren waste of thirsty land, and there the Syrtes raise the shifting sand; Barcaean troops besiege the narrow shore, and Pygmalion threatens still more from the sea. Propitious Heaven and gracious Juno have led this wandering fleet to your needful aid. How your empire will spread, your city will rise, from such a union, and with such allies! Implore the favor of the powers above, and leave the conduct of the rest to love. Continue still your hospitable way, and still invent occasions for their stay, until storms and winter winds cease to threaten, and planks and oars repair their shattered fleet."

These words, coming from a friend and sister, easily resolved the scruples of her fame, and added fury to the kindled flame. Inspired with hope, they pursued the project; they renewed sacrifice on every altar: a chosen ewe of two years old they paid to Ceres, Bacchus, and the God of Day; preferring above all Juno's power, for Juno ties the nuptial knot and grants the joys of marriage. The beauteous queen stood before her altar, and held the golden goblet in her hands. She adorned a milk-white heifer with flowers, and poured the ruddy wine between her horns. And while the priests invoked the gods with prayer, she fed the altars with Sabaean incense, hourly renewed the sacrifice, and anxiously viewed the panting entrails. What priestly rites, alas, what pious art, what vows can cure a bleeding heart? A gentle fire she fed within her veins, where the soft god reigned secure in silence.

Sick with desire, and seeking the one she loved, the raving Dido wandered from street to street. So when a watchful shepherd, from a hiding place, wounds a careless hind with a random shaft, distracted with her pain she flies the woods, bounds over the lawn, and seeks the silent streams, with fruitless care; for still the fatal dart sticks in her side, and rankles in her heart. And now she led the Trojan chief along the lofty walls, amidst the busy throng; she displayed her Tyrian wealth and rising town, which love, without his labor, made his own. She showed him this pomp to tempt her wandering guest; her faltering tongue forbade her to speak the rest. When day declined, and feasts renewed the night, still she fed her famished sight on his face; she longed again to hear the prince relate his own adventures and the Trojan fate. He told it over and over; but still in vain, for still she begged to hear it once again. The hearer hung upon the speaker's mouth, and thus the tragic story never ended.

Then, when they parted, when Phoebe's paler light withdrew, and falling stars invited sleep, she remained the last, when every guest had gone; she sat on the bed he had pressed, and sighed alone. Absent, she saw and heard her absent hero; or she carried young Ascanius in her bosom, and sought the father's image in the child, if love might be beguiled by likeness.

Meanwhile the rising towers stood at a halt; no labors exercised the youthful band, nor any use of arts, nor toils of arms; the mole was left unfinished to the enemy; the mounds, the works, the walls, lay neglected, short of their promised height that had seemed to threaten the sky.

But when imperial Juno, from above, saw Dido fettered in the chains of love, hot with the venom that inflamed her veins, and not to be reclaimed by any sense of shame, with soothing words she began to Venus: "High praises, endless honors you have won, and mighty trophies, with your worthy son! Two gods have undone a silly woman! Nor am I ignorant that you both suspect this rising city which my hands erect. But shall celestial discord never cease? It is better ended in a lasting peace. You stand possessed of all your soul desired: poor Dido is fired with consuming love. Let us join your Trojan with my Tyrian; so Dido shall be yours, Aeneas mine: one common kingdom, one united line. Eliza shall obey a Dardan lord, and lofty Carthage shall convey as her dower." Then Venus, who discerned her hidden fraud, which would misguide the scepter of the world to Libyan shores, replied thus artfully: "Who but a fool would choose wars with Juno, and refuse such alliance and such gifts, if Fortune would comply with our joint desires? The doubt is all from Jove and destiny—lest he forbid, with absolute command, the mixing of the peoples in one common land. Or will the Trojan and the Tyrian line be joined in lasting leagues and sure succession? But you, the partner of his bed and throne, may move his mind; my wishes are your own."

"Let the care be mine," said imperial Juno. "Time urges us now to perfect this affair. Attend my counsel, and share the secret. When next the Sun displays his rising light, and gilds the world below with purple rays, the queen, Aeneas, and the Tyrian court shall resort to the shady woods for sylvan game. There, while the huntsmen pitch their toils around, and cheerful horns resound from side to side, a pitchy cloud shall cover all the plain with hail, and thunder, and tempestuous rain. The fearful train shall take their speedy flight, dispersed, and all involved in gloomy night. One cave shall afford a grateful shelter to the fair princess and the Trojan lord. I will myself prepare the bridal bed, if you, to bless the nuptials, will be there. So shall their loves be crowned with due delights, and Hymen shall be present at the rites." The Queen of Love consented, and smiled closely at her vain project, its wiles now discovered.

The rosy morn had risen from the main, and horns and hounds woke the princely train. They issued early through the city gate, where the more wakeful huntsmen awaited them, ready with nets and toils and darts, besides the force of Spartan dogs and swift Massylian horses. The Tyrian peers and officers of state waited in antechambers for the slow queen. Her lofty courser, in the court below, seemed to know his majestic rider: proud of his purple trappings, he pawed the ground, champed the golden bit, and spread the foam around. The queen at length appeared; on either hand the brawny guards stood in martial order. She wore a flowered simar with golden fringe, and at her back bore a golden quiver; a golden caul restrained her flowing hair, and a golden clasp sustained the Tyrian robe. Then young Ascanius, with a sprightly grace, led on the Trojan youth to view the chase. But far above the rest in beauty shone great Aeneas, as he joined the troop; like fair Apollo, when he leaves the frost of wintry Xanthus, and the Lycian coast, to return to his native Delos, where he ordains the dances and renews the sports, where painted Scythians, mixed with Cretan bands, join hands before the joyful altars. Himself, walking on Cynthus, sees below the merry madness of the sacred show. Green wreaths of bay enclose the length of his hair; a golden fillet binds his awful brows; his quiver sounds. Not less was the prince to be seen in manly presence and lofty mien.

Now they had reached the hills, and stormed the seat of savage beasts in dens, their last retreat. The cry pursued the mountain goats; they bounded from rock to rock, and kept the craggy ground. Quite otherwise the stags—a trembling train—scoured the dusty plain in unseparated herds, and maintained a long chase in open view. The glad Ascanius, as he guided his courser, spurred through the valley, outriding both these and those. His horse's flanks and sides were forced to feel the clanking lash and the goring of the steel. Impatiently he viewed the feeble prey, wishing some nobler beast would cross his way, and rather would have preferred the tusky boar to attend him, or to see the tawny lion coming down.

Meanwhile, the gathering clouds obscured the skies; from pole to pole the forked lightning flew; the rattling thunders rolled, and Juno poured down a wintry deluge, and sounding showers. The company, dispersed, rode to coverts, and sought the homely cottages, or the mountain's hollow side. The rapid rains, descending from the hills, raised the creeping rills to rolling torrents. The queen and prince, as love or fortune guided, were hidden by one common cavern in her bosom. Then the trembling earth first gave the signal, and flashing fires enlightened all the cave; Hell from below, and Juno from above, and howling nymphs were conscious of their love. From this ill-omened hour in time arose debate and death, and all succeeding woes.
The queen, whom sense of honor could not move, no longer made a secret of her love, but called it marriage, with that specious name to veil the crime and sanctify the shame.

The loud report went through the Libyan cities. Fame, that great evil, grows from small beginnings: swift from the first, and every moment brings new vigor to her flights, new pinions to her wings. Soon the pygmy grows to gigantic size; her feet on earth, her forehead in the skies. Enraged against the gods, revengeful Earth produced her last of the Titanian brood. Swift is her walk, more swift her winged haste: a monstrous phantom, horrible and vast. As many plumes as raise her lofty flight, so many piercing eyes enlarge her sight; millions of opening mouths belong to Fame, and every mouth is furnished with a tongue, and round about the flying plague is hung with listening ears. She fills the peaceful universe with cries; no slumbers ever close her wakeful eyes. By day, from lofty towers she shows her head, and spreads disastrous news through trembling crowds; she haunts with court informers and royal spies; she relates things done, feigns things not done, and mingles truth with lies.

Talk is her business, and her chief delight is to tell of prodigies and cause affright. She filled the people's ears with Dido's name, who, lost to honor and the sense of shame, had admitted to her throne and nuptial bed a wandering guest who had fled from his country: whole days she passed with him in delights, and wasted long winter nights in luxury, forgetful of her fame and royal trust, dissolved in ease, abandoned to her lust.

The goddess spread the loud report widely, and at length flew to King Hyarbas' court. When first possessed by this unwelcome news, whom did he not accuse, of men and gods? This prince, born of ravished Garamantis, had adorned a hundred temples with spoils, in honor of Ammon, his celestial sire; a hundred altars fed with wakeful fire; and throughout his vast dominions had ordained priests whose watchful care maintained these holy rites. The gates and columns were crowned with garlands, and the blood of victim beasts enriched the ground.

He, when he heard that a fugitive could move the Tyrian princess, who had disdained his love, burned with fury in his breast, with fire in his eyes, mad with despair, impatient with desire. Then, pouring wine upon the sacred altars, he implored his divine sire with prayers: "Great Jove, propitious to the Moorish race, who feast on painted beds, who grace your temples with offerings, and adore your divine power with the blood of victims and sparkling wine—do you not see this? Or do we fear in vain your boasted thunder and your thoughtless reign? Do your broad hands hurl the forked lightnings? Are the bolts yours, or the blind work of chance? A wandering woman is building, within our state, a little town, bought at an easy rate; she pays me homage, and my grants allow her to plow a narrow space of Libyan lands; yet, scorning me, led blindly by passion, she admits a banished Trojan to her bed! And now this other Paris, with his train of conquered cowards, must reign in Africa! (Whom, what they are, their looks and garb confess—their locks perfumed with oil, their Lydian dress.) He takes the spoil, enjoys the princely dame; and I—I, rejected—adore an empty name."

He thus preferred his vows in haughty terms, and held the horns of his altar. The mighty Thunderer heard him; then he cast his eyes on Carthage, where he found the lustful pair drowned in lawless pleasure, lost in their loves, insensible of shame, and both forgetful of their better fame. He called Cyllenius, and the god attended, by whom he sent his menacing command: "Go, mount the western winds, and cleave the sky; then, with a swift descent, fly to Carthage. There find the Trojan chief, who is wasting his days in slothful riot and inglorious ease, and has no regard for the future city given him by fate. Relate to him this message from my mouth: 'Fair Venus did not hope for this, when twice she won your life with prayers, nor did she promise such a son. Hers was a hero, destined to command a martial race, and rule the Latian land, who should draw his ancient line from Teucer, and impose the law on the conquered world.' If glory cannot move so mean a mind, nor future praise wean him from fading pleasure, yet why should he defraud his son of fame, and grudge the Romans their immortal name? What are his vain designs! What more does he hope from his long lingering on a hostile shore, regardless of redeeming his lost honor, and of gaining the Ausonian coast for his race? Bid him with speed forsake the Tyrian court; wake the slumbering warrior with this command."

Hermes obeyed; he bound his flying feet with golden pinions, and mounted the western winds; and whether he flew over seas or earth, they bore him down the skies with rapid force. But first he grasped in his awful hand the mark of sovereign power, his magic wand. With this he draws ghosts from hollow graves; with this he drives them down the Stygian waves; with this he seals in sleep the wakeful sight, and restores eyes, though closed in death, to light.
