Thus armed, the god began his airy course, and drove the racking clouds along the liquid space. Now, as he flew, he saw the tops of Atlas, whose brawny back supports the starry skies—Atlas, whose head, crowned with piny forests, is beaten by the winds, bound with foggy vapors; snows hide his shoulders; from beneath his chin the founts of rolling streams begin their race; a beard of ice hangs upon his large breast. Here, poised upon his wings, the god descended; then, rested thus, from the towering height he plunged downward with precipitated flight, alighted on the seas, and skimmed along the flood. As waterfowl, seeking their fishy food, show less and less to distant prospect; by turns they dance aloft, and dive below—like these, he plied the steerage of his wings, and flew near the surface of the water, until, having passed the seas and crossed the sands, he closed his wings, and stooped upon the Libyan lands, where shepherds were once housed in homely sheds, but now towers advance their heads within the clouds. Arriving there, he found the Trojan prince raising new ramparts for the town's defense. He wore around his waist a purple scarf embroidered over with gold (Queen Dido's gift); a sword, diversified with glittering gems, for ornament, not use, hung idly by his side.

Then the god began thus, with winged words, resuming his own shape: "Degenerate man, woman's property, what are you doing here, raising these foreign walls and Tyrian towers, forgetful of your own? All-powerful Jove, who sways the world below and heaven above, has sent me down with this severe command: what do you mean by lingering in the Libyan land? If glory cannot move so mean a mind, nor future praise wean you from fleeting pleasure, regard the fortunes of your rising heir. Let young Ascanius wear the promised crown, to whom the Ausonian scepter, and the state of Rome's imperial name, is owed by fate." So spoke the god; and, speaking, took his flight, wrapped in clouds, and vanished out of sight.

The pious prince was seized with sudden fear; mute was his tongue, and upright stood his hair. Revolving the stern command in his mind, he longed to flee, and loathed the charming land. What should he say? Or how should he begin? What course, alas, remained to steer between the offended lover and the powerful queen? This way and that he turned his anxious mind, and tried all expedients, and could find none. Fixed on the deed, but doubtful of the means, after long thought he leaned to this advice: he called three chiefs, and commanded them to repair the fleet, and ship their men with silent care; he bade them find some plausible pretense, to color what he had secretly designed. He himself, meanwhile, would choose the softest hours, before the love-sick lady heard the news, to move her tender mind by slow degrees, to accept what the sovereign power decreed; Jove would inspire him, when and what to say. They heard with pleasure, and obeyed in haste.

But soon the queen perceived the thin disguise (what arts can blind a jealous woman's eyes?). She was the first to find the secret fraud, before the fatal news was blazed abroad. Love hears the first motions of the lover, quick to presage, and fearful even in safety. Nor was impious Fame lacking to report the ships repaired, the Trojans' thick resort, and their purpose to forsake the Tyrian court. Frantic with fear, impatient of the wound, and impotent of mind, she roved the city round. The Bacchanalian dames appear less wild, when from afar they hear their nightly god, and howl about the hills, and shake the wreathed spear. At length she found the dear perfidious man; preventing his formed excuse, she began: "Base and ungrateful! Could you hope to flee, and escape a lover's eye undiscovered? Could my kindness not move your compassion? Neither plighted vows, nor dearer bonds of love? Or is the death of a despairing queen not worth preventing, though too well foreseen? Even when the wintry winds command your stay, you dare the tempests and defy the sea. False as you are, suppose you were not bound to unknown lands, and foreign coasts to sound; were Troy restored, and Priam's happy reign, would you now dare the raging main for Troy? See whom you flee from! Am I the foe you shun? Now, by those holy vows so lately begun, by this right hand (since I have nothing more to claim but the faith you gave before), I beg you by these tears too truly shed, by the new pleasures of our nuptial bed: if ever Dido, when you were most kind, was pleasing in your eyes, or touched your mind; by these my prayers, if prayers may yet have place, pity the fortunes of a falling race. For you I have provoked a tyrant's hate, incensed the Libyan and the Tyrian state; for you alone I suffer in my fame, bereft of honor, and exposed to shame. Whom have I now to trust, ungrateful guest? (That only name remains of all the rest!) What have I left? Or where can I flee? Must I attend Pygmalion's cruelty, or wait until Hyarbas shall lead in triumph a queen who proudly scorned his proffered bed? Had you deferred, at least, your hasty flight, and left behind some pledge of our delight, some babe to bless the mother's mournful sight, some young Aeneas, to supply your place, whose features might express his father's face—I should not then complain to live bereft of all my husband, or be wholly left."

Here the queen paused. Unmoved he held his eyes, by Jove's command; nor suffered love to rise, though heaving in his heart; and thus at length he replied: "Fair queen, you can never recount your boundless favors enough, nor can I own my debt enough; nor can my mind forget Eliza's name while vital breath inspires this mortal frame. Only let me speak this in my defense: I never hoped a secret flight from here, much less pretended to the lawful claim of sacred nuptials, or a husband's name. For, if indulgent Heaven would leave me free, and not submit my life to fate's decree, my choice would lead me to the Trojan shore, to review those relics, to adore their dust, and to restore Priam's ruined palace. But now the Delphian oracle commands, and fate invites me to the Latian lands. That is the promised place to which I steer, and all my vows are terminated there. If you, a Tyrian and a stranger born, adorn a Libyan town with walls and towers, why may not we, like you, a foreign race, like you, seek shelter in a foreign place? As often as the night obscures the skies with humid shades, or twinkling stars arise, the angry ghost of Anchises appears in my dreams, chides my delay, and fills my soul with fears. And young Ascanius may justly complain of his defrauded and destined reign. Even now the herald of the gods appeared: waking I saw him, and heard his message. He came commissioned from Jove, heavenly bright with radiant beams, and manifest to sight (I attest both the sender and the sent): he entered these walls, and uttered those words. Fair queen, do not oppose what the gods command; forced by my fate, I leave your happy land."

Thus while he spoke, she had already begun, with sparkling eyes, to look upon the guilty man; she surveyed his person from head to foot, and no longer forbore these outrageous threats: "False as you are, and more than false, forsworn! Not sprung from noble blood, nor goddess-born, but hewn from the hardened entrails of a rock! And rough Hyrcanian tigers gave you suck! Why should I fawn? What have I worse to fear? Did he once look, or lend a listening ear, sigh when I sobbed, or shed one kindly tear? All symptoms of a base ungrateful mind—so foul that, what is worse, it is hard to find. Why should I complain of man's injustice? The gods, and Jove himself, behold in vain triumphant treason; yet no thunder flies, nor does Juno view my wrongs with equal eyes. Faithless is earth, and faithless are the skies! Justice is fled, and Truth is now no more! I saved the shipwrecked exile on my shore; I fed his hungry Trojans with needful food; I took the traitor to my throne and bed. Fool that I was—it is little to repeat the rest; I stored and rigged his ruined fleet. I rave, I rave! He pleads a god's command, and makes Heaven accessory to his deeds. Now it is Lycian lots, now the Delian god; now Hermes is employed from Jove's abode to warn him hence—as if the peaceful state of heavenly powers were touched with human fate! But go! I no longer detain your flight; go seek your promised kingdom through the main! Yet, if the heavens will hear my pious vow, the faithless waves—not half so false as you—or secret sands, shall afford sepulchers to your proud vessels, and their perjured lord. Then shall you call on injured Dido's name: Dido shall come in a black sulphurous flame, when death has once dissolved her mortal frame; she shall smile to see the traitor vainly weep. Her angry ghost, arising from the deep, shall haunt you waking, and disturb your sleep. At least my shade shall know your punishment, and Fame shall spread the pleasing news below."

Abruptly here she stops; then turns away her loathing eyes, and shuns the sight of day. Amazed he stood, revolving in his mind what speech to frame, and what excuse to find. Her fearful maids led their fainting mistress, and softly laid her on her ivory bed.

But good Aeneas, though he much desired to give the pity her grief required—though he mourned much, and labored with his love—resolved at length to obey the will of Jove. He reviewed his forces; they, with early care, unmoored their vessels, and prepared for sea. The fleet was soon afloat in all its pride, and well-caulked galleys rode in the harbor. They felled oaks for oars, or, as they stood, despoiled the growing wood of its green arms, studious of flight. The beach was covered all over with Trojan bands that blackened the entire shore; on every side were seen, descending downward, thick swarms of soldiers, laden from the town. Thus, in battle array, embodied ants march, fearful of winter and of future wants, to invade the corn, and convey to their cells the plundered forage of their yellow prey. The sable troops, along the narrow tracks, scarcely bear the weighty burden on their backs; some set their shoulders to the ponderous grain; some guard the spoil; some lash the lagging train; all ply their several tasks, and sustain equal toil.

What pangs tore the tender breast of Dido, when from the tower she saw the covered shore, and heard the shouts of sailors from afar, mixed with the murmurs of the watery war! All-powerful Love! What changes can you cause in human hearts, subjected to your laws! Once more the tyrant bent her haughty soul: to prayers and mean submissions she descended. No female arts or aids she left untried, no counsels unexplored, before she died. "Look, Anna! Look! The Trojans crowd to sea; they spread their canvas, and weigh their anchors. The shouting crew bind their ships with garlands, invoke the sea gods, and invite the wind. Could I have thought this threatening blow so near, my tender soul would have been forewarned to bear it. But do not deny my last request. Try your influence with that perfidious man, and bring me news whether I must live or die. You are his favorite; you alone can find the dark recesses of his inmost mind. You have a part in all his trusted secrets, and know the soft approaches to his heart. Haste, then, and humbly seek my haughty foe; tell him, I did not go with the Greeks, nor did I employ my fleet against his friends, nor did I swear the ruin of unhappy Troy, nor did I disturb his father's dust with profane hands. Why then should he reject so just a suit? Whom does he shun? Where would he flee? Can he deny this last, this only prayer? Let him at least delay his dangerous flight, wait for better winds, and hope for a calmer sea. I no longer urge the nuptials he disclaims; let him pursue the promised Latian shore. A short delay is all I ask of him now; a pause from grief, an interval from woe, till my soft soul is tempered to sustain its accustomed sorrows, and inured to pain. If you, in pity, grant this one request, my death shall glut the hatred of his breast." Pious Anna bore this mournful message, and seconded her sister's tears with her own; but all her arts were still employed in vain. Again she came, and again she was refused. His hardened heart neither prayers nor threatenings could move; Fate, and the god, had stopped his ears to love.

As when the winds try their airy quarrel, jostling from every quarter of the sky, they bend the mountain oak this way and that, shatter his boughs, and rend his branches; they spread the ground with leaves and falling mast; the hollow valleys echo to the sound. Unmoved, the royal plant mocks their fury, or, shaken, clings more closely to the rocks. As far as he shoots his towering head on high, so deep in earth his fixed foundations lie. No less a storm does the Trojan hero bear; thick messages and loud complaints he hears, and bandied words, still beating on his ears. Sighs, groans, and tears proclaim his inward pains; but the firm purpose of his heart remains.

The wretched queen, pursued by cruel fate, began at length to hate the light of heaven, and loathed to live. Then she saw dire portents to hasten the death her soul decreed. Strange to relate: for when, before the shrine, she poured the purple wine in sacrifice, the purple wine turned into putrid blood, and the white offered milk into mud. This dire presage, revealed to her alone, she concealed from all, even from her sister. A marble temple stood within the grove, sacred to death, and to her murdered love; that honored chapel she had hung around with snowy fleeces, and crowned with garlands. Often, when she visited this lonely dome, strange voices issued from her husband's tomb; she thought she heard him summon her away, invite her to his grave, and chide her stay. Every hour it was heard, when with a boding note the solitary screech owl strained her throat, and, on a chimney's top, or a turret's height, disturbed the silence of the night with obscene songs. Besides, old prophecies augmented her fears; and stern Aeneas appeared in her dreams, as disdainful as by day. She seemed, alone, to wander in her sleep, through ways unknown, guideless and dark; or, on a desert plain, to seek her subjects, and to seek in vain; like Pentheus, when, distracted with his fear, he saw two suns and double Thebes appear; or mad Orestes, when his mother's ghost tossed infernal torches full in his face, and shook her snaky locks: he shuns the sight, flies over the stage, surprised with mortal fright; the Furies guard the door and intercept his flight.

Now, sinking under a load of grief, she sought her last relief from death alone. Resolved in her breast on the time and means, she addressed her mournful sister thus (dissembling hope, she cleared her cloudy brow, and a false vigor appeared in her eyes): "Rejoice!" she said. "Instructed from above, I shall gain my lover, or lose my love. Near rising Atlas, next the falling sun, long tracts of Ethiopian climates run; there I have found a Massylian priestess, honored for age, renowned for magic arts: the Hesperian temple was her trusted care; it was she who supplied the food of the wakeful dragon. She taught poppy seeds to steep in honey, reclaimed his rage, and soothed him into sleep. She watched the golden fruit; her charms unbind the chains of love, or fix them on the mind; she stops the torrents, leaves the channel dry, repels the stars, and bears the sky backward; the yawning earth rebellows to her call; pale ghosts ascend, and mountain ashes fall. Witness, you gods, and you, my better part, how loth I am to try this impious art! Within the secret court, with silent care, erect a lofty pile, exposed in the air. Hang on the topmost part the Trojan vest, the spoils, arms, and presents, of my faithless guest. Next, under these, place the bridal bed, where I embraced my ruin in his arms. All relics of the wretch are doomed to fire, for so the priestess and her charms require."

Thus far she spoke, and forbore further speech; a mortal paleness appeared in her face. Yet the mistrustless Anna could not find the secret funeral designed in these rites, nor thought so dire a rage possessed her mind. Unknowing of a train concealed so well, she feared no worse than when Sichaeus fell; therefore she obeyed. They reared the fatal pile within the secret court, exposed in the air. The cloven holm-oaks and pines were heaped on high, and garlands lay on the hollow spaces. Sad cypress, vervain, and yew composed the wreath, and every baleful green denoting death. The queen, determined to the fatal deed, spread the spoils and sword he had left, in order, and the man's image on the nuptial bed.

And now (the sacred altars placed around) the priestess entered, with her hair unbound, and thrice invoked the powers below the ground. She proclaimed Night, Erebus, and Chaos, and threefold Hecate with her hundred names, and three Dianas; next, she sprinkled the hallowed ground with feigned Avernian drops; she culled hoary herbs, found by Phoebe's light, reaped with brazen sickles at noon of night; then she mixed baleful juices in the bowl, and cut the forehead of a newborn foal, robbing the mother's love. The destined queen observed, assisting at the obscene rites. A leavened cake she held in her devoted hands, and stood next to the highest altar; one of her tender feet was shod, the other bare; her gathered gown was girt, and her hair was loose. Thus dressed, she summoned, with her dying breath, the heavens and planets conscious of her death, and every power, if any rules above, who minds, or who avenges, injured love.

It was the dead of night, when weary bodies close their eyes in balmy sleep and soft repose: the winds no longer whispered through the woods, nor murmuring tides disturbed the gentle floods. The stars moved in silent order around; and Peace, with downy wings, was brooding on the ground. The flocks and herds, and party-colored fowl that haunt the woods or swim the weedy pool, lay stretched on the quiet earth, securely, forgetting the past labors of the day. All else shared in nature's common gift; unhappy Dido alone was awake. Neither sleep nor ease could the furious queen find; sleep fled her eyes, as quiet fled her mind. Despair, and rage, and love divided her heart; despair and rage had some of it, but love the greater part.

Then thus she said within her secret mind: "What shall I do? What aid can I find? Shall I become a suppliant to Hyarbas' pride, and take my turn to court and be denied? Shall I go with this ungrateful Trojan, forsake an empire, and attend a foe? Myself I refuged, and I relieved his train; it is true; but am I sure to be received? Can gratitude have any place in Trojan souls? Laomedon still lives in all his race! Then, shall I seek the churlish crew alone, or pursue their flying sails with my fleet? What force have I, but those I scarcely before drew reluctant from their native shore? Will they embark again at my desire, once more sustain the seas, and quit their second Tyre? Rather, with steel invade your guilty breast, and take the fortune you yourself have made. Your pity, sister, first seduced my mind, or seconded too well what I designed. Had I never known these dear-bought pleasures, had I continued free, and still my own, avoiding love, I would not have found despair, but would have shared the common air with savage beasts. Like them, I might have led a lonely life, not mourned the living, nor disturbed the dead." These thoughts she brooded in her anxious breast. On board, the Trojan found easier rest. Resolved to sail, he passed the night in sleep, and ordered all things for his early flight.

To whom once more the winged god appeared; he wore his former youthful mien and shape, and with this new alarm invaded his ears: "Do you sleep, O goddess-born! And can you drown your needful cares, so near a hostile town, beset with foes? Nor do you hear the western gales inviting your passage, and inspiring your sails? She harbors a furious hate in her heart, and you shall find its dire effects too late, fixed on revenge, and obstinate to die. Haste swiftly hence, while you have power to flee. The sea will soon be covered with ships, and blazing firebrands will kindle all the shore. Forestall her rage, while night obscures the skies, and sail before the purple morn arise. Who knows what hazards your delay may bring? A woman is a various and a changeful thing." Thus Hermes in the dream; then he took his flight, unseen, aloft in air, and mixed with night.

Twice warned by the celestial messenger, the pious prince arose with hasty fear, then roused his drowsy train without delay: "Haste to your benches; weigh your crooked anchors, spread your flying sails, and stand to sea. A god commands: he stood before my sight, and urged us once again to speedy flight. O sacred power, whatever power you are, I resign my heart to your blest orders. Lead the way; protect your Trojan bands, and prosper the design your will commands." He said, and drawing forth his flaming sword, his thundering arm divided the many-twisted cord. An emulating zeal inspired his train: they ran, they snatched, they rushed into the main. With headlong haste they left the deserted shores, and brushed the liquid seas with laboring oars.

Aurora had now left her saffron bed, and beams of early light overspread the heavens, when, from a tower, the queen with wakeful eyes saw the day point upward from the rosy skies. She looked seaward; but the sea was empty, and she scarcely descried the sailing ships in sight. Stung with resentment, and furious with despair, she struck her trembling breast and tore her hair. "And shall the ungrateful traitor go," she said, "my land forsaken, and my love betrayed? Shall we not arm? Not rush from every street, to follow, sink, and burn his perjured fleet? Haste, haul out my galleys! Pursue the foe! Bring flaming brands! Set sail, and swiftly row! What have I said? Where am I? Fury turns my brain; and my distempered bosom burns. Then, when I gave my person and my throne, this hate, this rage, should have been more timely shown. See now the promised faith, the vaunted name, the pious man, who, rushing through the flame, preserved his gods, and bore to the Phrygian shore the burden of his feeble father! I should have torn him piecemeal; strewn in floods his scattered limbs, or left them exposed in woods; destroyed his friends and son, and, from the fire, set the reeking boy before the sire. Events are doubtful, which depend on battles; yet where's the doubt to souls secure of fate? My Tyrians, at their injured queen's command, would have tossed their fires among the Trojan band; at once have extinguished all the faithless name; and I myself, in vengeance of my shame, would have fallen upon the pile, to mend the funeral flame. You Sun, who view at once the world below; you Juno, guardian of the nuptial vow; you Hecate, hearken from your dark abodes! You Furies, fiends, and violated gods, all powers invoked with Dido's dying breath, attend her curses and avenge her death! If so the Fates ordain, Jove commands, that the ungrateful wretch should find the Latian lands, yet let a race untamed, and haughty foes, oppose his peaceful entrance with dire arms; oppressed with numbers in the unequal field, his men discouraged, and himself expelled, let him sue for succor from place to place, torn from his subjects, and from his son's embrace. First let him see his friends slain in battle, and lament their untimely fate in vain; and when, at length, the cruel war shall cease, let him buy his peace on hard conditions; nor let him then enjoy supreme command, but fall, untimely, by some hostile hand, and lie unburied on the barren sand! These are my prayers, and this my dying will; and you, my Tyrians, fulfill every curse. Proclaim perpetual hate and mortal wars against the prince, the people, and the name. These grateful offerings bestow on my grave; let the hostile nations know neither league nor love! Now, and from hence, in every future age, when rage excites your arms, and strength supplies the rage, let some avenger of our Libyan blood arise, with fire and sword to pursue the perjured brood; our arms, our seas, our shores, opposed to theirs; and let the same hate descend on all our heirs!"

Having said this, she weighed in her anxious mind the means of cutting short her odious days. Then to Sichaeus' nurse she briefly said (for, when she left her country, her own nurse was dead): "Go, Barce, call my sister. Let her care prepare the solemn rites of sacrifice; bring the sheep, and all the atoning offerings, sprinkling her body from the crystal spring with living drops; then let her come, and do you bind your hoary brow with the sacred fillets. Thus will I pay my vows to Stygian Jove, and end the cares of my disastrous love; then I will cast the Trojan image on the fire, and, as that burns, my passions shall expire."

The nurse moved onward, with officious care, and all the speed her aged limbs could bear. But furious Dido, involved in dark thoughts, shook at the mighty mischief she had resolved. Her face was distinguished with livid spots; her rolling eyes were red, and her pace disordered; she gazed ghastly, drew her breath with pain, and nature shivered at her approaching death.

Then swiftly she passed to the fatal place, and mounted the funeral pile with furious haste; she unsheathed the sword the Trojan had left behind (not designed for so dire an enterprise). But when she viewed the garments loosely spread, which he once had worn, and saw the conscious bed, she paused, and with a sigh embraced the robes; then she cast her trembling body on the couch, repressed the ready tears, and spoke her last: "Dear pledges of my love, while Heaven so pleased, receive a soul eased of its mortal anguish. My fatal course is finished; and I go, a glorious name, among the ghosts below. A lofty city is raised by my hands; Pygmalion is punished, and my lord is appeased. What more could my fortune have afforded, had the false Trojan never touched my shore?" Then she kissed the couch, and, "Must I die," she said, "and unrevenged? It is doubly to be dead! Yet even this death I receive with pleasure. On any terms, it is better than to live. May the false Trojan view these flames from afar; may these boding omens pursue his base flight!"

She said, and struck; the piercing steel entered deep into her side, dyed with reeking purple. The cruel weapon stood clogged in the wound; the spouting blood came streaming on her hands. Her sad attendants saw the deadly stroke, and with loud cries shook the sounding palace. Distracted, they fled from the fatal sight, and the dismal rumor spread through the town. First the yell began from the frightened court; then, redoubled, it ran from house to house. The groans of men, with shrieks, laments, and cries of mingling women, mounted the vaulted skies. The clamor was no less than if ancient Tyre, or the new Carthage, had been set on fire by foes, and the rolling ruin, with their beloved abodes, had involved the blazing temples of their gods.

Her sister heard; and, furious with despair, she beat her breast, and tore her yellow hair, and, calling aloud on Eliza's name, ran breathless to the place, and broke through the crowd. "Was all that pomp of woe prepared for this? These fires, this funeral pile, these altars reared? Was all this train of plots contrived," she said, "only to deceive unhappy me? Which is worse? Did you, in death, pretend to scorn your sister, or delude your friend? Your summoned sister, and your friend, would have come; one sword would have served us both, one common tomb. Was I to raise the pile, to invoke the powers, and not to be present at the fatal stroke? At once you have destroyed yourself and me, your town, your senate, and your colony! Bring water; bathe the wound; while I, in death, lay my lips close to hers, and catch the flying breath." Having said this, she mounted the pile with eager haste, and embraced the gasping queen in her arms; she chafed her temples, and tore her own garments, to stanch the streaming blood and cleanse the gore. Three times Dido tried to raise her drooping head, and three times, fainting, fell groveling on the bed; three times opened her heavy eyes, and sought the light, but, having found it, sickened at the sight, and closed her lids at last in endless night.

Then Juno, grieving that she should sustain a death so lingering, and so full of pain, sent Iris down, to free her from the strife of laboring nature, and to dissolve her life. For since she died, not doomed by Heaven's decree, or by her own crime, but by human casualty, and by the rage of love that plunged her in despair, the Sisters had not cut the topmost hair, which Proserpine and they alone can know, nor made her sacred to the shades below. Downward the many-colored goddess took her flight, and drew a thousand colors from the light. Then she stood above the dying lover's head, and said: "I thus devote you to the dead. This offering I bear to the infernal gods." Thus while she spoke, she cut the fatal hair; the struggling soul was loosed, and life dissolved into air.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: Aeneas, setting sail from Africa, is driven by a storm upon the coast of Sicily, where he is hospitably received by his friend Acestes, king of part of the island, and born of Trojan parentage. He applies himself to celebrate his father's memory with divine honors, and accordingly institutes funeral games, appointing prizes for those who should conquer in them. While the ceremonies are being performed, Juno sends Iris to persuade the Trojan women to burn the ships. Upon her instigation, they set fire to them, burning four, and would have consumed the rest, had not Jupiter, by a miraculous shower, extinguished it. Upon this, Aeneas, by the advice of one of his generals, and a vision of his father, builds a city for the women, old men, and others, who were either unfit for war, or weary of the voyage, and sails for Italy. Venus procures from Neptune a safe voyage for him and all his men, except only for his pilot Palinurus, who was unfortunately lost.

Meanwhile the Trojan cut his watery way through the curling sea, fixed on his voyage. Then, casting back his eyes, he saw with dire amazement the mounting blaze on the Punic shore. The cause was unknown to him; yet his presaging mind divined Dido's fate from the fire. He knew the stormy souls of womankind, what secret springs move their eager passions, and how capable they are of death for injured love. From this the Trojans drew dire auguries, until they could see neither fires nor shining shores. Now only seas and skies bounded their prospect—an empty space above, a floating field around. But soon the heavens were overspread with shadows; a swelling cloud hung hovering over their heads, livid in appearance, the threatening of a storm. Then night and horror deformed the face of the ocean. The pilot, Palinurus, cried aloud: "What gusts of weather from that gathering cloud my thoughts presage! Before the tempest roars, stand to your tackle, mates, and stretch your oars; contract your swelling sails, and luff to the wind." The frightened crew performed the task assigned. Then, to his fearless chief he said: "Not Heaven, though Jove himself should promise Italy, can stem the torrent of this raging sea. Mark how the shifting winds rise from the west, and what collected night envelops the skies! Our shaken vessels cannot live at sea, much less force their way against the tempest. It is Fate that diverts our course, and Fate we must obey. Not far from here, if I observed the southing of the stars and the polar light aright, lies Sicily, whose hospitable shores we may reach in safety with struggling oars." Aeneas then replied: "Too surely I find we strive in vain against the seas and wind. Now shift your sails; what place can please me more than what you promise—the Sicilian shore, whose hallowed earth contains the bones of Anchises, and where a prince of Trojan lineage reigns?" The course resolved, they scudded amain before the western wind, and made the port assigned. Meanwhile Acestes, from a lofty stand, beheld the fleet descending on the land; and, not unmindful of his ancient race, he ran down from the cliff with eager pace, and held the hero in a close embrace. He wore the spoils of a rough Libyan bear, and bore a pointed javelin in each hand. His mother was a dame of Dardan blood; his sire was Crinisus, a Sicilian river. He welcomed his returning friends ashore with plentiful country fare and homely store.

Now, when the following morn had chased away the flying stars and restored the light of day, Aeneas called the Trojan troops around him, and thus addressed them from a rising ground: "Offspring of heaven, divine Dardanian race! The sun, revolving through the ethereal space, has filled the shining circle of the year since this island first held my father's ashes. And now the rising day renews the year: a day forever sad, forever dear. I would celebrate this with annual games, with gifts piled on altars, and holy flames, even though I were banished to Gaetulia's barren sands, or caught on the Grecian seas, or in hostile lands. But since this happy storm has driven our fleet (not, as I deem, without the will of Heaven) upon these friendly shores and flowery plains, which hide Anchises and his blessed remains, let us joyfully perform the honors due to him, and pray for prosperous winds to renew our voyage; let us pray that the name of great Anchises may be known in towns and temples of our own, and that yearly games may spread the gods' renown. Acestes, of the Trojan race, is pleased to grace our sports with royal gifts ordained: the king bestows two steers on every ship; his gods and ours shall share in your equal vows. Besides, if nine days hence the rosy morn shall adorn the skies with unclouded light, I mean to grace that day with solemn sports. Light galleys shall run a watery race on the seas; some shall contend in swiftness for the goal, and others shall try to bend the twanging bow; the strong, armed with iron gauntlets, shall stand opposed in combat on the yellow sand. Let all be present at the games prepared, and let joyful victors await their just reward. But now assist the rites, crowned with garlands." So he said, and first he bound his brows with myrtle. Then Helymus, led by his example, and old Acestes, each adorned his head; thus young Ascanius, with sprightly grace, tied his temples, and so did all the Trojan race.

Aeneas then advanced amidst the train, followed by thousands through the flowery plain, to the tomb of great Anchises. When he found it, he poured out, on the hallowed ground, two bowls of sparkling wine to Bacchus, two more of milk, and two of purple gore from offered bulls. He then strewed the sepulcher with roses, and thus addressed his father's ghost aloud: "Hail, O holy manes! Hail again, paternal ashes, now revisited in vain! The gods did not permit that you, with me, should reach the promised shores of Italy, or the flood of Tiber, whatever flood it may be." He had scarcely finished, when a serpent began to glide from the tomb, with speckled pride; his huge bulk rolled in seven high coils. Blue was his broad back, but streaked with scaly gold; riding thus on his own curls, he seemed to pass as a rolling fire along, and to singe the grass. More various colors ran through his body than Iris wears when her bow drinks in the sun. Between the rising altars, and around them, the sacred monster darted along the ground; with harmless play he passed amidst the bowls, and assayed the taste with his lolling tongue; thus fed with holy food, the wondrous guest retired to rest within the hollow tomb. The pious prince, surprised at what he viewed, renewed the funeral honors with more zeal, doubtful whether this were the genius of the place, or the guardian of his father's sepulcher. He slew five sheep, according to the rites; as many swine, and steers of sable hue; he poured fresh generous wine from the goblets, and called upon his father's ghost, restored from hell. The glad attendants came in long order, offering their gifts at great Anchises' tomb. Some added more oxen; some divided the spoil; some placed the chargers on the grassy soil; some blew the fires, and broiled the offered entrails.

Now came the desired day. The skies were bright with the rosy luster of the rising light. The bordering people, roused by sounding fame of the Trojan feasts and of great Acestes' name, filled the crowded shore with acclamations, part to behold, and part to prove their skill. First, the gifts were placed in public view: green laurel wreaths, and palms, the victors' grace. Within the circle lay arms and tripods, ingots of gold and silver heaped on high, and vests embroidered with the Tyrian dye. Then the trumpet's clangor proclaimed the feast, and all prepared for their appointed games. First four galleys, bearing equal rowers, advanced and appeared in the watery lists. The speedy Dolphin, that outstrips the wind, bore Mnestheus, founder of the Memmian kind; Gyas commanded the vast bulk of the Chimaera, which stood rising like a towering city; three Trojans tugged at every laboring oar; three banks of sailors in three degrees she bore; beneath their sturdy strokes the billows roared. Sergesthus, who began the Sergian race, took the leading place in the great Centaur; Cloanthus stood on the sea-green Scylla, from whom Cluentius draws his Trojan blood.

Far in the sea, against the foaming shore, there stood a rock. The raging billows roared above his head in storms; but when it was clear, they uncurled their ridgy backs, and appeared at his foot. In peace, the gentle waters ran below; the cormorants lay basking above in the sun. On this rock the hero fixed an oak in sight, as a mark to guide the mariners aright. They were to make this the bearing point, and steer around the rock, to seek the former shores again. The lots decided their place. Above the rest, each leader shone in his Tyrian vest; the common crew crowned their temples with wreaths of poplar boughs, and shaded their sweaty brows. Their naked shoulders shone, besmeared with oil. All took their seats, and awaited the sounding sign. They gripped their oars, and every panting breast was raised by turns with hope, and by turns depressed with fear. The clangor of the trumpet gave the sign; at once they started, advancing in a line. With shouts the sailors rent the starry skies; lashed with their oars, the smoky billows rose; the briny main sparkled, and the vexed ocean boiled. Exact in time, they rowed with equal strokes; at once the brushing oars and brazen prows dashed up the sandy waves, and opened the depths below. Not fiery coursers in a chariot race invade the field at half so swift a pace; not the fierce driver lends the sounding lash with more fury, bending his pliant body low to the wheels before the stroke descends. The partial crowd divided their hopes and fears, and aided the favored side with eager shouts. Cries, murmurs, clamors, with a mixing sound, rebounded from woods to woods, from hills to hills.

Amid the loud applauses of the shore, Gyas outstripped the rest and sprang before them; Cloanthus, better manned, pursued him fast, but his over-masted galley checked his haste. The Centaur and the Dolphin brushed the brine with equal oars, advancing in a line; and now the mighty Centaur seemed to lead, and now the speedy Dolphin got ahead; now the rival vessels rowed board to board; the billows lapped the skies, and the ocean groaned beneath. They reached the mark; proud Gyas and his train rode in triumph as victors of the main. But, steering round, he ordered his pilot to stand closer to shore, and skim along the sand. "Let others bear out to sea!" Menoetes heard; but he feared the hidden shoals too cautiously, and, fearing, sought the deep, and still steered aloof. With louder cries the captain called again: "Bear toward the rocky shore, and shun the main." He spoke, and, speaking, saw at his stern bold Cloanthus drawing near the shelvings. Between the mark and him the Scylla stood, and plowed the flood in a closer compass. He passed the mark, and, wheeling, got before him. Gyas blasphemed the gods, devoutly swore, cried out for anger, and tore his hair. Mindless of others' lives (so high had his rising rage grown) and careless of his own, he drew the trembling dotard to the deck; then hoisted him up, and threw him overboard. This done, he seized the helm; his fellows cheered; he turned short upon the shelves, and madly steered.

Hardly did the plunging pilot raise his head, clogged with his clothes and cumbered with his years. Now dripping wet, he climbed the cliff with pain. The crowd, who saw him fall and float again, shouted from the distant shore, and laughed aloud to see his heaving breast disgorge the briny draught. The following Centaur and the Dolphin's crew renewed their vanished hopes of victory. While Gyas lagged, they kindled in the race to reach the mark. Sergesthus took the place; Mnestheus pursued; and while they wound around, he came up, not half his galley's length behind. Then, on the deck, he appeared among his mates, and thus cheered their drooping courage: "My friends, and heretofore Hector's followers, exert your vigor; tug the laboring oar; stretch to your strokes, my still unconquered crew, whom I drew from the flaming walls of Troy. In this, our common interest, let me find that strength of hand, that courage of mind, which you showed when you stemmed the strong Malean flood, and rowed over the broken billows of the Syrtes. I do not now seek to gain the foremost palm—though yet... but ah! that haughty wish is vain; let those enjoy it whom the gods ordain. But to be last, the laggards of all the race! Redeem yourselves and me from that disgrace." Now, one and all, they tugged amain; they rowed at the full stretch, and shook the brazen prow. The sea beneath them sank; their laboring sides swelled, and sweat ran down in guttering tides. Chance aided their daring with unhoped success: Sergesthus, eager to press his beak between the rival galley and the rock, shut up the unwieldy Centaur in the lock. The vessel struck; and, with the dreadful shock, she shivered her oars, and broke her head. The trembling rowers arose from their benches, and, anxious for themselves, renounced the prize. With iron poles they heaved her off the shores, and gathered their floating oars from the sea. The crew of Mnestheus, with elated minds, urged on their success, and called the willing winds; then they plied their oars, and cut their liquid way, taking a wider compass on the roomy sea. As, when a dove forsakes her rocky hold, roused in a fright, she shakes her sounding wings; the cavern rings with clattering; out she flies, and leaves her callow young, and cleaves the skies; at first she flutters, but at length she springs to smoother flight, and shoots upon her wings—so Mnestheus in the Dolphin cut the sea; and, flying with a force, that force assisted his way. He soon passed Sergesthus in the Centaur, wedged in the rocky shoals, and sticking fast. In vain Sergesthus implored him with cries, and tried in vain to row with shattered oars. Then Mnestheus bore down on Gyas, and outflew him; the ship, without a pilot, yielded the prize. Only unvanquished Scylla now remained; he pursued her, and strained all his vigor. Shouts rose from the favoring multitude; applauding Echo replied to the shouts; shouts, wishes, and applause ran rattling through the skies. The Scylla's crew heard these clamors with disdain, grudging much the praise, but more the robbed reward. Resolved to hold their own, they mended their pace, all obstinate to die, or to gain the race. Raised by success, the Dolphin ran swiftly; for those who believe they can conquer can. Both urged their oars, and Fortune supplied both, and both perhaps would have shared an equal prize; when Cloanthus held his hands toward the sea, and demanded succor from the watery powers: "Gods of the liquid realms on which I row! If, given by you, the laurel binds my brow, assist me in making me guilty of my vow! A snow-white bull shall be slain on your shore; his offered entrails shall be cast into the main; and ruddy wine, thrown from golden goblets, shall acknowledge your gracious gift and my return." The choir of nymphs, and Phorcus, from below, with virgin Panopea, heard his vow; and old Portunus, with his broad hand, pushed on and sped the galley to the land. Swift as a shaft or a winged wind, she flew, and, darting into port, obtained the prize.

The herald summoned all, and then proclaimed Cloanthus conqueror of the naval games. The prince crowned the victor's head with laurel, and three fat steers were led to his vessel as the ship's reward; with generous wine besides, and sums of silver, which the crew divided. The leaders were distinguished from the rest; the victor was honored with a nobler vest, where gold and purple strove in equal rows, and needlework bestowed its happy cost. There Ganymede was wrought with living art, chasing the trembling hart through Ida's groves: he seemed breathless, yet eager to pursue, when from aloft, in open view, the bird of Jove descended, and, pouncing on his prey, bore the boy away with crooked talons. In vain, with lifted hands and gazing eyes, his guards beheld him soaring through the skies, and his dogs pursued his flight with imitated cries.

Mnestheus was declared the second victor; and, summoned there, he shared the second prize: a coat of mail which brave Demoleus had borne, and which braver Aeneas had torn from his shoulders in single combat on the Trojan shore. This was ordained for Mnestheus to possess; in war for his defense, for ornament in peace. The gift was rich, and glorious to behold, but yet so ponderous with its plates of gold, that scarce two servants could sustain the weight; yet, loaded thus, Demoleus had pursued and lightly seized the Trojan train over the plain. The third, succeeding to the last reward, shared two goodly bowls of massy silver, with figures prominent, and richly wrought, and two brass cauldrons brought from Dodona.

Thus all, rewarded by the hero's hands, bound their conquering temples with purple bands. And now Sergesthus, clearing from the rock, brought back his galley shattered by the shock. Forlorn she looked, without an aiding oar, and, hooted by the common folk, made it to shore. As when a snake, surprised upon the road, is crushed athwart her body by the load of heavy wheels; or is bruised in the belly by a mortal wound, and trodden to the ground: in vain, with loosened curls, she crawls along; yet, fierce above, she brandishes her tongue; glares with her eyes, and bristles with her scales; but, groveling in the dust, she trails her unsound parts—so slowly did the Centaur make for port; but what she wanted in oars she amended with sails. Yet, for his galley saved, the grateful prince was pleased to recompense the unhappy chief. Pholoe, the Cretan slave, rewarded his care, beautiful herself, with lovely twins equally fair.

From there the Trojan hero bent his way into the neighboring plain, pent with mountains, whose sides were shaded with surrounding wood. Full in the midst of this fair valley stood a natural theater, which, rising slowly by just degrees, overlooked the ground below. High on a sylvan throne the leader sat; a numerous train attended in solemn state. Here, those who delighted in the rapid footrace were invited by the desire of honor and the prize. The rival runners stood in no particular order; Trojans mingled with the Sicilian band. First Nisus appeared, with Euryalus; Euryalus, a boy of blooming years, crowned with sprightly grace and equal beauty; Nisus, renowned for his friendship to the youth. Next came Diores, of Priam's royal race; then Salius, joined with Patron, took their place. But Patron had his birth in Arcadia, and Salius his from the Acarnanian earth; then two Sicilian youths—Swift Helymus, and lovely Panopes—both jolly huntsmen, both bred in forest, and owning old Acestes for their head; and several others of less notable name, whom time has not delivered over to fame.

To these, the hero thus explained his thoughts, in words that gained general approval: "One common largess is designed for all, vanquished and victor shall be joined: two darts of polished steel and Gnosian wood, and a silver-studded axe, alike bestowed. The foremost three shall have olive wreaths decreed; the first of these shall obtain a stately steed, adorned with trappings; the next in fame shall have the quiver of an Amazonian dame, well supplied with feathered Thracian arrows; a golden belt shall gird his manly side, which shall be tied with a sparkling diamond. The third shall be content with this Grecian helmet." He said. They went to their appointed base; with beating hearts they received the expected sign, and, starting all at once, they left the barrier. Spread out as on winged winds, they flew, and eyed the distant goal with greedy view. Shot from the crowd, swift Nisus overpassed all; not storms, not thunder, equal half his haste. The next, though far behind, was Salius; and after him Euryalus; then Helymus, whom young Diores plied step after step, and almost side by side, pressing his shoulders; and in a longer space would have won, or at least left a dubious race.

Now, spent, they were almost at the goal, when eager Nisus, hapless in his haste, slipped first, and, slipping, fell upon the plain, soaked with the blood of oxen newly slain. The careless victor had not marked his way; but, treading where the treacherous puddle lay, his heels flew up; and on the grassy floor he fell, besmeared with filth and holy gore. Not then was he mindless of you, Euryalus, nor of the sacred bonds of amity; he strove to cross the hope of the immediate rival, and caught the foot of Salius as he rose. So Salius lay extended on the plain; Euryalus sprang out to gain the prize, and left the crowd: applauding peals attended the victor to the goal, vanquished by his friend. Next came Helymus; and then Diores, made by two misfortunes the third in fame.

But Salius entered the court, exclaiming loudly for justice, deafening and disturbing the crowd. He urged that his case be heard in the court, and pleaded that the prize had been wrongfully conferred. But favor appeared for Euryalus: his blooming beauty, with his tender tears, had bribed the judges for the promised prize. Besides, Diores filled the court with cries, who reached vainly for the last reward, if the first palm were conferred on Salius. Then thus the prince: "Let no disputes arise; I award the prize where Fortune placed it. But give me leave to mend Fortune's errors, or at least to pity my deserving friend." He said, and from among the spoils he drew a lion's hide (ponderous with shaggy mane and golden paws), which he gave to Salius. Nisus saw the gift with envy, and grieved: "If such rewards are due to vanquished men," he said, "and falling is rising by your favor, what prize may Nisus claim from your bounty, who merited the first rewards and fame? In falling, both of us tried an equal fortune; would that Fortune would so well provide for my fall!" With this he pointed to his face, and showed his hand and all his garments smeared with blood. The indulgent father of the people smiled, and caused an ample shield to be produced, of wondrous art, wrought by Didymaon, long since brought in triumph from Neptune's bars. This he gave to Nisus; he divided the rest, and expressed equal justice in his gifts.

The race thus ended, and the rewards bestowed, the prince once more addressed the attentive crowd: "If there is here a man whose dauntless courage dares to sustain his opponent in open view, in the gauntlet fight, with limbs and body bare, let him stand forth as champion, and renew the games. I propose two prizes, and thus I divide them: a bull with gilded horns and tied fillets shall be the portion of the conquering chief; a sword and helmet shall cheer the loser's grief."

Then haughty Dares appeared in the lists; stalking, he strode with erect head; his sinewy arms wielded the weighty gauntlet, and loud applauses echoed through the field. Dares was used to standing alone in combat as the match of mighty Paris, hand to hand; the same man, at Hector's funerals, had undertaken the gigantic Butes, of the Amycian stock, and by the stroke of his resistless hand had stretched the vast bulk upon the yellow sand. Such was Dares; and thus he strode along, and drew the wonder of the gazing throng. He showed his brawny back and ample breast; he threw his lifted arms around his head, and dealt empty blows in the whistling air. His match was sought; but through the trembling band, not one dared answer his proud demand. Presuming on his force, with sparkling eyes, he already devoured the promised prize. He claimed the bull with awless insolence, and, having seized its horns, accosted the prince: "If none dares oppose my matchless valor, how long shall Dares wait for his dastard foes? Permit me, chief, permit without delay, to lead this uncontested gift away." The crowd assented, and with redoubled cries demanded the prize for the proud challenger.

Acestes, fired with just disdain to see the palm usurped without a victory, reproached Entellus, who sat beside him, and heard and saw, unmoved, the Trojan's pride: "Once, but in vain, a champion of renown, can you so tamely bear the ravished crown? A prize in triumph borne before your sight, and shun, for fear, the danger of the fight? Where is our Eryx now, the boasted name, the god who taught your thundering arm the game? Where now is your baffled honor? Where the spoil that filled your house, and the fame that filled our isle?" Entellus replied: "My soul is still the same, unmoved by fear, and moved by martial fame; but my chill blood is curdled in my veins, and scarcely the shadow of a man remains. O could I return to that fair prime again, that prime of which this boaster is so vain, the brave, who defies this decrepit age, should feel my force, without the promised prize."

He said; and, rising at the word, he threw down two ponderous gauntlets in open view; gauntlets which Eryx was wont to wield in fight, and with which he sheathed his hands in the listed field. With fear and wonder seized, the crowd beheld the gloves of death, with seven distinguished folds of tough bull hides; the space within was spread with iron, or with loads of heavy lead. Dares himself was daunted at the sight, renounced his challenge, and refused to fight. Astonished at their weight, the hero stood, and poised the ponderous engines in his hands. "What would your wonder have been," said Entellus, "had you seen the gauntlets of Alcides, or viewed the stern debate on this unhappy green! These which I bear your brother Eryx bore, still marked with battered brains and mingled gore. With these he long sustained the Herculean arm; and these I wielded while my blood was warm, while better spirits fed this languished frame, before age unstrung my nerves, or time oversnowed my head. But if the challenger refuses these arms, and cannot wield their weight, or dare not use them; if great Aeneas and Acestes join in his request, I resign these gauntlets. Let us perform the fight with equal arms, and let him leave his fear, since I resign my right."

Having said this, Entellus prepared for the strife; stripped of his quilted coat, he bared his body. Composed of mighty bones and brawn he stood, a goodly towering object on the sands. Then just Aeneas supplied equal arms, which they tied around their shoulders to their wrists. Both stood on tiptoe at their full extent, their arms aloft, their bodies inwardly bent; they held their heads far from aiming blows; with clashing gauntlets they then provoked the war. One relied on his youth and pliant limbs; the other on his sinews and his giant size. The latter was stiff with age, his motion slow; he heaved for breath; he staggered to and fro, and clouds of issuing smoke blew loudly from his nostrils. Yet equal in success, they warded, they struck; their ways were different, but their art alike. Before, behind, the blows were dealt; around their hollow sides the rattling thumps resounded. A storm of strokes, well meant, flew with fury, and erred about their temples, ears, and eyes. Nor did they always err: for often the gauntlet drew a sweeping stroke along the cracking jaws. Heavy with age, Entellus stood his ground, but warded the wound with his warping body. His hand and his watchful eye kept an even pace; while Dares traversed, and shifted his place, like a captain who besieges some strong-built castle on a rising ground, views all the approaches with observing eyes: this and that other part in vain he tries, and relies more on industry than on force. With his hands on high, Entellus threatened his foe; but Dares watched the motion from below, and slipped aside, and shunned the long descending blow. Entellus wasted his forces on the wind, and, thus deluded of his designed stroke, fell headlong and heavy; his ample breast and weighty limbs pressed his ancient mother. So falls a hollow pine that had long stood on Ida's height, or in Erymanthus' wood, torn from the roots. The different nations rose, and shouts and mingled murmurs rent the skies. Acestes ran with eager haste to raise the fallen companion of his youthful days. Undaunted, he rose, and returned to the fight; his glowing cheeks burned with shame, his eyes with fury. Disdain and conscious virtue fired his breast, and with redoubled force he pressed his foe. He laid on load with either hand, amain, and drove the Trojan headlong over the plain. He did not stop, nor stay; he allowed neither rest nor breath; but storms of strokes descended about his brows, a rattling tempest, and a hail of blows. But now the prince, who saw the wild increase of wounds, commanded the combatants to cease, bounded Entellus' wrath, and bade peace. First to the Trojan, spent with toil, he came, and soothed his sorrow for the shame he had suffered. "What fury seized my friend?" he said. "The gods, propitious to him, and averse to you, have given his arm a force superior to yours. It is madness to contend with strength divine." The gauntlet fight thus ended; his faithful friends bore unhappy Dares from the shore. His mouth and nostrils poured out a purple flood, and pounded teeth came rushing with his blood. Faintly he staggered through the hissing throng, hung his head, and trailed his legs along. The sword and casque were carried by his train; but the palm and the ox remained with his foe.

The champion then came before Aeneas, proud of his prize, but prouder of his fame: "O goddess-born, and you, Dardanian host, mark with attention, and forgive my boast. Learn what I was, by what remains, and know from what impending fate you saved my foe." Sternly he spoke, and then confronted the bull; and, aiming full at his ample forehead, the deadly stroke, descending, pierced the skull. Down dropped the beast, nor needed a second wound, but sprawled in pangs of death, and spurned the ground. Then thus he said: "In Dares' stead, I offer this. Eryx, accept a nobler sacrifice; take the last gift my withered arms can yield: I resign your gauntlets, and here renounce the field."

This done, Aeneas ordered, for the close, the strife of archers with contending bows. With his own hands he raised on the shore the mast from Sergesthus' shattered galley. A fluttering dove was tied upon the top, the living mark at which their arrows would fly. The rival archers advanced in a line, to receive their turn of shooting from chance. A helmet held their names; the lots were drawn. On the first scroll was read Hippocoon; the people shouted. Upon the next was found young Mnestheus, late crowned with naval honors. The third contained the noble name of Eurytion, your brother, Pandarus, and next in fame—the man whom Pallas urged to confound the treaty, and to send a feathered wound among the Greeks. Acestes remained in the bottom last, not restrained by his age from youthful sports. Soon all, with vigor, bent their trusty bows, and each chose his arrow from the quiver. Hippocoon's was the first: with forceful sway it flew, and, whizzing, cut the liquid way. The feathered weapon stood fixed in the mast; the fearful pigeon fluttered in her bonds, and the tree trembled, and the shouting cries of the pleased people rent the vaulted skies. Then Mnestheus drove his arrow to the head; with lifted eyes he took his aim above, but made a glancing shot, and missed the dove; yet missed so narrowly, that he cut the cord that fastened the fluttering bird by the foot. The captive, thus released, flew away, and beat the yielding skies with clapping wings. With his bow already bent, Eurytion stood; and, having first invoked his brother god, he sped his winged shaft with eager haste. The fatal message reached her as she fled: she lost her life aloft; she struck the ground, and rendered back the weapon in the wound. Acestes, grudging at his lot, remained, without a prize to gratify his pains. Yet, shooting upward, he sent his shaft, to show an archer's art, and boast his twanging bow. The feathered arrow gave a dire portent, and later augurs judge from this event. Chafed by its speed, it caught fire; and as it flew, it drew a trail of following flames ascending; kindling, they mounted, and marked the shiny way; across the skies they played like falling meteors, and vanished into wind, or in a blaze decayed. The Trojans and Sicilians stared wildly, and, trembling, turned their wonder into prayer. The Dardan prince put on a smiling face, and strained Acestes in a close embrace; then, honoring him with gifts above the rest, turned the bad omen, nor confessed his fears. "The gods," he said, "have wrought this miracle, and ordained you the prize without the lot. Accept this goblet, rough with figured gold, which Thracian Cisseus gave my sire of old: receive this pledge of ancient amity, which I justly give to my second sire." He said; and, with the trumpets' cheerful sound, proclaimed him victor, and crowned him with laurel. Nor did good Eurytion envy him the prize, though he had transfixed the pigeon in the skies. He who cut the line was graced with second gifts; the third was his whose arrow pierced the mast.

Before the games were wholly done, the chief called Periphantes, tutor to his son, and whispered thus: "With speed find Ascanius; and if his childish troop is ready formed up, let him honor his grandsire's day on horseback, and lead his companions armed in just array." He said; and, calling out, cleared the ring. The crowd withdrawn, an open plain appeared. And now the noble youths, of form divine, advanced before their fathers in a line; the riders graced the steeds; the steeds shone with glory.

Thus, marching on in military pride, shouts of applause resounded from side to side. They wore casques adorned with laurel wreaths, each brandishing aloft a cornel spear. Some bore gilded quivers at their backs; their chains of burnished gold hung down before. They formed three graceful troops upon the green; three graceful leaders were seen at their head; twelve followed each chief, and left a space between. Young Priam led the first, a lovely boy, whose grandsire was the unhappy king of Troy. His race in after times was known to fame, adding new honors to the Latian name; and the royal boy well became his Thracian steed. The fetlocks of his forefeet were white, and on his forehead he bore a snowy star. Then beauteous Atys, bred with Iulus, of equal age, led the second squadron. Last in order, but first in place, first in the lovely features of his face, rode fair Ascanius on a fiery steed, Queen Dido's gift, and of the Tyrian breed. For the rest the king ordained sure coursers, adorned with golden bits and purple reins.

The pleased spectators renewed their peals of shouts, and all the parents viewed themselves in the children—their make, their motions, and their sprightly grace—with hopes and fears alternating on their faces.

The unfledged commanders and their martial train first made the circuit of the sandy plain around their sires, and, at the appointed sign, drew up in beauteous order and formed a line. At the second signal's sound, the troop divided into three distinguished parts, with three distinguished guides. Again they closed, and once again disjoined; troop opposed to troop, and line to line. They met; they wheeled; they threw their darts afar with harmless rage and well-dissembled war. Then in a round the mingled bodies ran: flying they followed, and pursuing they shunned; broken, they broke; and, rallying, they renewed the military show in other forms. At last, in order, undiscerned they joined, and marched together in a friendly line. And, as the Cretan labyrinth of old, with wandering ways and many a winding fold, involved the weary feet without redress, in a round error that denied recess—so fought the Trojan boys in warlike play, turned and returned, and still a different way. Thus dolphins in the deep chase each other in circles, when they swim around the watery race. This game, these carousels, Ascanius taught; and when he was building Alba, he brought it to the Latins. He showed them what he had learned; the Latin sires imparted the graceful art to their succeeding sons; from them imperial Rome received the game, and they call it 'Troy,' and the youths 'the Trojan troop.'

Thus far they celebrated the sacred sports; but Fortune soon resumed her ancient hate. For while they were paying the dead their annual dues, Saturnian Juno viewed these envied rites, and sent the goddess of the various bow to try new methods of revenge below; she supplied the winds to wing Iris' airy way, to where the navy lay secure in the port. Swiftly fair Iris descended from her arch, and, undiscerned, ended her fatal voyage. She saw the gathering crowd; and, gliding from there, saw the deserted shore and the fleet without defense. The Trojan matrons were on the sands alone, bemoaning Anchises' death with sighs and tears; then, turning their weeping eyes to the sea, their pity for themselves renewed their cries. "Alas," said one, "what oceans yet remain for us to sail! What labors to sustain!" All took up the word, and, with a general groan, implored the gods for peace, and for places of their own.

The goddess, great in mischief, viewed their pains, and restrained her heavenly limbs in a woman's form. In face and shape she became old Beroe, the wife of Doryclus, a venerable dame, once blest with riches and the name of mother. Thus changed, she ran amidst the crying crowd, mixed with the matrons, and began these words: "O wretched we, whom neither the Grecian power nor flames destroyed in Troy's unhappy hour! O wretched we, reserved by cruel fate beyond the ruins of the sinking state! Now seven revolving years are wholly run, since we began this unprosperous voyage; since, tossed from shore to shore, from land to land, through inhospitable rocks and barren sands, wandering in exile through the stormy sea, we have searched in vain for flying Italy. Now cast by Fortune on this kindred land, what should withstand our rest and our rising walls, or hinder us from fixing our banished band here? O country lost, and gods redeemed in vain, if we still remain in endless exile! Shall we no more renew the Trojan walls, or view the streams of some dissembled Simois? Haste, join with me, consume the unhappy fleet! Cassandra bids it; I declare her decree. I saw her in my sleep; she supplied my hands (this was more than a dream) with flaming brands: 'With these,' she said, 'destroy these wandering ships: these are your fatal seats, and this your Troy.' The time calls you now; employ the precious hour. Slacken not the good presage, while Heaven inspires our minds to dare, and gives the ready fires. See! Neptune's altars supply their brands; the god is pleased; the god supplies our hands." Then she drew a flaming firebrand from the pile, and, tossed in the air, threw it amid the galleys.

Wrapped in amazement, the matrons stared wildly. Then Pyrgo, reverenced for her hoary hair, Pyrgo, the nurse of Priam's numerous race: "This is not Beroe, though she belies her face! What terrors arise from her frowning front! Behold a goddess in her ardent eyes! What rays are seen around her heavenly face! Mark her majestic voice, and more than mortal mien! I just now left Beroe, pined with pain, whom her age and anguish detain from these rites." She said. The matrons, seized with new amazement, rolled their malignant eyes, and gazed on the navy. They feared, and hoped, and obeyed neither side: they hoped for the fated land, but feared the fatal way. The goddess, having done her task below, mounted up on equal wings, and bent her painted bow. Struck with the sight, and seized with rage divine, the matrons pursued their mad design; they shrieked aloud; with impious hands they snatched the food of altars, fires, and flaming brands. Green boughs and saplings, mingled in their haste, and smoking torches, they cast on the ships. The flame, unstopped at first, gained more fury, and Vulcan rode at large with loosened reins; he soared triumphant to the painted sterns, and seized, in this way, the benches and crackling oars. Eumelus was the first to bear the news, while they still crowded the rural theater. Then, what they heard was witnessed by their eyes: a storm of sparks and of flames arose. Ascanius took the alarm, while he still led his early warriors on his prancing steed, and, spurring on, soon outpaced his companions; nor could his frightened friends reclaim his haste. As soon as the royal youth appeared in view, he sent his voice before him as he flew: "What madness moves you, matrons, to destroy the last remainders of unhappy Troy! You burn not hostile fleets, but your own hopes, and turn your fatal fury on your friends. Behold your own Ascanius!" While he said this, he drew his glittering helmet from his head, in which he had led the youths to sportful arms. By this, Aeneas and his train appeared; and now the women, seized with shame and fear, dispersed, and took their flight to woods and caverns. They abhorred their actions, and avoided the light; they acknowledged their friends, and found their error, and shook the goddess from their altered mind.

Not so the raging fires cease their fury, but, lurking in the seams, with seeming peace, work their way amid the smoldering tow, sure in destruction, but slow in motion. The silent plague ate through the green timber, and vomited out a tardy flame by fits. Down to the keels, and upward to the sails, the fire descended, or mounted, but still prevailed; neither buckets poured, nor strength of human hand, could withstand the victorious element.

The pious hero rent his robe, and threw his hands, and with his hands his vows, to heaven. "O Jove," he cried, "if prayers can yet have place; if you do not abhor all the Dardan race; if any spark of pity still remains; if gods are gods, and not invoked in vain; yet spare the relics of the Trojan train! Yet free our burning vessels from the flames, or let your fury fall on me alone! Throw your thunder at this devoted head, and send the willing sacrifice below!"

He had scarcely spoken, when southern storms arose: from pole to pole the forked lightning flew; loud rattling shook the mountains and the plain; heaven bellied downward, and descended in rain. Whole sheets of water were sent from the clouds, which, hissing through the planks, prevented the flames, and stopped the fiery pest. Only four ships burned to the waterline, and atoned for the fleet.

But doubtful thoughts divided the hero's heart: whether he should still reside in Sicily, forgetful of his fates, or tempt the main, in hope of gaining the promised Italy. Then Nautes, old and wise, to whom alone the will of Heaven had been foreshown by Pallas; versed in portents, experienced, and inspired to tell events and what the fates required; while he stood, inclined to neither side, relieved his laboring mind with cheerful words: "O goddess-born, resigned in every state, bear your fate with patience, push it with prudence. By suffering well, we subdue our Fortune; flee when she frowns, and, when she calls, pursue. Your friend Acestes is of Trojan kind; to him disclose the secrets of your mind. Trust in his hands your old and useless train—too numerous for the ships that yet remain—the feeble, old, indulgent of their ease; the dames who dread the dangers of the seas; and all the dastard crew, who dare not stand the shock of battle against your foes by land. Here you may build a common town for all, and, from Acestes' name, call it Acesta." The reasons, joined with his friend's experience, encouraged much, but disturbed his mind more.

It was the dead of night; when to his slumbering eyes his father's shade descended from the skies, and thus he spoke: "O more than vital breath, loved while I lived, and dear even after death; O son, tossed in various toils and troubles, the King of Heaven employs my careful ghost on his commands—the god who saved your flaming fleet from fire, and heard your just desire. Receive the wholesome counsel of your friend, and here leave the cowardly train and the women. Transport the chosen youth, and those who nobly dare, to tempt the dangers of the war. The stern Italians will try their courage; their manners are rough, and their minds are high. But first you shall go to Pluto's palace, and seek my shade among the blessed below; for my soul does not remain with impious ghosts, nor does it suffer perpetual pains with the damned, but breathes the living air of soft Elysian plains. The chaste Sibyl shall convey your steps, and the blood of offered victims shall free the way. There you shall know what realms the gods assign, and learn the fates and fortunes of your line. But now, farewell! I vanish with the night, and feel the blast of heaven's approaching light." He said, and mingled with the shades, and took his airy flight. "Where so fast?" cried filial duty; "And why, ah why, deny the wished embrace?"

He said, and rose; as holy zeal inspired him, he raked hot embers and renewed the fires; then he adored his country gods and Vesta with cakes and incense, and implored their aid. Next he sent for his friends and his royal host, revealed his vision and the gods' intent, along with his own purpose. All, without delay, obeyed the will of Jove, and his desires. They listed with the women every degenerate name, who did not dare hazard life for future fame. These they dismissed; the brave remaining few renewed the oars, benches, and cables, half consumed. The prince designed a city with the plow; the lots allowed their several tenements. One part was named from Ilium, another from Troy; and the new king ascended the throne with joy. He drew a chosen senate from the people, appointed the judges, and ordained the laws. Then, on the top of Eryx, they began a rising temple to the Paphian queen. Anchises, last, was honored as a god; a priest was added, annual gifts were bestowed, and groves were planted around his blessed abode. Nine days they passed in feasts, their temples crowned; and fumes of incense abounded in the fanes. Then from the south arose a gentle breeze, which curled the smoothness of the glassy seas; the rising winds afforded a ruffling gale, and called the merry mariners aboard.

Now loud laments resounded along the shores, of parting friends bound in close embraces. The trembling women, the degenerate train who had shunned the frightful dangers of the main—even these desired to sail, and take their share of the rough passage and the promised war. Good Aeneas cheered them, and recommended his fearful friends to the care of their new master. On Eryx's altars he laid three fat calves; he offered a lamb new-fallen to the stormy seas. Then he slipped his hawsers, and weighed his anchors. High on the deck the godlike hero stood, crowned with olive, a charger in his hands; then he cast the reeking entrails into the brine, and poured the sacrifice of purple wine. Fresh gales arose; with equal strokes they vied, and brushed the buxom seas, and flew over the billows.

Meanwhile the mother goddess, full of fears, addressed Neptune thus with tender tears: "The pride of Jove's imperious queen, the rage, the malice that no sufferings can assuage, compel me to these prayers; since neither fate, nor time, nor pity, can remove her hate. Even Jove is thwarted by his haughty wife; she is still vanquished, yet she still renews the strife. As if it were too little to consume the town that awed the world and wore the imperial crown, she pursues the ghost of Troy with pains, and gnaws, even to the bones, the last remains. Let her tell the causes of her hatred; but you can witness its effects too well. You saw the storm she raised on Libyan floods, that mixed the mounting billows with the clouds; when, bribing Aeolus, she shook the main, and moved rebellion in your watery reign. With fury she possessed the Dardan dames, to burn their fleet with execrable flames, and forced Aeneas, when his ships were lost, to leave his followers on a foreign coast. For what remains, I implore your godhead, and trust my son to your protecting power. If neither Jove's nor Fate's decree withstands, secure his passage to the Latian land."

Then thus the mighty Ruler of the Main: "What may not Venus hope from Neptune's reign? My kingdom claims your birth; my recent defense of your endangered fleet may claim your confidence. My deeds declare, no less by land than by sea, how much your beloved Aeneas is my care. I call you to witness, Xanthus, and you, Simois. When proud Achilles pressed your Trojan troops, and drove them headlong before him on the plain, and dashed the trembling train against the walls; when the rivers were filled with the bodies of the slain; when crimson Xanthus, doubtful of his way, stood up on ridges to behold the sea; when new heaps came tumbling in, and choked his way; when your Aeneas fought, but fought with odds of unequal force, and unequal gods—then I spread a cloud before the victor's sight, sustained the vanquished, and secured his flight; even then I secured him, when I sought with joy the vowed destruction of ungrateful Troy. My will is the same: fair goddess, fear no more; your fleet shall safely gain the Latian shore. Their lives are given; only one destined head shall perish, and atone for the multitudes." Thus having armed her anxious mind with hopes, Saturnian Neptune yoked his finny team, then added the foamy bridle to their jaws, and gave the laws over to the loosened reins. High on the waves he guided his azure car; its axles thundered, and the sea subsided, and the smooth ocean rolled her silent tides. The tempests fled before their father's face; trains of inferior gods graced his triumph; and monster whales played before their master, and choirs of Tritons crowded the watery way. The marshaled powers divided in equal troops to right and left; the gods enclosed his better side, and the Nymphs and Nereids rode on the worse.

Now smiling Hope, with sweet vicissitude, renewed the hero's joys within his mind. He called to raise the masts, to display the sheets; the cheerful crew obeyed with diligence; they scudded before the wind, and sailed in the open sea. Ahead of all, the master pilot steered; and, as he led, the following navy veered.
