The steeds of Night had traveled half the sky; the drowsy rowers lay on their benches, when the soft God of Sleep, with easy flight, descended, and drew a trail of light behind him. You, Palinurus, were his destined prey; to you alone he took his fatal way. He bore to you dire dreams and iron sleep; and, lighting on your prow, he wore the form of Phorbas. Then thus the traitor god began his tale: "My friend, the winds inspire a pleasing gale; the ships sail securely without your care. Now steal an hour of sweet repose; and I will take the rudder, and supply your room." To whom the yawning pilot, half asleep: "Do you bid me trust the treacherous deep, the harlot smiles of her dissembling face, and commit the Trojan race to her faith? Shall I believe the Siren South again, and, often betrayed, not know the monster main?" He said: his fastened hands kept the rudder, and, fixed on heaven, his eyes repelled invading sleep. The god was wroth, and threw at his temples a branch dipped in Lethe, and drunk with Stygian dew. The pilot, vanquished by the divine power, soon closed his swimming eyes, and lay supine. Scarcely were his limbs extended at their length, when the god, insulting with superior strength, fell heavily upon him, plunged him in the sea, and tore away the rudder with the stern. Headlong he fell, and, struggling in the main, cried out for helping hands, but cried in vain. The victor demon mounted obscure in air, while the ship sailed without the pilot's care. The floating fleet relied on Neptune's faith; but what the man forsook, the god supplied, and the navy flew securely over the dangerous deep. It glided by the Sirens' cliffs, a shelvy coast, long infamous for ships and sailors lost, and white with bones. The impetuous ocean roared, and the rocks rebellowed from the sounding shores. The watchful hero felt the shocks, and found the tossing vessel sailing on shoal ground. Sure of his pilot's loss, he himself took the helm, and steered aloof, and shunned the shelf. Inly he grieved, and, groaning from the breast, deplored his death; and thus expressed his pain: "For faith reposed on seas, and on the flattering sky, your naked corpse is doomed to lie on unknown shores."

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: The Sibyl foretells to Aeneas the adventures he will meet with in Italy. She attends him to hell, describing to him the various scenes of that place, and conducting him to his father Anchises, who instructs him in those sublime mysteries of the soul of the world and of transmigration, and shows him that glorious race of heroes which was to descend from him and his posterity.

He spoke, and wept; then spread his sails before the winds, and at length reached the Cumaean shore. They dropped their anchors; his crew moored the vessels. They turned their heads to sea, their sterns to land, and greeted the Italian strand with greedy joy. Some struck their fiery seed from clashing flints; some gathered sticks to feed the kindled flames, or searched for hollow trees, and felled the woods, or traced the newly discovered streams through the valleys. Thus, while they fulfilled their several charges, the pious prince ascended the sacred hill where Phoebus is adored, and sought the shade that hid his venerable maid from sight. Deep in a cave the Sibyl makes her abode; from there she returns, full of fate and of the god. They walked through Trivia's grove; and now they beheld, and entered, the temple roofed with gold. When Daedalus, to flee the Cretan shore, bore his heavy limbs on jointed pinions (the first to sail in the air), Fame sings that he came at last to the Cumaean coast, and, alighting here, built this costly structure. Here, inscribed to Phoebus, he hung on high the steerage of his wings, that had cut the sky. Then, over the lofty gate, his art embossed Androgeos' death, and the offerings made to his ghost: seven youths from Athens yearly sent to meet the fate appointed by revengeful Crete. And next to these was placed the dreadful urn, in which the destined names were cast by lots. The mournful parents stand around in tears, and rising Crete appears over against their shore. There, too, in living sculpture, might be seen the mad affection of the Cretan queen; and then how she cheated her bellowing lover's eye; the rushing leap, the doubtful progeny—the lower part a beast, a man above—the monument of their polluted love. Not far from there he had graven the wondrous maze, a thousand doors, a thousand winding ways; here dwells the monster, hid from human view, not to be found but by the faithful clue; until the kind artist, moved with pious grief, lent to the loving maid this last relief, and described all those erring paths so well that Theseus conquered and the monster fell. Here hapless Icarus would have found his part, had not the father's grief restrained his art. Twice he essayed to cast his son in gold; twice from his hands he dropped the forming mold.

All this Aeneas viewed with wondering eyes; each varying object renewed his delight. Eager to read the rest, Achates came, and by his side the mad divining dame, the priestess of the god, Deiphobe by name. "Time does not suffer," she said, "to feed your eyes with empty pleasures; haste the sacrifice. Choose seven bullocks for Phoebus, yet unyoked, and seven unspotted ewes for Diana." This said, the servants urged on the sacred rites, while she invited the prince to the temple. A spacious cave, in its furthermost part, was hewn and fashioned by laborious art through the hollow sides of the hill; before the place a hundred doors, with a hundred entries, grace it; as many voices issue, and the sound of Sibyl's words rebounds as many times. Now to the mouth they came. She cried aloud: "This is the time; inquire your destinies. He comes; behold the god!" Thus while she spoke (and stood shivering at the sacred entry), her color changed; her face was not the same, and hollow groans came from her deep spirit. Her hair stood up; convulsive rage possessed her trembling limbs, and heaved her laboring breast. She seemed greater than humankind in her look, and spoke with an accent more than mortal. Her staring eyes rolled with sparkling fury, when all the god came rushing on her soul. Swiftly she turned, and, foaming as she spoke: "Why this delay?" she cried; "invoke the powers! Your prayers alone can open this abode; else my demands are vain, and the god is dumb."

She said no more. The trembling Trojans listened, overspread with a damp sweat and holy fear. The prince himself, possessed with awful dread, addressed his vows to great Apollo thus: "Indulgent god, propitious power to Troy, swift to relieve, unwilling to destroy, by whose hand the Dardan dart pierced the proud Grecian's only mortal part: thus far, by fate's decrees and your commands, through surrounding seas and through devouring sands, our exiled crew has sought the Ausonian ground; and now, at length, the fleeing coast is found. Thus far the fate of Troy, from place to place, has pursued her wandering race with fury. Here cease, you powers, and let your vengeance end: Troy is no more, and can no more offend. And you, O sacred maid, inspired to see the outcome of things in dark futurity, grant me what Heaven has promised to my fate: to conquer and command the Latian state; to fix my wandering gods, and find a place for the long exiles of the Trojan race. Then shall my grateful hands rear a temple to the twin gods, with vows and solemn prayer; and annual rites, and festivals, and games, shall be performed to their auspicious names. Nor shall you want your honors in my land; for there your faithful oracles shall stand, preserved in shrines; and every sacred lay, which Apollo shall convey through your mouth, all shall be treasured by a chosen train of holy priests, and shall remain forever. But, oh! do not commit your prophetic mind to flitting leaves, the sport of every wind, lest they disperse our empty fate in the air; do not write, but relate what the powers ordain."

Struggling in vain, impatient of her load, and laboring under the ponderous god, the more she strove to shake him from her breast, with more and far superior force he pressed; he commanded his entrance, and, without control, usurped her organs and inspired her soul. Now, with a furious blast, the hundred doors opened of themselves; a rushing whirlwind roared within the cave, and restored the Sibyl's voice: "Having escaped the dangers of the watery reign, yet more and greater ills remain by land. Your troops shall reach the coast so long desired (doubt not the event), but, having reached it, shall repent. Wars, horrid wars, I view; a field of blood, and Tiber rolling with a purple flood. Neither Simois nor Xanthus shall be wanting there; a new Achilles shall appear in arms, he too goddess-born. Fierce Juno's hate, added to hostile force, shall urge your fate. To what strange nations shall you not resort, driven to seek aid at every court! The cause the same which once oppressed Ilium: a foreign mistress, and a foreign guest. But you, secure of soul, unbent by woes, the more your fortune frowns, the more oppose. The dawnings of your safety shall be shown from where you shall least hope: a Grecian town."

Thus, from the dark recess, the Sibyl spoke, and the resisting air broke with thunder; the cave rebellowed, and the temple shook. The ambiguous god, who ruled her laboring breast, expressed his mind in these mysterious words: some truths revealed, the rest in terms involved. At length her fury fell, her foaming ceased, and, ebbing in her soul, the god decreased. Then thus the chief: "No terror to my view, no frightful face of danger can be new. Inured to suffer, and resolved to dare, the Fates, beyond my power, shall be beyond my care. This let me crave, since near your grove the road to hell lies open, and the dark abode which Acheron surrounds, the innavigable flood: conduct me through the regions void of light, and lead me, longing, to my father's sight. For him, I have sought a thousand dangers, and, rushing where the thickest Greeks fought, bore the sacred burden safe on my back. He, for my sake, tried the raging ocean and the wrath of Heaven, my still auspicious guide, and endured beyond the strength that decrepit age supplied. Often, since he breathed his last, in the dead of night his reverend image has stood before my sight; it enjoined me to seek his holy shade below, conducted there by your unerring aid. But you, if pious minds are won by prayers, oblige the father and protect the son. Yours is the power; nor has Proserpine made you priestess of her nightly reign in vain. If Orpheus, armed with his enchanting lyre, could inspire the ruthless king with pity, and redeem his wife from the shades below; if Pollux, offering his alternate life, could free his brother, and daily go by turns aloft, by turns descend below—why should I name Theseus, or his greater friend, who trod the downward path and could ascend upward? Not less than theirs did my lineage come from Jove; my mother is greater, my descent the same." So prayed the Trojan prince, and, while he prayed, laid his hand upon the holy altar.

Then thus replied the divine prophetess: "O goddess-born, of great Anchises' line, the gates of hell are open night and day; the descent is smooth, and easy is the way. But to return, and view the cheerful skies—in this the task and the mighty labor lies. To few does great Jupiter impart this grace, and those of shining worth and heavenly race. Between those regions and our upper light, deep forests and impenetrable night possess the middle space; the infernal bounds Cocytus surrounds with his sable waves. But if so dire a love invades your soul, as to view twice below the trembling shades; if you will undertake so hard a toil as to pass twice the innavigable lake, receive my counsel. In the neighboring grove there stands a tree; the queen of Stygian Jove claims it as her own; thick woods and gloomy night conceal the happy plant from human sight. It bears one bough, but wondrous to behold—the ductile rind and leaves of radiant gold; this must be torn from the common branches, and borne as a present to fair Proserpine, before leave is given to tempt the nether skies. After the first is thus torn off, a second will arise, and the same metal will supply the same place. Look round the wood, with lifted eyes, to see the lurking gold upon the fatal tree; then rend it off, as holy rites command; the willing metal will obey your hand, following with ease, if favored by your fate; you are foredoomed to view the Stygian state. If not, no labor can constrain the tree, and the strength of stubborn arms and steel are vain. Besides, you do not know, while you are here, the unworthy fate of your unhappy friend: he lies breathless; and his unburied ghost, deprived of funeral rites, pollutes your host. Pay first his pious dues, and let two sable sheep be led around his hearse for the dead; then lay living turfs upon his body. This done, securely take the destined way, to find the regions destitute of day."

She said, and held her peace. Aeneas went, sad from the cave, and full of discontent, not knowing whom the sacred Sibyl had meant. Achates, the companion of his breast, walked grieving by his side, oppressed with equal cares. Walking, they talked, and fruitlessly divined which friend the priestess had designed by those words. But soon they found an object to deplore: Misenus lay extended on the shore, the son of the God of Winds; none so renowned in sounding the warrior trumpet in the field, kindling fierce alarms with breathing brass, and rousing men to dare their fate in honorable arms. He had served great Hector, and was ever near him, not only with his trumpet, but with his spear. But when, by the arms of Pelides, Hector fell, he chose Aeneas, and he chose well. Swollen with applause, and aiming always at more, he now provoked the sea gods from the shore; with envy Triton heard the martial sound, and drowned the bold champion for his challenge; then he cast his mangled carcass on the strand. The gazing crowd stood around the body. All wept; but most Aeneas mourned his fate, and hastened to perform the funeral state. They reared a stately pile, like an altar, the basis broad below, and the top advanced in the air. The Trojans found an ancient wood, fit for the work designed (the shady covert of the wild kind); the sounding axe was plied; firs, pines, and pitch trees, and the towering pride of forest ashes, felt the fatal stroke, and piercing wedges cleaved the stubborn oak. Huge trunks of trees, felled from the steepy crown of the bare mountains, rolled down in ruin. Armed like the rest, the Trojan prince appeared, and by his pious labor urged theirs.

Thus while he wrought, revolving in his mind the ways to accomplish what his wish designed, he cast his eyes upon the gloomy grove, and then with vows implored the Queen of Love: "O may your power, still propitious to me, conduct my steps to find the fatal tree in this deep forest, since the Sibyl's breath foretold, alas, too truly, Misenus' death." Scarcely had he said this when, full before his sight, two doves, descending from their airy flight, alighted securely upon the grassy plain. He knew his mother's birds; and thus he prayed: "Be you my guides, with your auspicious aid, and lead my footsteps until the branch is found, whose glittering shadow gilds the sacred ground. And you, great parent, with celestial care, be present to my prayer in this distress." Having said this, he stopped with watchful sight, observing still the motions of their flight, what course they took, what happy signs they showed. They fed, and, fluttering, by degrees withdrew still farther from the place, but still in view. Hopping and flying, thus they led him on to the slow lake, whose baleful stench to shun they winged their flight aloft; then, stooping low, perched on the double tree that bears the golden bough. Through the green leaves the glittering shadows glowed; as, on the sacred oak, the wintry mistletoe, where the proud mother views her precious brood, and happier branches that she never sowed. Such was the glittering; such the ruddy rind, and dancing leaves, that wantoned in the wind. He seized the shining bough with gripping hold, and rent away the lingering gold with ease; then bore the prize to the Sibyl's palace. Meanwhile the Trojan troops, with weeping eyes, paid their obsequies to dead Misenus. First, from the ground they reared a lofty pile of pitch trees, oaks, and pines, and unctuous fir. They strewed the front of the structure with cypress twigs, and stuck the sides with boughs of baleful yew. The topmost part was adorned with his glittering arms; then warm waters, borne in brazen cauldrons, were poured to wash his body, joint by joint, and fragrant oils anointed his stiffened limbs. With groans and cries they bewailed Misenus; then they laid his breathless body on a bier, covered over with purple, and fired the pile, their faces turned away—such reverend rites their fathers had been wont to pay. Pure oil and incense they threw on the fire, and the fat of victims that his friends bestowed. The greedy flames devoured these gifts to dust; then they poured red wine on the living coals, and last, the priests themselves disposed of the relics, which they enclosed in a brazen urn. Old Corynaeus encompassed the crew thrice, and dipped an olive branch in holy dew, which thrice he sprinkled round, and thrice aloud invoked the dead, and then dismissed the crowd. But good Aeneas ordered a stately tomb on the shore, whose top bore a trumpet, a soldier's falchion, and a seaman's oar. Thus was his friend interred; and deathless fame still consigns his name to the lofty cape. These rites performed, the prince, without delay, hastened his destined way to the nether world. Deep was the cave; and, as it went downward from the wide mouth, it was a rocky rough descent. Here a gloomy grove defended the access, and there extended the unnavigable lake, over whose unhappy waters, void of light, no bird presumes to steer his airy flight; such deadly stenches arose from the depths, and steaming sulphur, that infected the skies. From this the Grecian bards make their legends, and give the lake the name Avernus. Four sable bullocks, untaught to the yoke, the pious hero brought for sacrifice. The priestess poured wine between their horns, then cut the curling hair; that first oblation burned, invoking Hecate to repair there—a powerful name in hell and in upper air. The sacred priests with ready knives bereaved the beasts of life, and received the streaming blood in full bowls. Aeneas offered a lamb to Hell and Night (the sable wool without a streak of white); and, by fate's decree, a barren heifer to you, Proserpine. He filled Pluto's altar with holocausts; seven brawny bulls he killed with his own hand; then he poured oil on the broiling entrails, which, anointed thus, the raging flame devoured. Late began the nocturnal sacrifice, nor ended until the next returning sun. Then earth began to bellow, trees to dance, and howling dogs to advance in glimmering light, before Hecate came. "Far hence be profane souls!" cried the Sibyl, "and abstain from the grove! Now, Trojan, take the way your fates afford; assume your courage, and unsheathe your sword." She said, and passed along the gloomy space; the prince pursued her steps with equal pace.
You realms, yet unrevealed to human sight, you gods who rule the regions of the night, you gliding ghosts, permit me to relate the mystic wonders of your silent state!

Obscure they went through dreary shades, that led along the waste dominions of the dead. Thus travelers wander in woods by night, by the moon's doubtful and malignant light, when Jove involves the skies in dusky clouds, and the faint crescent shoots by fits before their eyes.

Just at the gate and in the jaws of hell, revengeful Cares and sullen Sorrows dwell, and pale Diseases, and repining Age, Want, Fear, and Famine's unresisted rage; here Toils, and Death, and Death's half-brother, Sleep—forms terrible to view—keep their sentry; with anxious Pleasures of a guilty mind, Deep Frauds before, and open Force behind; the Furies' iron beds, and Strife, that shakes her hissing tresses and unfolds her snakes. Full in the midst of this infernal road, an elm displays her dusky arms abroad: the God of Sleep there hides his heavy head, and empty dreams are spread on every leaf. More unnumbered specters of various forms, Centaurs, and double shapes, besiege the door. Before the passage stood horrid Hydra, and Briareus with all his hundred hands; Gorgons, Geryon with his triple frame, and vain Chimaera vomits empty flame. The chief unsheathed his shining steel, prepared, though seized with sudden fear, to force the guard, offering his brandished weapon at their face, had not the Sibyl stopped his eager pace, and told him what those empty phantoms were: forms without bodies, and impassive air. Hence they took their way to deep Acheron, whose troubled eddies, thick with ooze and clay, are whirled aloft, and lost in Cocytus. There Charon stands, who rules the dreary coast: a sordid god; down from his hoary chin a length of beard descends, uncombed, unclean; his eyes are like hollow furnaces on fire; a girdle, foul with grease, binds his obscene attire. He spreads his canvas; with his pole he steers; in his thin bottom he bears the freight of flitting ghosts. He looked aged; yet in his years were seen a youthful vigor and autumnal green. An airy crowd came rushing where he stood, which filled the margin of the fatal flood: husbands and wives, boys and unmarried maids, and the more majestic shades of mighty heroes, and youths entombed before their fathers' eyes, with hollow groans, and shrieks, and feeble cries. Thick as the leaves strew the woods in autumn, or as fowls, forced by winter, forsake the floods, and wing their hasty flight to happier lands—such, and so thick, the shivering army stood, and pressed for passage with extended hands. Now these, now those, the surly boatman bore; the rest he drove to distance from the shore. The hero, who beheld with wondering eyes the tumult mixed with shrieks, laments, and cries, asked of his guide what the rude concourse meant; why the thronging people bent toward the shore; what forms of law were used among the ghosts; why some were ferried over, and some refused.

"Son of Anchises, offspring of the gods," the Sibyl said, "you see the Stygian floods, the sacred stream by which heaven's imperial state attests its oaths, and fears to violate. The ghosts rejected are the unhappy crew deprived of sepulchers and funeral due. The boatman, Charon, ferries those, the buried host, over to the farther coast; nor does his transport vessel dare cross the waves with such whose bones are not composed in graves. They wander for a hundred years on the shore; at length, their penance done, they are wafted over." The Trojan chief repressed his forward pace, revolving anxious thoughts within his breast. He saw his friends who, whelmed beneath the waves, claimed their funeral honors, and asked for quiet graves. In the crowd he knew the lost Leucaspis, and the brave leader of the Lycian crew, whom, on the Tyrrhene seas, the tempests had met, whose sailors had been mastered, and whose ship had been overset.

Amidst the spirits, Palinurus pressed forward, yet fresh from life, a newly admitted guest; who, while he was steering and watching the stars, and bearing his course from Africa to the Latian shore, had fallen headlong down. The Trojan fixed his gaze, and scarcely through the gloom knew the sullen shadow. Then thus the prince: "What envious power, O friend, brought your beloved life to this disastrous end? For Phoebus, always true in all he said, has betrayed my faith only in your fate. The god foretold that you should not die before you reached the Italian shore, safe from the seas. Is this the unerring power?" The ghost replied: "Neither did Phoebus flatter, nor did his answers lie; nor have envious gods sent me to the deep. But, while I kept the stars and the course of heaven, my wearied eyes were seized with fatal sleep. I fell; and, with my weight, the helm I had gripped was dragged along, which I still held in my grasp. Now by the winds and raging waves I swear, your safety, more than mine, was then my care, lest, bereft of its guide, and the rudder lost, your ship should run against the rocky coast. For three blustering nights, borne by the southern blast, I floated, and at last discovered land: high on a mounting wave I bore my head, forcing my strength, and gathering to the shore. Panting, but past the danger, I now seized the craggy cliffs, and eased my tired limbs. While I lay, cumbered with my dripping clothes, the cruel people, covetous of prey, stained the inhospitable coast with my blood. Now, by winds and waves, my lifeless limbs are tossed. Which, oh, avert, by yon ethereal light, which I have lost for this eternal night! Or, if by dearer ties you may be won, by your dead sire and by your living son, redeem my wandering ghost from this reproach. Or seek the Velian coast with your navy, and compose my corpse in a peaceful grave; or, if a nearer way your mother shows—without whose aid you would not dare to undertake this frightful passage over the Stygian lake—lend to this wretch your hand, and waft him over to the sweet banks of yon forbidden shore." Scarcely had he said this, when the prophetess began: "What hopes delude you, miserable man? Do you think, unentombed, to cross the floods, to view the Furies and infernal gods, and visit the dark abodes without leave? Attend the term of long revolving years; Fate, and the dooming gods, are deaf to tears. Take this comfort in your dire misfortune: the wrath of Heaven, inflicted for your sake, shall with vengeance pursue the inhuman coast, till they propitiate your offended ghost, and raise a tomb, with vows and solemn prayer; and the place shall bear Palinurus' name." This calmed his cares; soothed by his future fame, and pleased to hear his propagated name.

Now they drew nearer to the Stygian lake. The surly boatman saw them from the shore, observed their passage through the shady wood, and marked their near approaches to the flood. Then thus he called aloud, inflamed with wrath: "Mortal, whoever you are, who in arms presume to tread this forbidden path, I charge you, stand, and tell your name, and your business in the land. Know this: the realm of night, the Stygian shore. My boat conveys no living bodies over; nor was I once pleased to bear great Theseus, who forced a passage with his pointed spear, nor strong Alcides, men of mighty fame, who derived their lineage from the immortal gods. One tied the barking porter in fetters, and took him trembling from his sovereign's side; two sought by force to seize his beauteous bride." To whom the Sibyl thus: "Compose your mind; no frauds are contrived here, nor force designed. Still may the dog constrain the wandering troops of airy ghosts, and vex the guilty train, and may his lovely queen remain with her grisly lord. The Trojan chief, whose lineage is from Jove, much famed for arms, and more for filial love, is sent to seek his sire in your Elysian grove. If neither piety nor Heaven's command can gain his passage to the Stygian strand, this fatal present shall prevail, at least." Then she showed the shining bough, concealed within her vest. No more was needed: for the gloomy god stood mute with awe, to see the golden rod; he admired the destined offering to his queen—a venerable gift, so rarely seen. His fury thus appeased, he put to land. The ghosts forsook their seats at his command; he cleared the deck, received the mighty freight; the leaky vessel groaned beneath the weight. Slowly she sailed, and scarcely stemmed the tides; the pressing water poured in at her sides. His passengers at length were wafted over, exposed, in muddy weeds, upon the miry shore.

No sooner landed, in his den they found the triple porter of the Stygian sound, grim Cerberus, who soon began to rear his crested snakes, and arm his bristling hair. The prudent Sibyl had before prepared a sop, steeped in honey, to charm the guard; which, mixed with powerful drugs, she cast before his greedy grinning jaws, just opened to roar. With three enormous mouths he gaped; and straightaway, pressed by hunger, devoured the pleasing bait. Long draughts of sleep enslaved his monstrous limbs; he reeled, and, falling, filled the spacious cave. The keeper charmed, the chief without delay passed on, and took the irremeable way. Before the gates, the cries of babes newly born, whom fate had torn from their tender mothers, assaulted his ears; then those whom the form of laws had condemned to die, when traitors had judged their cause. Nor did they want for lots, nor judges to review the wrongful sentence, and award a new one. Minos, the strict inquisitor, appears; and hears their lives and crimes, with his assessors. He rolls the blended balls in his urn, absolves the just, and dooms the guilty souls. Next in place and punishment are those who prodigally throw their souls away: fools, who, repining at their wretched state, and loathing anxious life, suborned their fate. With late repentance they would now retrieve the bodies they forsook, and wish to live; they desire to bear their pains and poverty, to view the light of heaven, and breathe the vital air. But fate forbids; the Stygian floods oppose, and enclose the captive souls with circling streams.

Not far from there, the Mournful Fields appear—so called from the lovers who inhabit them. The souls whom that unhappy flame invades, in secret solitude and myrtle shades, make endless moans, and, pining with desire, lament too late their unextinguished fire. Here he found Procris, and Eriphyle, baring her breast, still bleeding with the wound made by her son. He saw Pasiphae there, with Phaedra's ghost, a foul incestuous pair. There Laodamia and Evadne moved, both unhappy, but loyal in their loves; Caeneus, once a woman, and once a man, but ending in the sex she first began. Not far from these stood Phoenician Dido, fresh from her wound, her bosom bathed in blood. When the Trojan hero hardly knew her, obscure in shades, and with a doubtful view (doubtful as one who sees, through dusky night, or thinks he sees, the moon's uncertain light), with tears he first approached the sullen shade; and, as his love inspired him, thus he said: "Unhappy queen! Then is the common breath of rumor true in your reported death? And I, alas, the cause? By Heaven, I vow, and by all the powers that rule the realms below, unwilling I forsook your friendly state, commanded by the gods, and forced by fate. Those gods, that fate, whose unresisted might has sent me to these regions void of light, through the vast empire of eternal night. Nor did I dare to presume that my flight, pressed with grief, should urge you to this dire relief. Stay, stay your steps, and listen to my vows: it is the last interview that fate allows!" In vain he thus attempted to move her mind with tears, and prayers, and late-repenting love. Disdainfully she looked; then, turning round, she fixed her eyes unmoved upon the ground, and what he said and swore she regarded no more than deaf rocks regard the loud billows' roar. Then she whirled away, to shun his hateful sight, hid in the forest and the shades of night; then she sought Sichaeus through the shady grove, who answered all her cares, and equaled all her love.

The pitying hero paid some pious tears, and followed the flitting shade with his eyes. Then he took the forward way ordained by fate, and, with his guide, attained the farther fields, where, severed from the rest, the warrior souls remained. He met Tydeus, with Meleager's race, the pride of armies and the soldiers' grace, and pale Adrastus, with his ghastly face. Of Trojan chiefs he viewed a numerous train, all much lamented, all slain in battle: Glaucus and Medon, high above the rest, Antenor's sons, and Ceres' sacred priest; and proud Idaeus, Priam's charioteer, who shakes his empty reins, and aims his airy spear. The gladsome ghosts, in circling troops, attended, and beheld their friend with unwearied eyes; they delighted to hover near him, and longed to know what business brought him to the realms below. But the Argive chiefs, and Agamemnon's train, when his refulgent arms flashed through the shady plain, fled from his well-known face, with their wonted fear, as when his thundering sword and pointed spear had driven them headlong to their ships, and gleaned the routed rear. They raised a feeble cry, with trembling notes; but the weak voice deceived their gasping throats.

Here he found Priam's son, Deiphobus, whose face and limbs were one continued wound. Dishonest, with lopped-off arms, the youth appeared, spoiled of his nose, and shortened of his ears. He scarcely knew him, striving to disown his blotted form, and blushing to be known; and therefore Aeneas first began: "O Teucer's race, who dared thus to deface your faultless figure? What heart could wish, what hand inflict, this dire disgrace? It was famed that, on our last and fatal night, your single prowess long sustained the fight, until tired, not forced, you chose a glorious fate, and fell upon a heap of slaughtered foes. But, in remembrance of so brave a deed, I decreed a tomb and funeral honors; three times I called your manes on the Trojan plains; the place retains your armor and your name. I also sought your body, and, had I found it, I intended burial in your native ground."

The ghost replied: "Your piety has paid all needful rites to rest my wandering shade; but cruel fate, and my more cruel wife, betrayed my sleeping life to Grecian swords. These are the monuments of Helen's love: the shame I bear below, the marks I bore above. You know in what deluding joys we passed the night that was by Heaven decreed our last: for, when the fatal horse, descending down, pregnant with arms, overwhelmed the unhappy town, she feigned nocturnal orgies; she left my bed, and, mixed with Trojan dames, led the dances. Then, waving her torch high, she made the signal which roused the Greeks from their ambush. Worn out with watching, oppressed with cares, unhappy I had laid myself down to rest, and heavy sleep possessed my weary limbs. Meanwhile my worthy wife mislaid our arms, and conveyed my sword from beneath my head. She unlatched the door, and with repeated calls, invited her former lord into my halls. Thus she placed her confidence in her crime, and hoped with new treasons to redeem the past. What more need I say? They ran into the room, and basely murdered a defenseless man. Ulysses, basely born, led the way first. Avenging powers! With justice, if I pray, may their fortune one day be the same! But answer me, and in your turn relate, what brought you, living, to the Stygian state: driven by the winds and errors of the sea, or did you obey Heaven's superior doom? Or tell what other chance conducts your way, to view with mortal eyes our dark retreats, the tumults and torments of the infernal seats."

While thus, in talk, they passed the flying hours, the sun had finished more than half his race; and they, perhaps, would have spent in words and tears the little time of stay which Heaven had lent, but thus the Sibyl chided their long delay: "Night rushes down, and headlong drives the day. Here, in different paths, the way divides: the right leads to Pluto's golden palace; the left tends to that unhappy region which descends to the depth of Tartarus—the seat of night profound, and of punished fiends." Then thus Deiphobus: "O sacred maid, forbear to chide, and let your will be obeyed! Look! To the secret shadows I retire, to pay my penance till my years expire. Proceed, auspicious prince, crowned with glory, and born to better fates than I have found." He said; and, while he said it, turned his steps to secret shadows, and mourned in silence.

The hero, looking on the left, espied a lofty tower, strong on every side with triple walls, which Phlegethon surrounded, whose fiery flood bounded the burning empire; and, pressed between the rocks, the bellowing noise resounded. Wide was the fronting gate, raised on high with adamantine columns, threatening the sky. Vain is the force of man, and of Heaven as vain, to crush the pillars that sustain the pile. Sublime on these was reared a tower of steel; and dire Tisiphone kept the ward there, girt in her bloody gown, by night and by day, observant of the souls that passed the downward way. From here were heard the groans of ghosts, the pains of sounding lashes, and of dragging chains. The Trojan stood astonished at their cries, and asked his guide from where those yells arose; and what the crimes, and what the tortures were, and the loud laments that rent the liquid air.

She thus replied: "The chaste and holy race are all forbidden this polluted place. But Hecate, when she gave me to rule the woods, then led me trembling through these dire abodes, and taught me the tortures of the avenging gods. These are the realms of unrelenting fate; and awful Rhadamanthus rules the state. He hears and judges each committed crime; he inquires into the manner, place, and time. The conscious wretch must reveal all his acts, loth to confess, unable to conceal, from the first moment of his vital breath to his last hour of unrepenting death. Straightaway, over the guilty ghost, the Fury shakes the sounding whip and brandishes her snakes, and takes the pale sinner, with her sisters. Then of itself, the eternal door unfolds; with dreadful sounds the brazen hinges roar. You see, before the gate, what stalking ghost commands the guard, what sentries keep the post. More formidable Hydra stands within, whose jaws severely grin with iron teeth. The gaping gulf lies low to the center, and is twice as deep as earth is distant from the skies. The rivals of the gods, the Titan race, here, singed with lightning, roll within the unfathomed space. Here lie the Aloean twins (I saw them both), enormous bodies of gigantic growth, who dared in fight to defy the Thunderer, aspiring to his heaven, and to force him from the sky. I found Salmoneus suffering cruel pains, for emulating Jove with the rattling sound of mimic thunder, and the glittering blaze of pointed lightnings, and their forked rays. Through Elis and the Grecian towns he flew; the audacious wretch drove four fiery coursers; he waved a torch aloft, and, madly vain, sought godlike worship from a servile train. Ambitious fool! With horny hoofs to pass over hollow arches of resounding brass, to rival thunder in its rapid course, and to imitate inimitable force! But he, the King of Heaven, obscure on high, bared his red arm, and, launching from the sky his writhen bolt—not shaking empty smoke—struck the flaming felon down to the deep abyss. There was to see Tityus also, who took his birth from heaven, and his nursing from the fruitful earth. Here his gigantic limbs, with large embrace, enfold nine acres of infernal space. A ravenous vulture, in his opened side, tried her crooked beak and cruel talons; still she dug in his breast for the growing liver; the growing liver still supplied the feast; still are his entrails fruitful to their pains: the immortal hunger lasts, the immortal food remains. Ixion and Perithous I could name, and more Thessalian chiefs of mighty fame. High over their heads a moldering rock is placed, that promises a fall, and shakes at every blast. They lie below, displayed on golden beds; and genial feasts with regal pomp are made. The Queen of Furies is set by their sides, and snatches from their mouths the untasted meat. If they touch it, she rears her hissing snakes, tossing her torch, and thundering in their ears. Then those who deny brothers' better claim, who expel their parents, and usurp the throne; who defraud their clients, and, sold to lucre, sit brooding on unprofitable gold; who dare not give, and even refuse to lend to their poor kindred, or to a friend in need. Vast is the throng of these; nor less the train of lustful youths, slain for foul adultery; hosts of deserters, who sold their honor, and basely broke their faith for bribes of gold. All these remain within the dungeon's depth, despairing of pardon, and expecting pain. Do not ask what pains; nor seek further to know their process, or the forms of law below. Some roll a weighty stone; some, laid along, and bound with burning wires, are hung on the spokes of wheels. Unhappy Theseus, doomed forever there, is fixed by fate on his eternal chair; and wretched Phlegyas warns the world with cries (could warning make the world more just or wise): 'Learn righteousness, and dread the avenging deities.' To tyrants others have sold their country, imposing foreign lords for foreign gold; some have repealed old laws and made new statutes, not as the people pleased, but as they paid; with incest some have profaned their daughters' beds: all dared the worst of ills, and, what they dared, they attained. Had I a hundred mouths, a hundred tongues, and throats of brass, inspired with iron lungs, I could not repeat half those horrid crimes, nor half the punishments those crimes have met. But let us haste to pursue our voyage: the walls of Pluto's palace are in view; the gate, and the iron arch above it, stand on anvils labored by the Cyclops' hands. Before the Fates allow us to go further, here we must fix on high the golden bough."

She said, and through the gloomy shades they passed, and chose the middle path. Arrived at last, the prince sprinkled his limbs and body over with living water; then he approached the door, took possession of the porch, and on the front above he fixed the fatal bough required by Pluto's love. These holy rites performed, they took their way to where long extended plains of pleasure lay. The verdant fields might vie with those of heaven, vested with ether, and with a purple sky—the blissful seats of happy souls below. They know their own stars, and their own suns; they exercise their airy limbs in sports, and on the green they contend for the wrestler's prize. Some sing in heroic verse divinely; others in artful measures lead the ring. The Thracian bard, surrounded by the rest, stands conspicuous there in his flowing vest; his flying fingers, and harmonious quill, strike seven distinguished notes, and seven at once fill the air. Here they found Teucer's old heroic race, born to grace better times and happier years. Assaracus and Ilus here enjoy perpetual fame, with him who founded Troy. The chief beheld their chariots from afar, their shining arms, and coursers trained to war: their lances fixed in earth, their steeds around, free from their harness, graze the flowery ground. The love of horses, and the care of chariots, that they had while alive, survive after death. Some cheerful souls were feasting on the plain; some maintained the song, and some the choir, beneath a laurel shade, where mighty Po mounts up to woods above, and hides his head below. Here live patriots who, for their country's good, were prodigal of their blood in fighting fields; priests of unblemished lives made their abode here, and poets worthy of their inspiring god; and searching wits, of more mechanical parts, who graced their age with newly invented arts; those who extended their bounty to worth, and those who knew how to commend that bounty. The heads of these were bound with holy fillets, and all their temples were crowned with garlands.

To these the Sibyl addressed her speech, and first to him who, surrounded by the rest, towered above them in height, and in ample breast: "Tell us, happy souls, divine Musaeus, tell us, where does Anchises live, and where is our way to find the hero, for whose sake alone we have sought the dark abodes, and crossed the bitter lake?" To this the sacred poet thus replied: "The happy souls reside in no fixed place. We live in groves, and lie on mossy beds, by crystal streams that murmur through the meads. But pass yon easy hill, and descend from there; the path will conduct you to your journey's end." This said, he led them up the mountain's brow, and showed them all the shining fields below. They wound around the hill, and passed through the blissful meadows.

But old Anchises, in a flowery vale, was reviewing his mustered race, and taking the tale—those happy spirits who, ordained by fate, were awaiting future beings and new bodies. With studious thought he observed the illustrious throng, as they passed along in nature's order; their names, their fates, their conduct, and their care, in peaceful senates and in successful war. When he saw Aeneas on the plain, he met him with open arms, and falling tears. "Welcome," he said, "undoubted race of the gods! O long expected by my dear embrace! Once more I am given to behold your face! The love and pious duty which you pay have passed the perils of so hard a way. It is true, in computing the times, I now believed the happy day approached; nor are my hopes deceived. What length of lands, what oceans have you passed; what storms sustained, and on what shores been cast? How have I feared your fate! But feared it most when love assailed you on the Libyan coast." To this filial duty thus replied: "Your sacred ghost, before my sleeping eyes, appeared, and often urged this painful enterprise. After long tossing on the Tyrrhene sea, my navy rides at anchor in the bay. But reach your hand, O parent shade, and do not shun the dear embraces of your longing son!" He said; and falling tears bedewed his face; then three times around his neck he threw his arms; and three times the flitting shadow slipped away, like winds, or empty dreams that flee the day.

Now, in a secret vale, the Trojan sees a separate grove, through which a gentle breeze plays with a passing breath, and whispers through the trees; and, just before the confines of the wood, gliding Lethe leads her silent flood. About the boughs flew an airy nation, thick as the humming bees that hunt the golden dew; in summer's heat they feed on tops of lilies, and creep within their bells to suck the balmy seed. The winged army roamed the fields around; the rivers and the rocks remurmured to the sound. Aeneas stood wondering, and then asked the cause that drew the crowding people to the stream. Then thus the sire: "The souls that throng the flood are those to whom, by fate, other bodies are owed. In Lethe's lake they taste long oblivion, secure of future life, forgetful of the past. Long has my soul desired this time and place, to set before your sight your glorious race, so that this presaging joy may fire your mind to seek the shores designed by destiny." "O father, can it be that sublime souls return to visit our terrestrial clime, and that the generous mind, released by death, can covet lazy limbs and mortal breath?"

Anchises then, in order, thus began to clear those wonders to his godlike son: "Know, first, that heaven and earth's compacted frame, and flowing waters, and the starry flame, and both the radiant lights, are inspired and fed by one common soul, which animates the whole. This active mind, infused through all the space, unites and mingles with the mighty mass. Hence men and beasts obtain the breath of life, and the birds of the air, and monsters of the main. The ethereal vigor is in all the same, and every soul is filled with equal flame, as much as earthly limbs, and gross alloy of mortal members, subject to decay, do not blunt the beams of heaven and the edge of day. From this coarse mixture of terrestrial parts, desire and fear by turns possess their hearts, and grief, and joy; nor can the groveling mind, confined in the dark dungeon of the limbs, assert the native skies, or own its heavenly kind. Nor can death itself wholly wash their stains; but long-contracted filth even in the soul remains. The relics of inveterate vice they wear, and spots of obscene sin appear in every face. For this various penances are enjoined; and some are hung to bleach upon the wind, some plunged in waters, others purged in fires, till all the dregs are drained, and all the rust expires. All have their manes, and bear those manes; the few, thus cleansed, repair to these abodes, and breathe, in ample fields, the soft Elysian air. Then are they happy, when by length of time the scurf of each committed crime is worn away; no speck is left of their habitual stains, but the pure ether of the soul remains. But when a thousand rolling years are past (so long their punishments and penance last), whole droves of minds are, by the driving god, compelled to drink the deep Lethaean flood, to steep the cares of their past labors and their irksome years in large forgetful draughts, so that, not remembering its former pain, the soul may suffer mortal flesh again."

Thus having said, the father spirit led the priestess and his son through swarms of shades, and took a rising ground, from which to see the long procession of his progeny. "Survey," pursued the sire, "this airy throng, as they pass along, offered to your view. These are the Italian names which fate will join with ours, and graft upon the Trojan line. Observe the youth who first appears in sight, and holds the nearest station to the light: already he seems to sniff the vital air, and leans just forward on a shining spear. Silvius is he, your last-begotten race, but first in order sent, to fill your place; an Alban name, but mixed with Dardan blood, born in the covert of a shady wood. Him fair Lavinia, your surviving wife, shall breed in groves, to lead a solitary life. In Alba he shall fix his royal seat, and, born a king, a race of kings beget. Then Procas, honor of the Trojan name; Capys, and Numitor, of endless fame. A second Silvius appears after these: Silvius Aeneas, for he bears your name; equally renowned for arms and justice; who, restored late, shall be crowned in Alba. How great they look! How vigorously they wield their weighty lances, and sustain the shield! But they who appear crowned with oaken wreaths shall rear Gabian walls and strong Fidena; Nomentum, Bola, with Pometia, they shall found; and raise Collatian towers on rocky ground. All these shall then be towns of mighty fame, though now they lie obscure, and lands without a name. See the great Romulus, born to restore the crown that his injured grandsire once wore. A priestess of your blood shall bear this prince, and he shall appear in arms like his sire. Two rising crests adorn his royal head, born from a god, himself to godhead born: his sire already signs him for the skies, and marks his seat amidst the deities. Auspicious chief! Your race, in times to come, shall spread the conquests of imperial Rome. Rome, whose ascending towers shall invade heaven, involving earth and ocean in her shade, high as the Mother of the Gods in place, and proud, like her, of an immortal race. Then, when in pomp she makes the Phrygian round, with golden turrets on her temples crowned, a hundred gods shall supply her sweeping train, all her offspring, and all commanding the sky.

"Now fix your sight, and stand intent, to see your Roman race and Julian progeny. The mighty Caesar awaits his vital hour, impatient for the world, and grasps his promised power. But next behold the youth of form divine, Caesar himself, exalted in his line; Augustus, often promised and long foretold, sent to the realm that Saturn ruled of old; born to restore a better age of gold. Africa and India shall obey his power; he shall extend his propagated sway beyond the solar year, without the starry way, where Atlas turns the rolling heavens around, and his broad shoulders are crowned with their lights. At his foreseen approach, already the Caspian kingdoms and the Maeotian lake quake; their seers behold the tempest from afar, and threatening oracles denounce the war. Nile hears him knocking at her sevenfold gates, and seeks her hidden spring, and fears her nephew's fates. Not even Hercules knew more lands or labors, though he slew the brazen-footed hind, freed Erymanthus from the foaming boar, and dipped his arrows in Lernaean gore; nor Bacchus, turning from his Indian war, drawn triumphant by tigers in his car, descending from Nysa's top onto the plains, with curling vines around his purple reins. And do we yet doubt, through dangers, to pursue the paths of honor, and a crown in view? But what is the man who from afar appears? His head crowned with olive, a censer in his hand; his hoary beard and holy vestments bring his lost idea back—I know the Roman king. He shall ordain new laws for peaceful Rome, called from his mean abode to sustain a scepter. Tullus next succeeds him in dignity, an active prince, prone to martial deeds. He shall prepare his troops for fighting fields, disused to toils, and to the triumphs of war. By dint of sword he shall increase his crown, and scour his armor from the rust of peace. Whom Ancus follows, with a fawning air, but vain within, and proudly popular. Next view the Tarquin kings, and the avenging sword of Brutus, justly drawn, and Rome restored. He first renews the severe rods and axe, and gives the consuls royal robes to wear. His sons, who seek to sustain the tyrant, and long again for arbitrary lords, he dooms to a deserved death, scourged with ignominy in open sight, asserting the public right. Unhappy man, to break the pious laws of nature, pleading in his children's cause! However the doubtful fact is understood, it is love of honor, and of his country's good; the consul, not the father, sheds the blood. Behold Torquatus pursues the same track; and, next, view the two devoted Decii, the Drusian line, Camillus loaded home with standards well redeemed, and foreign foes overcome. The pair you see shine in equal armor, now, friends below, joined in close embraces; but, when they leave the shady realms of night, and, clothed in bodies, breathe your upper light, they shall pursue each other with mortal hate. What wars, what wounds, what slaughter shall ensue! From Alpine heights the father first descends; his daughter's husband awaits him on the plain; his daughter's husband arms his eastern friends. Embrace again, my sons, be foes no more; nor stain your country with her children's gore! And you, the first, lay down your lawless claim, you, of my blood, who bear the Julian name! Another comes, who shall ride in triumph, and guide his chariot to the Capitol, rich with Grecian spoils from conquered Corinth. And yet another, famed for warlike toils, shall impose the Roman laws on Argos, and on the Greeks revenge the Trojan cause; shall drag their Achillean race in chains; shall vindicate his ancestors' disgrace, and Pallas, for her violated place. Great Cato is there, renowned for gravity, and conquering Cossus walks crowned with laurels. Who can omit the Gracchi? Who can declare the worth of the Scipios, those thunderbolts of war, the double bane of Carthage? Who can see without esteem for virtuous poverty, severe Fabricius, or cease to admire the plowman consul in his coarse attire? Tired as I am, the Fabii claim my praise; and you, great hero, greatest of your name, ordained in war to save the sinking state, and, by delays, to put a stop to fate! Let others better mold the running mass of metals, and inform the breathing brass, and soften into flesh a marble face; let them plead better at the bar; let them describe the skies, and tell when the stars descend, and when they rise. But, Rome, it is yours alone, with awful sway, to rule mankind, and make the world obey, disposing peace and war by your own majestic way; to tame the proud, to free the fettered slave: these are imperial arts, and worthy of you."

He paused; and, while they viewed the passing spirits with wondering eyes, he thus renewed his speech: "See great Marcellus! How, untired in toils, he moves with manly grace, how rich with regal spoils! He, when his country, threatened with alarms, requires his courage and his conquering arms, shall more than once affright the Punic bands; shall kill the Gaulish king in single fight; then move in triumph to the Capitol, and his third spoils shall grace Feretrian Jove." Here Aeneas beheld, of form divine, a godlike youth shining in glittering armor, keeping equal pace with great Marcellus; but his eyes were gloomy, his face dejected. He saw, and, wondering, asked his airy guide what and from where was he, who pressed the hero's side: "His son, or one of his illustrious name? How like the former, and almost the same! Observe the crowds that surround him; all gaze, and all admire, and raise a shouting sound. But hovering mists are spread around his brows, and night, with sable shades, envelops his head." "Seek not to know," the ghost replied with tears, "the sorrows of your sons in future years. This youth (the blissful vision of a day) shall just be shown on earth, and snatched away. The gods had raised the Roman state too high, were their gifts as permanent as they were great. What groans of men shall fill the Martian field! How fierce a blaze his flaming pile shall yield! What funeral pomp shall the floating Tiber see, when, rising from his bed, he views the sad solemnity! No youth shall give equal hopes of glory, no youth afford so great a cause to grieve: the Trojan honor, and the Roman boast, admired when living, and adored when lost! A mirror of ancient faith in early youth! Undaunted worth, inviolable truth! No foe, unpunished, in the fighting field shall dare you, foot to foot, with sword and shield; much less in arms oppose your matchless force, when your sharp spurs shall urge your foaming horse. Ah! Could you break through fate's severe decree, a new Marcellus shall arise in you! Bring full canisters of fragrant lilies, mixed with the purple roses of the spring; let me strew his body with funeral flowers; this gift which parents owe to their children, this unavailing gift, at least I may bestow!" Thus having said, he led the hero round the confines of the blest Elysian ground; which when Anchises had shown to his son, and fired his mind to mount the promised throne, he told the future wars, ordained by fate, the strength and customs of the Latian state, the prince and the people, and forearmed his care with rules, to push his fortune, or to bear.

Two gates adorn the silent house of Sleep: this of polished ivory, that of transparent horn. True visions rise through transparent horn; through polished ivory pass deluding lies. Discoursing of various things as he passed, Anchises bent his steps here at last. Then, through the gate of ivory, he dismissed his valiant offspring, and his divining guest. Straight to the ships Aeneas took his way, embarked his men, and skimmed along the sea, still coasting, until he gained Caieta's bay. At length on oozy ground his galleys moored; their heads were turned to sea, their sterns to shore.

chapters.title: Book VII
paragraphs: King Latinus entertains Aeneas, and promises him his only daughter, Lavinia, the heiress of his crown. Turnus, being in love with her, and favored by her mother, by Juno, and by Alecto, breaks the treaty that had been made, and engages in his quarrel Mezentius, Camilla, Messapus, and many other of the neighboring princes, whose forces, and the names of their commanders, are particularly related.

And you, O matron of immortal fame, here dying, have left your name to the shore. The place is still called Caieta from you, the nurse of the infancy of great Aeneas. Here your bones rest in the rich plains of Hesperia; your name (which is all a ghost can have) remains.

Now, when the prince had paid her funeral rites, he plowed the Tyrrhene seas with sails displayed. A gentle breeze arose from the land by night; the stars shone serenely, the moon was bright, and the sea trembled with her silver light. Now they ran near the shelves of Circe's shores (Circe, the rich, the daughter of the Sun)—a dangerous coast: the goddess wastes her days in joyous songs; the rocks resound her lays; in spinning, or at the loom, she spends the night, and cedar brands supply her father's light. From there were heard, rebellowing to the main, the roars of lions that refuse the chain, the grunts of bristled boars, and the groans of bears, and the herds of howling wolves that stun the sailors' ears. These, from their caverns, at the close of night, fill the sad island with horror and fright. In the darkness they mourn their fate, whom Circe's power (who watched the moon and the planetary hour), with words and wicked herbs, had altered from humankind and confined in brutal shapes. Lest the Trojans' pious host should bear these monsters or touch upon the enchanted coast, propitious Neptune steered their course by night with rising gales that sped their happy flight. Supplied with these, they skimmed the sounding shore, and heard the swelling surges vainly roar. Now, when the rosy morn began to rise, and waved her saffron streamer through the skies; when Thetis blushed in a purple not her own, and the breathing winds were blown from her face, a sudden silence sat upon the sea, and sweeping oars, with struggling, urged their way. From the main, the Trojan beheld a wood, which stood thick with shades and a brown horror; between the trees the Tiber took his course, dimpled with whirlpools, and with downward force, which drove the sand along, he took his way, and rolled his yellow billows to the sea. About him, and above, and round the wood, the birds that haunt the borders of his flood, that bathed within, or basked upon his side, applied their narrow throats to tuneful songs. The captain gave the command; the joyful train glided through the gloomy shade, and left the main.

Now, Erato, inspire your poet's mind, and fill his soul with your celestial fire! Relate what Latium was; tell of her ancient kings; declare the past and present state of things, when the Trojan fleet first sought Ausonia, and how the rivals loved, and how they fought. These are my theme, and how the war began, and how it was concluded by the godlike man. For I shall sing of battles, blood, and rage, which princes and their people did engage; and haughty souls, who, moved with mutual hate, pursued and found their fate in fighting fields; that roused the Tyrrhene realm with loud alarms, and involved peaceful Italy in arms. A larger scene of action is displayed; and, rising hence, a greater work is weighed.

Latinus, old and mild, had long possessed the Latin scepter, and had blessed his people. His father was Faunus; his mother a Laurentian dame, fair Marica by name. But Faunus came from Picus; Picus drew his birth from Saturn, if records be true. Thus King Latinus, in the third degree, had Saturn as author of his family. But this old peaceful prince, as Heaven decreed, was blessed with no male issue to succeed: his sons in blooming youth were snatched by fate; one only daughter inherited the royal state. Fired with her love, and led by ambition, the neighboring princes courted her nuptial bed. Among the crowd, but far above the rest, young Turnus addressed himself to the beauteous maid. Turnus, for high descent and graceful mien, was first, and favored by the Latian queen; with him she strove to join Lavinia's hand, but dire portents withstood the purposed match.

Deep in the palace, of long growth, there stood the trunk of a laurel, a venerable wood; where divine rites were paid, whose holy hair was kept and cut with superstitious care. Latinus, when he walled his town, then found this plant, and from the tree called it Laurentum; and last, in honor of his new abode, he vowed the laurel to the laurel's god. It happened once (a boding prodigy) that a swarm of bees, which cut the liquid sky, unknown from where they took their airy flight, alighted in clouds on the topmost branch. There with their clasping feet they clung together, and a long cluster hung from the laurel. An ancient augur prophesied from this: "Behold on Latian shores a foreign prince! From the same parts of heaven his navy comes, to the same parts on earth; his army lands; the town he conquers, and commands the tower."

Yet more: when fair Lavinia fed the fire before the gods, and stood beside her sire, strange to relate, the flames, involved in the smoke of incense, broke from the sacred altar, and caught her disheveled hair and rich attire. Her crown and jewels crackled in the fire; from there the fuming trail began to spread, and lambent glories danced about her head. This new portent the seer viewed with wonder; then, pausing, he thus renewed his prophecy: "The nymph, who scatters flaming fires around, shall shine with honor, shall herself be crowned; but, caused by her irrevocable fate, war shall waste the country, and change the state."

Latinus, frightened with this dire omen, went for counsel to his father Faunus, and sought the shades renowned for prophecy, which lie near Albunea's sulphurous fountain. To these the Latian and the Sabine land flee, when distressed, and from thence demand relief. The priest takes his ease on the skins of offerings, and sees nightly visions in his slumber; a swarm of thin aerial shapes appears, and, fluttering round his temples, deafens his ears. These he consults, to know the future fates from the powers above, and from the fiends below. Here Latinus flew for the gods' advice, offering a hundred sheep for sacrifice. Their woolly fleeces, as the rites required, he laid beneath him, and retired to rest. No sooner were his eyes bound in slumber, when from above, a more than mortal sound invaded his ears; and thus the vision spoke: "Do not seek, my offspring, to yoke our fair Lavinia in Latian bonds, nor provoke the gods. A foreign son descends upon your shore, whose martial fame extends from pole to pole. His race, renowned in arms and in arts of peace, neither Latium shall contain, nor Europe bound: theirs shall be whatever the sun surveys." These answers, received in the silent night, the king himself divulged, and the land believed. Fame flew through all the neighboring nations, when now the Trojan navy was in view.

Beneath a shady tree, the hero spread his table on the turf, with cakes of bread; and with his chiefs, he fed on forest fruits. They sat, and (not without the gods' command), having dispatched their homely fare, the hungry band invaded their trenchers next, and soon devoured, to mend the scanty meal, their very cakes of flour. Ascanius observed this, and, smiling, said: "See, we devour the plates on which we fed!" The speech had an omen in it, that the Trojan race should find rest, and that this was the time and place. Aeneas took up the word, and thus replied, confessing fate with wonder in his eyes: "All hail, O earth! All hail, my household gods! Behold the destined place of your abodes! For thus Anchises prophesied of old, and foretold this our fatal place of rest: 'When, on a foreign shore, instead of meat, forced by famine, you shall eat your trenchers, then ease will attend your weary Trojans, and the long labors of your voyage shall end. Remember, on that happy coast, to build, and to enclose the fruitful field with a trench.' This was that famine, and this the fatal place, which ends the wandering of our exiled race. Then, on tomorrow's dawn, employ your care to search the land, and where the cities lie, and what the men are; but give this day to joy. Now pour libations to Jove; and, after Jove is blessed, call great Anchises to the genial feast. Crown the goblets high with a cheerful draught; enjoy the present hour; adjourn the future thought."

Thus having said, the hero bound his brows with leafy branches; then performed his vows, adoring first the genius of the place; then Earth, the mother of the heavenly race; the nymphs, and native godheads yet unknown; and Night, and all the stars that gild her sable throne; and ancient Cybele, and Idaean Jove; and last his sire below, and his mother queen above. Then heaven's high monarch thundered three times aloud, and three times shook a golden cloud aloft. Soon through the joyful camp a rumor flew that the time had come for them to renew their city. Then every brow was crowned with cheerful green; the feasts were doubled, and the bowls went round.

When next the rosy morn disclosed the day, the scouts divided their way to several parts, to learn the names of the natives, to explore their towns, and the coasts and bends of the crooked shore: here flows Tiber, and here stands Numicus; here warlike Latins hold the happy lands. The pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways to found his empire and to raise his town, selected a hundred youths from all his train, and directed their course to the Latian court (the spacious palace where their prince resides), and veiled all their heads with wreaths of olive. They went commissioned to ask for peace, and to carry presents to procure access. Thus while they hastened their pace, the prince designed his newly elected seat, and drew the lines. The Trojans cast a rampart round the place, and set palisades about the trenches.

Meanwhile the train, proceeding on their way, surveyed the town and the lofty towers from afar. At length they approached the walls. Outside the gate, they saw the boys and Latian youth contend for the martial prizes on the dusty plain: some drove the cars, some reined the coursers; some bent the stubborn bow for victory, and some tried their active sinews with darts. A posting messenger, dispatched from there, advised their aged prince of this fair troop, that foreign men of mighty stature had come, uncouth in habit, and unknown in name. The king ordained their entrance, and ascended his regal seat, surrounded by his friends.

The palace built by Picus, vast and proud, stood supported by a hundred pillars, and was surrounded by a rising wood. The pile overlooked the town, and drew the sight, surprising at once with reverence and delight. There kings received the marks of sovereign power; in state the monarchs marched; the lictors bore their awful axes, and the rods before. Here the tribunal stood, the house of prayer, and here the sacred senators repaired; all set at large tables in long order, a ram their offering, and a ram their meat. Above the portal, carved in cedar wood, stood their godlike grandsires placed in their ranks: old Saturn, with his crooked scythe on high; and Italus, who led the colony; and ancient Janus, with his double face, and bunch of keys, the porter of the place. There good Sabinus, planter of the vines, reclined his head on a short pruning hook, and studiously surveyed his generous wines. Then warlike kings, who fought for their country, and brought honorable wounds from battle. Around the posts hung helmets, darts, and spears, and captive chariots, axes, shields, and bars, and broken beaks of ships, the trophies of their wars. Above the rest, as chief of all the band, was placed Picus, with a buckler in his hand; his other hand waved a long divining wand. The hero sat girt in his Gabine gown, yet he could not with his art avoid his fate: for Circe had long loved the youth in vain, till love, refused, converted to disdain. Then, mixing powerful herbs with magic art, she changed his form, since she could not change his heart; she constrained him into a bird, and made him fly as a chattering magpie, with party-colored plumes.

In this high temple, on a chair of state, the seat of audience, old Latinus sat; then gave admission to the Trojan train, and thus began with pleasing accents: "Tell me, you Trojans (for that name you own, nor is your course unknown upon our coasts), say what you seek, and where you were bound. Were you cast aground by stress of weather, such dangers as are often seen at sea, and often befall miserable men? Or have you come to lay your shipping in our ports, spent and disabled by so long a way? Say what you want; you shall find the Latians not forced to goodness, but inclined by will; for, since the time of Saturn's holy reign, we retain his hospitable customs. I call to mind (though time has worn the tale) that the Aurunci said that Dardanus, though born on Latian plains, yet sought the Phrygian shore, and Samothracia, formerly called Samos. From Tuscan Corythus he claimed his birth; but afterwards, when exempt from mortal earth, he ascended from there to his kindred skies, a god, and, as a god, augments their sacrifice."

He said. Ilioneus made this reply: "O king, of Faunus' royal family! Neither did wintry winds force our way to Latium, nor did the stars betray our wandering course. Willingly we sought your shores; and, bound here, we at length found the long-desired port; expelled from our sweet homes and ancient realms, once as great as the greatest the sun beheld. The god who rules above began our line; and, as our race, our king descends from Jove; and here we have come, by his command, to crave admission in your happy land. How dire a tempest, poured from Mycenae, devoured our plains, our temples, and our town; what was the waste of war, what fierce alarms shook Asia's crown with European arms—even such have heard of it, if any such there be, whose earth is bounded by the frozen sea, and such as, born beneath the burning sky and sultry sun, lie between the tropics. From that dire deluge, through the watery waste, having past such length of years and various perils, we have at last escaped, and we repair to Latium, to beg what you without your own want may spare: the common water, and the common air; and sheds which we ourselves will build, and mean abodes, fit to receive and serve our banished gods. Nor shall our admission disgrace your realm, nor shall length of time efface our gratitude. Besides, what endless honor shall you gain, to save and shelter Troy's unhappy train! Now, by my sovereign, and by his fate, I swear—renowned for faith in peace, for force in war—often our alliance has been desired by other lands, and what we seek of you has been required of us. Do not despise, then, that in our hands we bear these holy boughs, and sue with words of prayer. Fate and the gods, by their supreme command, have doomed our ships to seek the Latian land. Apollo sends our fleet to these abodes; here Dardanus was born, and here he tends; where Tuscan Tiber rolls with rapid force, and where Numicus opens his holy source. Besides, our prince presents, with his request, some small remains of what his sire possessed: this golden charger, snatched from burning Troy, Anchises employed in sacrifice; old Priam wore this royal robe and this tiara, and bore this golden scepter in full assemblies, and in solemn games; these purple vests were woven by Dardan dames."

Thus while he spoke, Latinus rolled his eyes around, and fixed them for a while upon the ground. He seemed intent, and anxious in his breast; not moved by the scepter or the kingly vest, but pondering future things of wondrous weight: succession, empire, and his daughter's fate. On these he mused within his thoughtful mind, and then revolved what Faunus had divined. This was the foreign prince, decreed by fate to share his scepter and Lavinia's bed; this was the race that sure portents foreshow would sway the world, and subdue land and sea. At length he raised his cheerful head, and spoke: "The powers," he said, "the powers we both invoke, to you, and to yours, and to mine, may they be propitious, and confirm our purpose with their augury! Have what you ask; I receive your presents; land, where and when you please, with ample leave; partake and use my kingdom as your own; all shall be yours, while I command the crown. And, if my wished alliance pleases your king, tell him he should not send the peace, but bring it. Then let him not fear a friend's embraces; the peace is made when I behold him here. Besides this answer, tell my royal guest, I add my own request to his commands: one only daughter inherits my crown and state, whom neither our oracles, nor Heaven, nor fate, nor frequent prodigies, permit to join with any native of the Ausonian line. A foreign son-in-law shall come from far (such is our doom), a chief renowned in war, whose race shall bear aloft the Latian name, and diffuse our fame through the conquered world. That he himself is the man the fates require, I firmly judge, and, what I judge, I desire."

He said, and then bestowed a steed on each. Three hundred horses, fed in high stables, stood ready, all shining, and smoothly dressed. Of these he chose the fairest and the best, to mount the Trojan troop. At his command, the steeds stood caparisoned with purple, with golden trappings, glorious to behold, and champed the foaming gold between their teeth. Then to his absent guest the king decreed a pair of coursers born of heavenly breed, which breathed ethereal fire from their nostrils—which Circe had stolen from her celestial sire, by substituting mares produced on earth, whose wombs had conceived a more than mortal birth. These drew the chariot which Latinus sent, and commended the rich present to the prince. Borne sublime on stately steeds, the Trojans returned to their expecting lord with peace.

But jealous Juno, from the height of Pachynus, as she took her airy flight from Argos, beheld with envious eyes this hateful sight. She saw the Trojan and his joyful train descending upon the shore, deserting the main, designing a town, and, with unhoped success, the ambassadors returning with a promised peace. Then, pierced with pain, she shook her haughty head, sighed from her inward soul, and thus she said: "O hated offspring of my Phrygian foes! O fates of Troy, that oppose Juno's fates! Could they not fall unpitied on the plain, but revive slain, and, taken, escape again? When execrable Troy lay in ashes, through fires and swords and seas they forced their way. Then vanquished Juno must contend in vain, her rage disarmed, her empire at an end. Is all my fury spent, breathless and tired? Or does my glutted spleen at length relent? As if it were too little to chase them from their town, I pursued their exiled race through the seas; I engaged the heavens, opposed the stormy main; but billows roared, and tempests raged in vain. What have my Scyllas and my Syrtes done, when they overpass these, and shun those? On Tiber's shores they land, secure of fate, triumphant over the storms and over Juno's hate. Mars could bathe the Centaurs in mutual blood, and Jove himself gave way to Cynthia's wrath, who sent the tusky boar to Calydon; what great offense had either people done? But I, the consort of the Thunderer, have waged a long and unsuccessful war, with various arts and arms have toiled in vain, and at length am foiled by a mortal man. If native power does not prevail, shall I doubt to seek needful succor from without? If Jove and Heaven deny my just desires, Hell shall supply the power of Heaven and Jove. Grant that the Fates have firmed, by their decree, that the Trojan race shall reign in Italy; at least I can defer the nuptial day, and delay the peace with protracted wars. The dear alliance shall be bought with blood, and both peoples brought near destruction; so shall the son-in-law and father join, with ruin, war, and the waste of either line. O fatal maid, your marriage is endowed with Phrygian, Latian, and Rutulian blood! Bellona leads you to your lover's hand; another queen brings forth another brand, to burn another land with foreign fires! A second Paris, differing only in name, shall fire his country with a second flame."

Thus having said, she sinks beneath the ground, with furious haste, and shoots across the Stygian sound, to rouse Alecto from the infernal seat of her dire sisters, and from their dark retreat.
