This Fury, fit for her intent, she chose—one who delights in wars and human woes. Even Pluto hates his own misshapen race; her sister Furies fly her hideous face; so frightful are the forms the monster takes, so fierce the hissings of her speckled snakes. Juno finds her, and thus inflames her spite: "O virgin daughter of eternal Night, give me this once your labor, to sustain my right, and to execute my just disdain. Let not the Trojans, with a feigned pretense of proffered peace, delude the Latian prince. Expel that odious name from Italy, and let not Juno suffer in her fame. It is yours to ruin realms, to overturn a state, to raise debate between the dearest friends, and to kindle kindred blood into mutual hate. Your hand displays the funeral torch over towns, and forms a thousand ills in ten thousand ways. Now shake out from your fruitful breast the seeds of envy, discord, and of cruel deeds. Confound the established peace, and prepare their souls for hatred, and their hands for war."

Smeared as she was with black Gorgonian blood, the Fury sprang above the Stygian flood; and on her wicker wings, sublime through night, she took her flight to the Latian palace. There she sought the queen's apartment, stood before the peaceful threshold, and besieged the door. Restless Amata lay, her swelling breast fired with disdain over Turnus' dispossession, and over the new nuptials of the Trojan guest. From her black bloody locks the Fury shook her darling plague, the favorite of her snakes; with her full force she threw the poisonous dart, and fixed it deep within Amata's heart, that, thus envenomed, she might kindle rage, and sacrifice to strife her house and her husband's age. Unseen, unfelt, the fiery serpent skimmed between her linen and her naked limbs, inspiring his baleful breath as he glided; now like a chain around her neck he rode; now like a fillet he repaired to her head, and folded her hair with his circling coils. At first the silent venom slid with ease, and seized her cooler senses by degrees; then, before the infected mass was fired too far, in plaintive accents she began the war, and thus bespoke her husband: "Shall," she said, "a wandering prince enjoy Lavinia's bed? If nature does not plead in a parent's heart, pity my tears, and pity her desert. I know, my dearest lord, the time will come when you would, in vain, reverse your cruel doom; the faithless pirate will soon set to sea, and bear the royal virgin far away! A guest like him, a Trojan guest before, in the show of friendship sought the Spartan shore, and ravished Helen from her husband. Think on a king's inviolable word; and think on Turnus, her once plighted lord. To this false foreigner you give your throne, and wrong a friend, a kinsman, and a son. Resume your ancient care; and, if the god your sire, and you, resolve on foreign blood, know that all are foreign, in a larger sense, who are not born your subjects, or derived from here. Then, if you trace the line of Turnus, he springs from Inachus, of Argive race."

But when she saw her reasons idly spent, and that she could not move him from his fixed intent, she flew to rage; for now the snake possessed her vital parts, and poisoned all her breast. She raved, she ran with a distracted pace, and filled the public place with horrid howls. And, as young striplings whip the top for sport on the smooth pavement of an empty court—the wooden engine flies and whirls about, admired, with clamors, by the beardless rout; they lash aloud; they provoke one another, and lend their little souls at every stroke—thus fared the queen; and thus her fury blew amid the crowd, and kindled as she went. Nor yet content, she strained her malice more, and added new ills to those contrived before. She fled the town, and, mixing with a throng of madding matrons, bore the bride along, wandering through woods and wilds, and devious ways, and with these arts delayed the Trojan match. She feigned the rites of Bacchus, cried aloud, and vowed the virgin to the buxom god. "Evoe! O Bacchus!" thus began the song; and "Evoe!" answered all the female throng. "O virgin! Worthy of you alone!" she cried; "O worthy of you alone!" the crew replied. "For you she feeds her hair, she leads your dance, and wreathes her lance with your winding ivy." Like fury seized the rest; the progress known, all sought the mountains, and forsook the town. All, clad in the skins of beasts, bore the javelin; they gave their flowing hair to the wanton winds, and shrieks and shoutings rent the suffering air. The queen herself, inspired with divine rage, shook a flaming pine high above her head; then rolled her haggard eyes around the throng, and sang, in Turnus' name, the nuptial song: "Io, you Latian dames! If any here hold your unhappy queen, Amata, dear; if there be here," she said, "who dare maintain my right, nor think the name of mother vain, unbind your fillets, loose your flowing hair, and prepare orgies and nocturnal rites."

Thus the Fury invades Amata's breast, and fires her with rage, amid the sylvan shades. Then, when she found her venom had spread so far, and that the royal house was embroiled in civil war, raised on her dusky wings, she cleaved the skies, and sought the palace where young Turnus lay. His town, as fame reports, was built of old by Danae, pregnant with almighty gold, who fled her father's rage, and, with a train of following Argives, through the stormy main, driven by the southern blasts, was fated to reign here. It was once called Ardua; now it bears the name of Ardea, once a fair city, now consumed with years. Here, in his lofty palace, Turnus lay, between the confines of night and day, secure in sleep. The Fury laid aside her looks and limbs, and tried, with new methods, to hide the foulness of her infernal form. Propped on a staff, she took on a trembling mien; her face was furrowed, and her front obscene; she drew deep-dinted wrinkles on her cheek; her eyes were sunk, and her jaws toothless; her hoary hair was bound with holy fillets, and her temples were crowned with an olive wreath. Old Chalybe, who kept the sacred fane of Juno, she now seemed to be; and thus, appearing in a dream, began to rouse the careless man: "Shall Turnus, then, sustain such endless toil in fighting fields, and conquer towns in vain? Win, for a Trojan head to wear the prize, usurp your crown, enjoy your victories? The bride and scepter which your blood has bought, the king transfers, and foreign heirs are sought. Go now, deluded man, and seek again new toils, new dangers, on the dusty plain. Repel the Tuscan foes; seize their city; protect the Latians in luxurious ease. This dream all-powerful Juno sends; I bear her mighty mandates, and her words you hear. Haste; arm your Ardeans; issue to the plain; with Fate as your friend, assault the Trojan train; their thoughtless chiefs, their painted ships that lie in Tiber's mouth, destroy with fire and sword. The Latian king, unless he submits, and owns his old promise, and forgets his new; let him prove, in arms, the power of Turnus, and learn to fear whom he disdains to love. For such is Heaven's command." The youthful prince replied with scorn, and made this bold defense: "You tell me, mother, what I knew before: the Phrygian fleet is landed on the shore. I neither fear nor will provoke the war; my fate is Juno's most peculiar care. But time has made you dote, and you vainly tell of arms imagined in your lonely cell. Go; let the temple and the gods be your care; permit the thought of peace and war to men."

These haughty words provoked Alecto's rage, and frightened Turnus trembled as she spoke. Her eyes grew stiffened, and with sulphur burned; her hideous looks and hellish form returned; her curling snakes filled the place with hissings, and opened all the furies of her face. Then, darting fire from her malignant eyes, she cast him backward as he strove to rise, and, lingering, sought to frame some new replies. High on her head she reared two twisted snakes; her chains she rattled, and her whip she shook; and, churning bloody foam, thus loudly spoke: "Behold whom time has made to dote, and tell of arms imagined in her lonely cell! Behold the Fates' infernal minister! War, death, destruction, I bear in my hand."

Thus having said, she plunged her smoldering torch, impressed with her full force, into his breast. Aghast he woke; and, starting from his bed, cold sweat overspread his limbs in clammy drops. "Arms! Arms!" he cried. "Prepare my sword and shield!" He breathed defiance, blood, and mortal war. So, when with crackling flames a cauldron fries, the bubbling waters rise from the bottom; above the brims they force their fiery way; black vapors climb aloft, and cloud the day.

The peace thus polluted, he first commissioned a chosen band to the Latian land in threatening embassy; then he raised the rest, to meet in arms the intruding Trojan guest, to force the foes from the Lavinian shore, and to restore Italy's endangered peace. He boasted himself alone an equal match, to fight the Phrygian and Ausonian hosts. The gods invoked, the Rutuli prepared their arms, and warned each other to the war. His beauty engaged these, his blooming age engaged those; the rest were engaged by his house and his own fame.

While Turnus thus urges his enterprise, the Stygian Fury flew to the Trojans; she invented new frauds, and took a steepy stand, which overlooked the vale with wide command, where fair Ascanius and his youthful train, with horns and hounds, were ordaining a hunting match, and pitching their toils around the shady plain. The Fury fired the pack; they snuffed, they vented, and fed their hungry nostrils with the scent. It was of a well-grown stag, whose antlers rose high above his brow; his beams invaded the skies. From this light cause the infernal maid prepared the country churls for mischief, hate, and wars.

The two Tyrrhidae had bred the stately beast, having snatched him from his dam, and fed the tame young thing. Their father Tyrrheus brought him fodder; Tyrrheus was chief ranger to the Latian king. Their sister Silvia cherished with her care the little wanton, and prepared wreaths to hang on his budding horns; she tied ribbons around his tender neck, and combed his silken hide, and bathed his body. Patient of command, in time he grew, and, growing, used to the hand, he waited at his master's board for food; then he sought his wild kindred in the wood, where, grazing all the day, at night he came to his known lodgings, and to his country dame.

This household beast, that was used to the woodland grounds, was viewed first by the young hero's hounds, as he swam down the stream to seek retreat in the cool waters, and to quench his heat. Young Ascanius, eager for his game, soon bent his bow, uncertain in his aim; but the dire fiend guided the fatal arrow, which pierced his bowels through his panting sides. The bleeding creature issued from the floods, possessed with fear, and sought his known abodes, his old familiar hearth and household gods. He fell; he filled the house with heavy groans; implored their pity, and bemoaned his pain. Young Silvia beat her breast, and cried aloud for succor from the clownish neighborhood. The churls assembled; for the fiend, who lay in the close woody covert, urged their way. One came with a brand still burning from the flame, another armed with a knotty club; whatever they caught or found, without their care, their fury made an instrument of war. Tyrrheus, the foster father of the beast, then clenched a hatchet in his horny fist, but held his hand from the descending stroke, and left his wedge within the cloven oak, to whet their courage and provoke their rage. And now the goddess, exercised in ill, who watched an hour to work her impious will, ascended the roof, and added all her breath to her crooked horn, such as was then borne by Latian shepherds. The rocks, the woods around, and the mountains, trembled at the infernal sound. The sacred lake of Trivia from afar, the Veline fountains, and sulphureous Nar, shook at the baleful blast, the signal of the war. Young mothers stared wildly, possessed with fear, and strained their helpless infants to their breasts.

The clowns, a boisterous, rude, ungoverned crew, with furious haste flew to the loud summons. The powers of Troy, then issuing on the plain, sustained their youthful chief with fresh recruits—not a raw and inexperienced train, but a firm body of embattled men. At first, while fortune favored neither side, the fight was tried with clubs and burning brands; but now, both parties reinforced, the fields were bright with flaming swords and brazen shields. A shining harvest was displayed by either host, and each shot against the sun with equal rays. Thus, when a black-browed gust begins to rise, white foam at first boils on the curled ocean; then roars the main, and the billows mount the skies, until, fully blown by the fury of the storm, the muddy bottom is thrown over the clouds. Almon fell first, old Tyrrheus' eldest care, pierced with an arrow from the distant war: the flying weapon stood fixed in his throat, and stopped his breath, and drank his vital blood. Huge heaps of slain rose about the body; among the rest, rich Galesus lies, a good old man, who had in vain preached peace amidst the madness of the unruly train: five herds, five bleating flocks, filled his pastures; his lands were tilled by a hundred yoke of oxen.

Thus, while their fortune stood in equal scales, the Fury bathed them in each other's blood. Then, having fixed the fight, she exulting flew, and bore word to the skies that her promise was fulfilled. To Juno thus she speaks: "Behold! It is done, the blood already drawn, the war begun; the discord is complete; nor can they cease the dire debate, nor can you command the peace. Now, since the Latian and the Trojan brood have tasted vengeance and the sweets of blood, speak, and my power shall add this office more: the neighboring nations of the Ausonian shore shall hear the dreadful rumor, from afar, of armed invasion, and shall embrace the war." Then Juno thus: "The grateful work is done, the seeds of discord sown, the war begun; frauds, fears, and fury have possessed the state, and fixed the causes of a lasting hate. A bloody Hymen shall join the alliance between the Trojan and the Ausonian line. But you, with speed, repair to night and hell; for neither the gods, nor angry Jove, will bear your lawless wandering walks in upper air. Leave what remains to me." Saturnia said; the sullen fiend displayed her sounding wings, unwilling she left the light, and sought the nether shade.

In midst of Italy, well known to fame, there lies a lake, Amsanctus is its name, below the lofty mounts. On either side thick forests hide the forbidden entrance. Full in the center of the sacred wood an arm arises of the Stygian flood, which, breaking from beneath with bellowing sound, whirls the black waves and rattling stones around. Here Pluto pants for breath from out his cell, and opens wide the grinning jaws of hell. To this infernal lake the Fury flies; here hides her hated head, and frees the laboring skies.

Saturnian Juno now, with double care, attended the fatal process of the war. The clowns, returned from battle, bore the slain, implored the gods, and complained to their king. The corpses of Almon and the rest were shown; shrieks, clamors, murmurs, filled the frightened town. Ambitious Turnus appeared in the press, and, aggravating crimes, augmented their fears; he proclaimed his private injuries aloud, a solemn promise made, and disavowed: a foreign son is sought, and a mixed mongrel brood. Then those whose mothers, frantic with their fear, in woods and wilds bore the flags of Bacchus, and led his dances with disheveled hair, increased the clamor, and demanded war (such was Amata's interest in the land), against the public sanctions of the peace, against all omens of their ill success. With fates averse, the rout resorted in arms, to force their monarch, and to insult the court. But, like a rock unmoved, a rock that braves the raging tempest and the rising waves, propped upon himself he stood; his solid sides washed off the seaweeds and the sounding tides. So stood the pious prince, unmoved, and long he sustained the madness of the noisy throng. But when he found that Juno's power prevailed, and all the methods of cool counsel failed, he called the gods to witness their offense, disclaimed the war, asserted his innocence. "Hurried by fate," he cried, "and borne before a furious wind, we have wronged the faithful shore. O more than madmen! You yourselves shall bear the guilt of blood and sacrilegious war. You, Turnus, shall atone for it by your fate, and shall pray to Heaven for peace, but pray too late. For me, my stormy voyage at an end, I securely tend to the port of death. The funeral pomp which you pay to your kings is all I want, and all you take away." He said no more, but, confined in his walls, shut out the woes which he too well divined; nor would he vainly strive with the rising storm, but left the helm, and let the vessel drive.

A solemn custom was observed of old, which Latium held, and which now the Romans hold, when they rear their standard in fighting fields against the fierce Hyrcanians, or declare war upon the Scythian, Indian, or Arabian, or would regain from the boasting Parthians their eagles, lost in Carrhae's bloody plain. Two gates of steel (which bear the name of Mars, and are still worshiped with religious fear) stand before his temple: the dire abode, and the feared issues of the furious god, are fenced with brazen bolts; outside the gates, the wary guardian Janus doubly waits. Then, when the sacred senate votes the wars, the Roman consul declares their decree, and, in his robes, unbars the sounding gates. The youth rise in military shouts, and the loud trumpets break the yielding skies. These rites, of old used by sovereign princes, were the king's office; but the king refused, deaf to their cries, nor would he unbar the gates of sacred peace, or loose the imprisoned war; but hid his head, and, safe from loud alarms, abhorred the wicked ministry of arms. Then heaven's imperious queen shot down from high: at her approach the brazen hinges flew; the gates were forced, and every falling bar; and, like a tempest, the war issued out.

The peaceful cities of the Ausonian shore, lulled in their ease, and undisturbed before, were all on fire. Some, with studious care, prepared their restive steeds in sandy plains; some tried their soft limbs in painful marches, and war was all their wish, and arms the general cry. Part scoured the rusty shields with seam; part ground anew the blunted axe, and pointed the dart; with joy they viewed the waving ensigns fly, and heard the trumpet's clangor pierce the sky. Five cities forged their arms: the Atinian powers, Antemnae, Tibur with her lofty towers, Ardea the proud, the Crustumerian town: all these of old were places of renown. Some hammered helmets for the fighting field; some twined young willows to support the shield; some molded the corselet, and some the cuisses, plated with silver, and with ductile gold. The rustic honors of the scythe and share gave place to swords and plumes, the pride of war. Old falchions were newly tempered in the fires; the sounding trumpet inspired every soul. The word was given; with eager speed they laced the shining headpiece, and embraced the shield. The neighing steeds were tied to the chariot; the trusty weapon sat on every side.

And now the mighty labor has begun. You Muses, open all your Helicon. Sing, you, the chiefs that swayed the Ausonian land, their arms, and the armies under their command; what warriors were bred in our ancient clime; what soldiers followed, and what heroes led. For you alone know well, and can record, what fame conveys to future times but darkly. Mezentius first appeared upon the plain: scorn sat upon his brows, and sour disdain, defying earth and heaven. Etruria lost, he brought his baffled host to Turnus' aid. The charming Lausus, full of youthful fire, rode in the rank, next to his sullen sire; second only to Turnus in the grace of manly mien and features of the face. A skillful horseman, and a huntsman bred, with fates averse, he led a thousand men: his sire unworthy of so brave a son; himself well worthy of a happier throne.

Next Aventinus drove his chariot round the Latian plains, crowned with palms and laurels. Proud of his steeds, he smoked along the field; his father's hydra filled his ample shield: a hundred serpents hissed about the brim. He justly seemed the son of Hercules, by his broad shoulders and gigantic limbs; of heavenly part, and part of earthly blood, a mortal woman mixing with a god. For strong Alcides, after he had slain the triple Geryon, drove his captive herds from conquered Spain; and, thence in triumph led, they fed on the flowery banks of Tuscan Tiber. Then on Mount Aventine the son of Jove found the priestess Rhea, and forced her to love. For arms, his men bore long pikes and javelins, and gored their foes in battle with poles of pointed steel. Like Hercules himself his son appeared, in savage pomp; he wore a lion's hide; about his shoulders hung the shaggy skin; the teeth and gaping jaws severely grinned. Thus, like his father the god, homely dressed, he strode into the hall, a horrid guest.

Then two twin brothers came from fair Tibur (which took its name from their brother Tiburs), fierce Coras and Catillus, void of fear. They led armed Argive horse, and appeared in the front. Like cloud-born Centaurs, descending rapidly from the mountain's height to the fight, they rushed along; the rattling woods gave way; the branches bent before their sweepy sway.

Nor was Praeneste's founder wanting there, whom fame reports was the son of Mulciber: found in the fire, and fostered in the plains, he reigned a shepherd and a king at once, and led to Turnus' aid his country swains. His own Praeneste sent a chosen band, with those who plow Saturnia's Gabine land; besides the succor which cold Anien yields, the rocks of Hernicus, and the dewy fields, fat Anagnia, and Father Amasene—a numerous rout, but all of naked men: nor did they wear arms, nor wield swords and bucklers, nor drive the chariot through the dusty field, but whirled huge balls of lead from leathern slings, and the spoils of yellow wolves adorned their heads; the left foot naked, when they marched to fight, but in a bull's raw hide they sheathed the right. Next Messapus (great Neptune was his sire), secure of steel, and fated from the fire, appeared in pomp, and warmed with his ardor a heartless train, unexercised in arms. He brought the just Faliscans to battle, and those who live where Lake Ciminius springs; and where Feronia's grove and temple stand, who till Fescennian or Flavinian lands. All these marched in order, and marching they sang the warlike actions of their sea-born king; like a long team of snowy swans on high, which clap their wings, and cleave the liquid sky, when, borne homeward from their watery pastures, they sing, and Asia's lakes return their notes. Not one who heard their music from afar would think these troops an army trained to war, but flocks of fowl, which, when the tempests roar, seek the silent shore with their hoarse gabbling.

Then Clausus came, who led a numerous band of troops embodied from the Sabine land, and, in himself alone, brought an army. It was he who begot the noble Claudian race—the Claudian race, ordained, in times to come, to share in the greatness of imperial Rome. He led forth the Cures, of old renown; the Mutuscans from their olive-bearing town; and all the Eretian powers; besides a band that followed from the dewy land of Velinum; and the Amiternian troops of mighty fame; and the mountaineers, who came from Severus, and from the craggy cliffs of Tetrica; and those where yellow Tiber takes his way, and where Himella's wanton waters play. Casperia sent her arms, with those that lie by Fabaris, and by fruitful Foruli. The warlike aids of Horta next appeared, and the cold Nursians came to close the rear, mixed with the natives born of Latin blood, whom Allia washes with her fatal flood. Not thicker billows beat the Libyan main, when pale Orion sets in wintry rain; nor thicker harvests rise on rich Hermus, or in the Lycian fields, when Phoebus burns the skies, than stood these troops: their bucklers rang around; their trampling turned the turf, and shook the solid ground.

High in his chariot then Halesus came, a foe by birth to Troy's unhappy name: born of Agamemnon; to Turnus' aid the youthful hero led a thousand men, who till the Massic soil, renowned for wine, and the fierce Auruncans from their hilly ground, and those who live by the Sidicinian shores, and where Vulturnus roars with shoaly fords; the old inhabitants of Cales and of Osca, and the rough Saticulans, inured to wants. From afar they throw light demi-lances, fastened with leathern thongs, to gall the foe. In closer fight they wear short crooked swords; and on their warding arm they bear light bucklers.

Nor, Oebalus, shall you be left unsung, sprung from the nymph Semethis and old Telon, who then reigned in Teleboan Capri. But the ambitious youth disdained that short isle, and stretched his ample sway over Campania, where swelling Sarnus seeks the Tyrrhene sea; over Batulum, and where Abella sees, from her high towers, the harvest of her trees. And these (as was the Teuton use of old) wielded brazen swords and held brazen bucklers; slung weighty stones, when they fought from afar; their casques were cork, a covering thick and light.

Next these in rank, the warlike Ufens went, and led the mountain troops that Nursia sent. The rude Equicoli obeyed his rule: hunting was their sport, and plundering was their trade. They plowed in arms, ever ready for battle: their soil was barren, and their hearts were hard.

Umbro the priest led the proud Marrubians, sent by King Archippus to Turnus' aid, and peaceful olives crowned his hoary head. With his wand and holy words he could assuage the viper's rage and the venomed wounds of serpents. When he pleased to steep their temples with powerful juice, he shut their eyes in pleasing sleep. But vain were Marsian herbs and magic art to cure the wound given by the Dardan dart: yet the Angitian woods remurmured his untimely fate in sighs to the Fucine floods.

The son of famed Hippolytus was there, famed like his sire, and, like his mother, fair; whom in the Egerian groves Aricia bore, and nursed his youth along the marshy shore, where great Diana's peaceful altars flame, in fruitful fields; and Virbius was his name. Hippolytus, as old records have said, was sought by his stepmother to share her bed; but when no female arts could move his mind, she turned her impious love to furious hate. Torn by wild horses on the sandy shore, the unhappy hunter bore another's crimes, glutting his father's eyes with guiltless gore. But chaste Diana, who deplored his death, restored his life with Aesculapian herbs. Then Jove, who saw from on high, with just disdain, the dead inspired with vital breath again, struck to the center, with his flaming dart, the unhappy founder of the godlike art. But Trivia kept her care, Hippolytus, alone in secret shades, unknown to fate, and called him Virbius in the Egerian grove, where then he lived obscure, but safe from Jove. For this reason, from Trivia's temple and her wood, horses that shed their master's blood are driven, affrighted by the monsters of the flood. His son, the second Virbius, retained his father's art, and reined warrior steeds.

Amid the troops, and like the leading god, high above the rest in arms rode the graceful Turnus: a triple plume adorned his crest, on which Chimaera burned with belching flames: the higher the kindled combat rises, the more fiercely the blazing fire burns. Fair Io graced his shield; but Io now stands with horns exalted, and seems to low—a noble charge! Her keeper, by her side, to watch her walks, applied his hundred eyes; and on the brims her sire, the watery god, rolled his crystal flood from a silver urn. A cloud of foot succeeded, and filled the fields with swords, and pointed spears, and clattering shields; of Argives, and of old Sicanian bands, and those who plow the rich Rutulian lands; Auruncan youth, and those whom Sacrana yielded, and the proud Labicans, with painted shields; and those who reside near the Numician streams, and those whom Tiber's holy forests hide, or whom Circe's hills divide from the main land; where Ufens glides along the lowly lands, or where the black water of Pomptina stands.

Last, from the Volscians fair Camilla came, and led her warlike troops, a warrior dame; unbred to spinning, unskilled in the loom, she chose the nobler Pallas of the field. Mixed with the first, the fierce Virago fought, sustained the toils of arms, sought the danger, outstripped the winds in speed upon the plain, flew over the fields, nor hurt the bearded grain. She swept the seas, and, as she skimmed along, her flying feet hung unbathed on the billows. Men, boys, and women, stupid with surprise, wherever she passed, fixed their wondering eyes; longingly they looked, and, gaping at the sight, devoured her over and over with vast delight. Her purple habit sat with such a grace on her smooth shoulders, and so suited her face; her head was crowned with the ringlets of her hair, and the curls were bound in a golden caul. She shook her myrtle javelin; and, behind, her Lycian quiver danced in the wind.

chapters.title: Book VIII
paragraphs: The war having now begun, both generals make all possible preparations. Turnus sends to Diomedes. Aeneas goes in person to beg succors from Evander and the Tuscans. Evander receives him kindly, furnishes him with men, and sends his son Pallas with him. Vulcan, at the request of Venus, makes arms for her son Aeneas, and draws on his shield the most memorable actions of his posterity.

When Turnus had assembled all his powers, and planted his standard on Laurentum's towers; when now the sprightly trumpet, from afar, had given the signal of approaching war, had roused the neighing steeds to scour the fields, while the fierce riders clattered on their shields; trembling with rage, the Latian youth prepared to join the allies, and headlong rushed to war. Fierce Ufens and Messapus led the crowd, with bold Mezentius, who blasphemed aloud. These took their wasteful course through the country, to forage the fields and to gather force. Then they sent Venulus to Diomedes, to beg his aid in defending Ausonia, declaring the common danger, and informing the Grecian leader of the growing storm: "Aeneas, landed on the Latian coast, with banished gods and with a baffled host, yet now aspired to conquest of the state, and claimed a title from the gods and from fate; what numerous nations came in his quarrel, and how they spread his formidable name. What he designed, what mischief might arise, if fortune favored his first enterprise, was left for Diomedes himself to weigh, whose equal fears, and common interest, were involved in theirs."

While Turnus and the allies thus urged the war, the Trojan, floating in a flood of care, beheld the tempest which his foes prepared. This way and that he turned his anxious mind; he thought, and rejected the counsels he had designed; he explored himself in vain, in every part, and gave no rest to his distracted heart. So, when the sun by day, or the moon by night, strikes on polished brass their trembling light, the glittering species divide here and there, and cast their dubious beams from side to side; now they play on the walls, now on the pavement, and flash the glaring day to the ceiling.

It was night; and weary nature had lulled asleep the birds of the air, and the fishes of the deep, and beasts, and mortal men. The Trojan chief lay on Tiber's banks, oppressed with grief, and found a late relief in silent slumber. Then, through the shadows of the poplar wood, arose the father of the Roman flood. An azure robe was spread over his body; a wreath of shady reeds adorned his head. Thus, manifest to sight, the god appeared, and with these pleasing words cheered his sorrow: "Undoubted offspring of ethereal race, O long expected in this promised place, who has borne your banished gods through the foes, restored them to their hearths and old abodes: this is your happy home, the clime where fate ordains you to restore the Trojan state. Fear not! The war shall end in lasting peace, and all the rage of haughty Juno shall cease. And, so that this nightly vision may not seem the effect of fancy, or an idle dream, a sow shall lie along beneath an oak, all white herself, and white her thirty young. When thirty rolling years have run their race, your son Ascanius, on this empty space, shall build a royal town, of lasting fame, which from this omen shall receive its name. Time shall approve the truth. For what remains, and how to crown your pains with sure success, attend next with patience. A banished band, driven with Evander from the Arcadian land, have planted here, and placed their walls on high; their founder calls their town Pallanteum, derived from Pallas, his great-grandsire's name. But the fierce Latians claim old possession, infesting the new colony with war. Make these your friends, and rely on their aid. I submit my streams to your free passage. Wake, son of Venus, from your pleasing dreams; and, when the setting stars are lost in day, pay your just devotion to Juno's power; appease the wrathful queen with sacrifice: her pride at length shall fall, her fury cease. When you return victorious from the war, perform your vows to me with grateful care. I am the god whose yellow water flows around these fields, and fattens as it goes: my name is Tiber; among the rolling floods I am renowned on earth, esteemed among the gods. This is my certain seat. In times to come, my waves shall wash the walls of mighty Rome."

He said, and plunged below. While he yet spoke, his dream and his sleep forsook Aeneas. He rose, and, looking up, beheld the skies with purple blushing, and the day arising. Then he took water in his hollow palm from Tiber's flood, and thus addressed the powers: "Laurentian nymphs, by whom the streams are fed, and Father Tiber, in your sacred bed, receive Aeneas, and keep him from danger. Whatever fount, whatever holy deep, conceals your watery stores; wherever they rise, and, bubbling from below, salute the skies; you, king of horned floods, whose plenteous urn suffices fatness to the fruitful corn, for this your kind compassion on our woes, you shall share my morning song and evening vows. But, O be present to the aid of your people, and confirm the gracious promise you have made!" Thus having said, he chose two galleys with care from his stores, manned them, and fitted them with oars. Now on the shore the fated swine was found. Wondrous to tell!—she lay along the ground, her well-fed offspring hanging at her udders, she white herself, and white her thirty young. Aeneas takes the mother and her brood, and all are bestowed upon Juno's altar.

The following night, and the succeeding day, propitious Tiber smoothed his watery way: he rolled his river back, and stood poised, a gentle swelling, a peaceful flood. The Trojans mounted their ships; they put out from shore, borne on the waves, and scarcely dipped an oar. Shouts from the land gave omen to their course, and the pitched vessels glided with easy force. The woods and waters wondered at the gleam of shields, and at the painted ships that stemmed the stream. One summer's night and one whole day they passed between the greenwood shades, and cut the liquid glass. The fiery sun had finished half his race, looked back, and doubted in the middle space, when they from far beheld the rising towers, the tops of sheds, and the shepherds' lowly bowers, thin as they stood, which, then of homely clay, now rise in marble, from the Roman sway. These cottages (Evander's kingdom, mean and poor) the Trojan saw, and turned his ships to shore. It was a solemn day: the Arcadian states, the king and prince, without the city gates, were then paying their offerings in a sacred grove to Hercules, the warrior son of Jove. Thick clouds of rolling smoke involved the skies, and fat of entrails fried on his altar.

But, when they saw the ships that stemmed the flood, and glittered through the covert of the wood, they rose in fear, and left the unfinished feast, until dauntless Pallas reassured the rest to continue the rites. Without delay, he himself seized a javelin, and singly took his way; then he gained a rising ground, and called from afar: "Resolve me, strangers, from where you come, and what you are; your business here; and do you bring peace or war?" High on the stern Aeneas took his stand, and held a branch of olive in his hand, while thus he spoke: "You see the Phrygians' arms, expelled from Troy, provoked in Italy by Latian foes, in a war unjustly made; at first affianced, and at last betrayed. Bear this message: 'The Trojans and their chief bring holy peace, and beg the king's relief.'" Struck with so great a name, and all on fire, the youth replied: "Whatever you require, your fame exacts. Descend upon our shores. A welcome guest, and, what you wish, a friend." He said, and, hastening downward to the strand, embraced the stranger prince, and joined his hand.

Conducted to the grove, Aeneas first broke the silence, and thus addressed the king: "Best of the Greeks, to whom, by fate's command, I bear these peaceful branches in my hand, undaunted I approach you, though I know your birth is Grecian, and your land my foe; though your ancient lineage came from Atreus, and both the brother kings claim your kindred; yet my self-conscious worth, your high renown, your virtue, blown through the neighboring nations, our fathers' mingled blood, and Apollo's voice, have led me hither, less by need than by choice. Our founder Dardanus, as fame has sung, and as the Greeks acknowledge, sprang from Electra: Electra came from the loins of Atlas; Atlas, whose head sustains the starry frame. Your sire is Mercury, whom long before fair Maia bore on cold Cyllene's top. Maia the fair, if we rely on fame, was Atlas' daughter, who sustains the sky. Thus from one common source our streams divide; ours is the Trojan, yours the Arcadian side. Raised by these hopes, I sent no news before, nor asked your leave, nor did I implore your faith; but I come, without a pledge, as my own ambassador. The same Rutulians who pursue the Trojan race with arms are equal foes to you. Our host expelled, what further force can stay the victor troops from universal sway? Then will they stretch their power athwart the land, and command either sea from side to side. Receive our offered faith, and give us yours; ours is a generous and experienced line: we do not lack hearts or bodies for the war; we are cautious in council, and daring in the field."

He said; and while he spoke, Evander viewed the man with piercing eyes and vast surprise, pleased with his action, ravished with his face. Then he answered briefly, with a royal grace: "O valiant leader of the Trojan line, in whom the features of your father shine, how I recall Anchises! How I see in you his motions, mien, and all of my friend! Long ago though it be, it is fresh within my mind, when Priam designed a welcome visit to his sister's court, with a friendly stay, and took his way through the Arcadian kingdom. Then, past a boy, the callow down began to shade my chin, and to call me first a man. I saw the shining train with vast delight, and Priam's goodly person pleased my sight; but great Anchises, far above the rest, fired my youthful breast with awful wonder. I longed to join our mutual hearts in friendship's holy bands, and to plight our mutual hands. I first accosted him: I sued, I sought, and, with a loving force, brought him to Pheneus. He gave me, when at length constrained to go, a Lycian quiver and a Gnossian bow, an embroidered vest, glorious to behold, and two rich bridles, with their bits of gold, which my son's coursers hold in obedience. I offer the league you ask, as your right; and, when tomorrow's sun reveals the light, you shall be sent away with swift supplies. Now celebrate with us this solemn day, whose holy rites admit no long delay. Honor our annual feast; and take your seat, with friendly welcome, at a homely treat." Thus having said, the bowls (removed for fear) the youths replaced, and soon restored the cheer. On sods of turf he set the soldiers round: a maple throne, raised higher from the ground, received the Trojan chief; and, over the bed, they spread a lion's shaggy hide for ornament. The loaves were served in baskets; the wine in bowls; the priest renewed the divine rites. Broiled entrails were their food, and a continued chine of beef.

But when the rage of hunger was repressed, Evander thus spoke to his royal guest: "These rites, these altars, and this feast, O king, spring from no vain fears or superstition, nor from blind devotion, nor from blinder chance, nor from heady zeal, or brutal ignorance; but, saved from danger, we recompense the labors of a god with a grateful sense. See, from afar, yon rock that mates the sky, about whose feet such heaps of rubbish lie—such undigested ruin; bleak and bare, how desert it stands now, exposed in air! It was once a robber's den, enclosed around with living stone, and deep beneath the ground. The monster Cacus, more than half a beast, possessed this hold, impervious to the sun. The pavement was ever foul with human gore; heads, and their mangled members, hung on the door. Vulcan begot this plague; and, like his sire, he belched black clouds, and flakes of livid fire. Time, long expected, eased us of our load, and brought the needful presence of a god. The avenging force of Hercules arrived in triumph from Spain, Geryon slain: the giant lived three times, and three times lived in vain. Alcides drove his prize, the lowing herds, near Tiber's bank, to graze in the shady grove. Allured with hope of plunder, and intent on robbing by force and circumventing by fraud, the brutal Cacus, as they strayed by chance, conveyed four oxen and four fair kine from there; and, lest the printed footsteps might be seen, he dragged them backwards to his rocky den. The reversed tracks gave a lying notice, and led the searcher backward from the cave.

"Meanwhile the herdsman hero shifted his place, to find fresh pasture and untrodden grass. The beasts, who missed their mates, filled all around with bellowings, and the rocks restored the sound. One heifer, who had heard her love complain, roared from the cave, and made the project vain. Alcides found the fraud; with rage he shook, and tossed about his head his knotted oak. Swift as the winds, or the flight of Scythian arrows, he climbed the aerial height with eager haste. Then first we saw the monster mend his pace; fear in his eyes, and paleness in his face, confessed the god's approach. Trembling he sprang, as if terror had increased his feet with wings; nor did he stay for stairs, but threw his body down the depth, drew the door over his back (the door, a rib of living rock; with pains his father had hewn it out, and bound it with iron chains); he broke the heavy links, the mountain closed, and opposed bars and levers to his foe. The wretch had hardly made his dungeon fast, when the fierce avenger came with bounding haste; he surveyed the mouth of the forbidden hold, and rolled his raging eyes here and there. He gnashed his teeth; and three times he compassed, with winged speed, the circuit of the ground. Three times at the cavern's mouth he pulled in vain, and, panting, three times desisted from his pain. A pointed flinty rock, all bare and black, grew gibbous from behind the mountain's back; owls, ravens, all ill omens of the night, built their nests here, and winged their flight hither. The leaning head hung threatening over the flood, and nodded to the left. The hero stood adverse, with planted feet, and, from the right, tugged at the solid stone with all his might. Thus heaved, the fixed foundations of the rock gave way; heaven echoed at the rattling shock. Tumbling, it choked the flood: on either side the banks leaped backward, and the streams divided; the sky shrunk upward with unusual dread, and trembling Tiber dived beneath his bed. The court of Cacus stood revealed to sight; the cavern glared with new-admitted light. So the pent vapors, with a rumbling sound, heave from below, and rend the hollow ground; a sounding cleft succeeds; and from on high the gods with hate beheld the nether sky: the ghosts repined at violated night, cursed the invading sun, and sickened at the sight. The graceless monster, caught in open day, enclosed, and in despair to fly away, howled horribly from underneath, and filled his hollow palace with unmanly yells. The hero stood above, and from afar plied him with darts, and stones, and distant war. He, from his huge mouth and nostrils, expired black clouds of smoke, amidst his father's fires, gathering, with each repeated blast, the night, to make aim uncertain, and sight erring. The wrathful god then plunged from above, and, where the sparkles drove in thickest waves, there he alighted; he waded through fumes, and groped his way, half singed, half stifled, till he grasped his prey. He found the monster, spewing fruitless flames; he squeezed his throat; he writhed his neck around, and bound his crippled members in a knot; then from their sockets tore his burning eyes. Rolled on a heap, the breathless robber lay. The doors, unbarred, received the rushing day, and thorough lights disclosed the ravished prey. The bulls, redeemed, breathed the open air again. Next, by the feet, they dragged him from his den. The wondering neighborhood, with glad surprise, beheld his shaggy breast, his giant size, his mouth that flamed no more, and his extinguished eyes. From that auspicious day, with rites divine, we worship at the hero's holy shrine. Potitius first ordained these annual vows; the Pinarian house were added as priests, who raised this altar in the sacred shade, where the honors forever due shall forever be paid. For these deserts, and for this high virtue shown, you warlike youths, crown your heads with garlands; fill high the goblets with a sparkling flood, and with deep draughts invoke our common god."

This said, Evander twined a double wreath, and poplars black and white bound his temples. Then he filled his ample bowl. With like design the rest invoked the gods, with sprinkled wine. Meanwhile the sun descended from the skies, and the bright evening star began to rise. And now the priests, Potitius at their head, involved in the skins of beasts, led the long procession; they held high the flaming tapers in their hands, as custom had prescribed their holy bands. Then they loaded the tables with a second course, and offered to the god with full chargers. The Salii sang, and censed his altars round with Saban smoke, their heads bound with poplar: one choir of the old, another of the young, to dance, and to bear the burden of the song. The lay recorded the labors and the praises, and all the immortal acts of Hercules: first, how the mighty babe, when swathed in bands, strangled the serpents with his infant hands; then, as he grew in years and matchless force, he overthrew the Oechalian walls, and the Trojan. Besides, they related a thousand hazards procured by Juno's and by Eurystheus' hate: "Your hands, unconquered hero, could subdue the cloud-born Centaurs and the monster crew; neither did the bull withstand your resistless arm, nor he, the roaring terror of the wood. The triple porter of the Stygian seat, with lolling tongue, lay fawning at your feet, and, seized with fear, forgot his mangled meat. The infernal waters trembled at your sight; no face of danger, O god, could affright you; neither huge Typhoeus, nor the unnumbered snake, increased with hissing heads, in Lerna's lake. Hail, Jove's undoubted son! An added grace to heaven and to the great author of your race! Receive the grateful offerings which we pay, and smile propitious on your solemn day!" In such verses they sang; above the rest, the den and death of Cacus crowned the feast. The woods conveyed the sound to the hollow vales, the vales to the hills, and the hills rebounded the notes. The rites performed, the cheerful train retired.

Between young Pallas and his aged sire, the Trojan passed, to survey the city, and pleasing talk beguiled the tedious way. The stranger cast his curious eyes around, still viewing new objects with new surprise; with greedy joy he inquired of various things, and of the acts and monuments of ancient kings. Then thus the founder of the Roman towers: "These woods were first the seat of sylvan powers, of Nymphs and Fauns, and of savage men, who took their birth from trunks of trees and stubborn oak. They knew neither laws, nor manners, nor the care of laboring oxen, nor the shining plowshare, nor arts of gain, nor what they gained, to spare. Their exercise was the chase; the running flood supplied their thirst, the trees supplied their food. Then Saturn came, who fled the power of Jove, robbed of his realms, and banished from above. He brought the men, dispersed on hills, to towns, and ordained laws, and taught civil customs, and called the land Latium, where he safely lay hid from his unduteous son, and his usurping sway. With his mild empire, peace and plenty came; and hence the golden times derived their name. A more degenerate and discolored age succeeded this, with avarice and rage. Then the Ausonians, and the bold Sicanians, came; and Saturn's empire often changed its name. Then kings, gigantic Tybris, and the rest, oppressed the land with arbitrary sway: for Tiber's flood was called Albula before, till, from the tyrant's fate, it bore his name. I last arrived, driven from my native home by fortune's power, and by fate's resistless doom. Long tossed on seas, I sought this happy land, warned by my mother nymph, and called by Heaven's command."

Thus, walking on, he spoke, and showed the gate, since called the Carmental by the Roman state, where stood an altar, sacred to the name of old Carmenta, the prophetic dame, who had foretold to her son the Aenean race, sublime in fame, and the imperial place of Rome. Then he showed the forest, which, in after times, fierce Romulus made a sacred refuge for perpetrated crimes; and, with this, the shrine where Pan below the rock had divine rites. Then he told of Argus' death, his murdered guest, whose grave and tomb attest his innocence. Thence he led to the steep Tarpeian rock, now roofed with gold, then thatched with homely reeds. A reverent fear (such superstition reigns among the rude) possessed the swains even then. Some god, they knew—what god, they could not tell—dwelt there amidst the sacred horror. The Arcadians thought him Jove; and they said they saw the mighty Thunderer with majestic awe, who took his shield, and dealt his bolts around, and scattered tempests on the teeming ground. Then they saw two heaps of ruins (once they stood as two stately towns, on either side of the flood), the remains of Saturnia and of Janiculum; each place retained the founder's name. Thus discoursing together, they arrived where poor Evander kept his country court. They viewed the ground of Rome's litigious hall (once oxen lowed, where now the lawyers bawl); then, stooping, they pressed through the narrow gate, when thus the king bespoke his Trojan guest: "Mean as it is, this palace, and this door, received Alcides, then a conqueror. Dare to be poor; accept our homely food, which feasted him, and emulate a god." Then beneath a lowly roof he led the weary prince, and laid him on a bed—the stuffing leaves, overspread with hides of bears. Now night had shed her silver dews around, and with her sable wings embraced the ground, when love's fair goddess, anxious for her son (new tumults rising, and new wars begun), couched with her husband in his golden bed, with these alluring words invokes his aid; and, so that her pleasing speech may move his mind, she inspires each accent with the charms of love: "While cruel fate conspired with Grecian powers to level with the ground the Trojan towers, I asked not aid to restore the unhappy, nor did I implore the succor of your skill; nor did I urge in vain the labors of my lord, to sustain a sinking empire longer, though I owed much to Priam's house, and more, deplored the dangers of Aeneas. But now, by Jove's command, and fate's decree, his race is doomed to reign in Italy. With humble suit I beg your needful art, O power still propitious, that rules my heart! A mother kneels a suppliant for her son. By Thetis and Aurora you were won to forge impenetrable shields, and to grace a less illustrious race with fated arms. Behold what haughty nations are combined against the relics of the Phrygian kind, to destroy my people with fire and sword, and to conquer Venus twice, in conquering Troy." She said; and straightaway she threw her snow-white arms about her unresolving husband. Her soft embraces soon infused desire; his bones and marrow inspired sudden warmth; and all the godhead felt the wonted fire. Not half so swift flies the rattling thunder, nor forky lightnings flash along the skies. The goddess, proud of her successful wiles, and conscious of her form, smiled in secret.

Then thus the power, obnoxious to her charms, panting, and half dissolving in her arms: "Why seek reasons for a cause so just, or distrust your own beauties or my love? Had you long since required my helpful hand, you might have commanded the artificer and the art, to labor arms for Troy: neither Jove, nor fate, confined their empire to so short a date. And, if you now desire to wage new wars, I promise my skill, and engage my pains. Whatever melting metals can conspire, or breathing bellows, or the forming fire, is freely yours: remove your anxious fears, and think no task is difficult to love." Trembling he spoke; and, eager for her charms, he snatched the willing goddess to his arms; till, infused in her lap, he lay possessed of full desire, and sunk into pleasing rest. Now when the night had ridden her middle race, and his first slumber had refreshed the god—the time when early housewives leave the bed; when they spread living embers on the hearth, supply the lamp, and call the maids to rise; with yawning mouths, and with half-opened eyes, they ply the distaff by the winking light, and add the night to their daily labor: thus frugally they earn their children's bread, and uncorrupted keep the nuptial bed—no less concerned, nor at a later hour, the forging power rose from his downy couch.

Sacred to Vulcan's name, an island lay between the coasts of Sicily and Lipare, raised high on smoking rocks; and, deep below, the fires of Aetna glow in hollow caves. Here the Cyclops deal their heavy hammers; loud strokes and hissings of tormented steel are heard around; the boiling waters roar, and smoky flames soar through fuming tunnels. Hither the Father of the Fire, by night, precipitated his flight through the brown air. Here, on their eternal anvils, he found the brethren beating, and the blows going round. A load of pointless thunder now lay before their hands, to ripen for the skies: these darts, for angry Jove, they daily cast; consumed on mortals with prodigious waste. Three rays of writhen rain, three more of fire, as many parts of winged southern winds and cloudy store, frame the dreadful mixture; and fears are added, and avenging flame. Inferior ministers repair the broken axletrees and the blunted war of Mars, and send him forth again with furbished arms, to wake the lazy war with trumpets' loud alarms. The rest refresh the scaly snakes that fold the shield of Pallas, and renew their gold. Full on the crest they place the Gorgon's head, with eyes that roll in death, and with distorted face.

"My sons," said Vulcan, "set your tasks aside; your strength and master-skill must now be tried. Forge arms for a hero; arms that require your force, your speed, and all your forming fire." He said. They set their former work aside, and divided their new toils with eager haste. A flood of molten silver, brass, and gold, and deadly steel, rolled in the large furnace. Of this, their artful hands prepared a shield, alone sufficient to sustain the war. They closed seven orbs within a spacious round: one stirred the fire, and one blew the bellows. The hissing steel was drowned in the smithy; the grotto groaned around with beaten anvils. By turns their arms advanced, in equal time; by turns their hands descended, and the hammers chimed. They turned the glowing mass with crooked tongs; the fiery work proceeded, with rustic songs.

While, at the Lemnian god's command, they thus urged their labors, and plied the Aeolian forge, the cheerful morn saluted Evander's eyes, and the songs of chirping birds invited him to rise. He left his lowly bed: his buskins met above his ankles; sandals sheathed his feet; he set his trusty sword upon his side, and threw a panther's hide over his shoulder. Two menial dogs pressed before their master. Thus clad, and thus guarded, he sought his kingly guest. Mindful of promised aid, he mended his pace, but met Aeneas in the middle space. Young Pallas attended his father's steps, and true Achates waited on his friend. They joined their hands; they chose a secret seat. The Arcadian first renewed their former talk: "Undaunted prince, I never can believe the Trojan empire lost, while you survive. Command the assistance of a faithful friend; but the succors I can send are feeble. Our narrow kingdom here is bounded by the Tiber; on that other side the Latian state surrounds us, insults our walls, and wastes our fruitful grounds. But I prepare mighty nations to join their arms with yours, and to aid your just design. You come, as if sent by your better genius, and fortune seems to favor your intent. Not far from here stands a hilly town, of ancient building, and of high renown, torn from the Tuscans by the Lydian race, who gave the place the name of Caere, once called Agyllina. It flourished long, strong in pride of wealth and in warlike people, until cursed Mezentius, in a fatal hour, assumed the crown, with arbitrary power. What words can paint those execrable times, the subjects' sufferings, and the tyrant's crimes? That blood, those murders, O you gods, visit back on his own head, and on his impious race! The living and the dead were coupled at his command, face to face, and hand to hand, till, choked with stench, tied in loathed embraces, the lingering wretches pined away and died. Thus plunged in ills, and meditating more—the people's patience, tired, no longer bore the raging monster; but they beset his house with arms, and threatened vengeance and destruction. They fired his palace; while the flame ascended, they forced his guards, and executed his friends. He cleaved the crowd, and, favored by the night, directed his flight to Turnus' friendly court. Set on fire by just revenge, the Tuscans require their king's punishment by lawful arms: their numerous troops, now mustered on the strand, shall submit to your command by my counsel. Their navy swarms upon the coasts; they cry to hoist their anchors, but the gods deny. An ancient augur, skilled in future fate, restrains their hate with these foreboding words: 'You brave in arms, you Lydian blood, the flower of Tuscan youth, and choice of all their power, whom just revenge against Mezentius arms, to seek your tyrant's death by lawful arms: know this—no native of our land may lead this powerful people; seek a foreign head.' Awed by these words, they still abide in camps, and await with longing looks their promised guide. Tarchon, the Tuscan chief, has sent me their crown, and every regal ornament: the people join their own desire with his; and all require my conduct, as their king. But the chill blood that creeps within my veins, and age, and listless limbs unfit for pains, and a soul conscious of its own decay, have forced me to refuse imperial sway. My Pallas would be more fit to mount the throne, and should, but he is a Sabine mother's son, and half a native; but in you combine a manly vigor and a foreign line. Where Fate and smiling Fortune show the way, pursue the ready path to sovereign sway. The staff of my declining days, my son, shall make your good or ill success his own; in fighting fields, from you, he shall learn to dare, and serve the hard apprenticeship of war; view your matchless courage and your conduct, and early begin to admire and copy you. Besides, he shall command two hundred horse; though few, a warlike and well-chosen band. These are enlisted in my name; and my son has added as many more in his own."

Scarcely had he said this, when Achates and his guest, with downcast eyes, expressed their silent grief; they, short of succors, and in deep despair, shook at the dismal prospect of the war. But his bright mother, from a breaking cloud, to cheer her offspring, thundered three times aloud; three times forky lightning flashed along the sky, and Tyrrhene trumpets were heard three times on high. Then, gazing up, they heard repeated peals; and, in a serene heaven, refulgent arms appeared: reddening the skies, and glittering all around, the tempered metals clashed, and yielded a silver sound. The rest stood trembling, struck with divine awe; Aeneas only, conscious of the sign, presaged the event, and joyfully viewed, above, the accomplished promise of the Queen of Love. Then, to the Arcadian king: "This prodigy (dismiss your fear) belongs to me alone. Heaven calls me to the war: the expected sign is given of promised aid, and arms divine. My goddess mother, whose indulgent care foresaw the dangers of the growing war, gave this omen, when bright Vulcanian arms, fated from the force of steel by Stygian charms, suspended, shone on high. She then foreshowed approaching fights, and fields to float in blood. Turnus shall dearly pay for faith forsworn; and corpses, and swords, and shields, borne on Tiber, shall choke his flood. Now sound the loud alarms; and, Latian troops, prepare your perjured arms."

He said, and, rising from his homely throne, began the solemn rites of Hercules, and woke the sleeping fires on his altars; then cheerfully retired to his household gods; there he offered chosen sheep. The Arcadian king and the Trojan youth brought the same oblations. Next he reviewed his men and ships; he drew out the best and ablest of the crew. Down with the falling stream the refuse ran, to raise with joyful news his drooping son. Steeds were prepared to mount the Trojan band, who waited their leader to the Tyrrhene land. A sprightly courser, fairer than the rest, the king himself presented to his royal guest: a lion's hide enfolded his back and limbs, precious with studded work, and with paws of gold. Fame spread aloud through the little city the intended march, amid the fearful crowd. The matrons beat their breasts, dissolved in tears, and doubled their devotion in their fears. The war at hand appeared with more affright, and rose at every moment to the sight.

Then old Evander, with a close embrace, strained his departing friend, and tears overflowed his face. "Would Heaven," he said, "recall my strength and youth, such as I was beneath Praeneste's wall, when I made the foremost foes retire, and set whole heaps of conquered shields on fire; when I slew Herilus in single fight, whom Feronia had endued with three lives; and three times I sent him to the Stygian shore, till the last ebbing soul returned no more. If I stood renewed like that, no alarms, nor death, should rend me from my Pallas' arms; nor should proud Mezentius, thus unpunished, boast his rapes and murders on the Tuscan coast. You gods, and mighty Jove, in pity bring relief, and hear a father and a king! If fate and you reserve these eyes to see my son return with peace and victory; if the beloved boy shall bless his father's sight; if we shall meet again with more delight; then draw out my life in length; let me sustain, in hopes of his embrace, the worst of pain. But if your hard decrees (which, O, I dread) have doomed his undeserving head to death; this, O, this very moment, let me die! While hopes and fears lie in equal balance; while, still possessed of all his youthful charms, I strain him close within these aged arms; before that fatal news shall wound my soul!" He said, and, swooning, sank upon the ground. His servants bore him off, and softly laid his languished limbs upon his homely bed.

The horsemen marched; the gates were opened wide; Aeneas at their head, Achates by his side. Next these, the Trojan leaders rode along; last followed in the rear the Arcadian throng. Young Pallas shone conspicuous over the rest; his arms were gilded, his vest embroidered. So, from the seas, the star by whom the lights of heaven are led exerts his radiant head; shakes the pearly dews from his rosy locks, dispels the darkness, and renews the day. The trembling wives crowded the walls and turrets, and followed with their eyes the dusty cloud, which the winds dispersed by fits, and showed from far the blaze of arms, and shields, and shining war. The troops, drawn up in beautiful array, pursued the ready way over heathy plains. Repeated peals of shouts were heard around; the neighing coursers answered to the sound, and shook the solid ground with horny hoofs.

A greenwood shade, known for long religion, stood by the streams that wash the Tuscan town, encompassed round with gloomy hills above, which added a holy horror to the grove. The first inhabitants, of Grecian blood, vowed that sacred forest to Silvanus, the guardian of their flocks and fields; and they pay their due devotions on his annual day. Not far from here, along the river's side, in tents secure, the Tuscan troops abode, led by Tarchon. Now, from a rising ground, Aeneas cast his wondering eyes around, and all the Tyrrhene army had in sight, stretched on the spacious plain from left to right. Thither the Trojan led his warlike train; he refreshed his men, and fed his wearied horses.

Meanwhile the mother goddess, crowned with charms, broke through the clouds, and brought the fated arms. Within a winding vale she found her son, retired alone on the cool river's banks. She showed her heavenly form without disguise, and gave herself to his desiring eyes. "Behold," she said, "performed in every part, my promise made, and Vulcan's labored art. Now secure, seek the Latian enemy, and defy haughty Turnus to the field." She said; and, having first embraced her son, she placed the radiant arms beneath an oak. Proud of the gift, he rolled his greedy sight around the work, and gazed with vast delight. He lifts, he turns, he poises, and admires the crested helm, that vomits radiant fires: his hands hold the fatal sword and corslet, one keen with tempered steel, one stiff with gold: both ample, flaming both, and beamy bright; so shines a cloud, when edged with adverse light. He shakes the pointed spear, and longs to try the plated cuisses on his manly thigh; but he most admires the shield's mysterious mold, and the Roman triumphs rising on the gold. For the heavenly smith had wrought these on it, embossed (not untaught in the rolls of future fate)—the wars in order, and the divine race of warriors issuing from the Julian line. The cave of Mars was dressed with mossy greens; there, by the wolf, were laid the martial twins. Intrepid on her swelling dugs they hung; the foster dam lolled out her fawning tongue; they sucked secure, while, bending back her head, she licked their tender limbs, and formed them as they fed. Not far from there new Rome appears, with games projected for the rape of Sabine dames. The pit resounds with shrieks; a war succeeds, for breach of public faith, and unexampled deeds. Here for revenge the Sabine troops contend; the Romans there with arms defend the prey. Wearied with tedious war, at length they cease; and both the kings and kingdoms plight the peace. The friendly chiefs before Jove's altar stand, both armed, each with a charger in his hand: a fatted sow is led for sacrifice, with imprecations on the perjured head. Near this, the traitor Metius, stretched between four fiery steeds, is dragged along the green, by Tullus' doom: the brambles drink his blood, and his torn limbs are left as the vulture's food. There, Porsena brings proud Tarquin to Rome, and would by force restore the banished kings. One tyrant fights for his fellow-tyrant; the Roman youth assert their native rights. Before the town the Tuscan army lies, to win by famine, or by fraud to surprise. Their king, half-threatening, half-disdaining, stood, while Cocles broke the bridge, and stemmed the flood. The captive maids there tempt the raging tide, escaped from their chains, with Cloelia for their guide. High on a rock heroic Manlius stood, to guard the temple, and the temple's god. Then Rome was poor; and there you might behold the palace thatched with straw, now roofed with gold. The silver goose flew there before the shining gate, and, by her cackle, saved the state. She told the Gauls' approach; the approaching Gauls, obscure in night, ascended, and seized the walls. The gold well dissembled their yellow hair, and they wore golden chains on their white necks. Their vests were gold; they wielded long Alpine spears, and their left arm sustained a length of shield. Nearby, the leaping Salian priests advanced; and the mad Luperci danced naked through the streets, in caps of wool; the targets fallen from heaven. Here modest matrons, driven in soft litters, appeared to pay their vows in solemn pomp, and bore odorous gums in their chaste hands. Far hence removed, the Stygian seats are seen; the pains of the damned, and punished Catiline hung on a rock—the traitor; and, around, the Furies hissing from the nether ground. Apart from these, he draws the happy souls, and Cato's holy ghost dispensing laws.

Between the quarters flows a golden sea; but there foaming surges play in silver. The dancing dolphins divide the glittering waves with their tails, and cut the precious tide. Amid the main, two mighty fleets engaged their brazen beaks, opposed with equal rage. Actium surveyed the well-disputed prize; Leucate's watery plain fried with foamy billows. Young Caesar, on the stern, in armor bright, here leads the Romans and their gods to fight: his beamy temples shoot their flames afar, and the Julian star hangs over his head. Agrippa seconds him, with prosperous gales, and, with propitious gods, assails his foes: a naval crown, that binds his manly brows, foreshows the happy fortune of the fight. Ranged on the line opposed, Antonius brings barbarian aids, and troops of Eastern kings; the Arabians near, and the Bactrians from afar, of discordant tongues, and a mingled war; and, rich in gaudy robes, amidst the strife, his ill fate follows him—the Egyptian wife. Moving they fight; with oars and forky prows the froth is gathered, and the water glows. It seems as if the Cyclades were rooted up again, and jostled in the main; or as if floating mountains met floating mountains: such was the fierce encounter of the fleet. Fireballs are thrown, and pointed javelins fly; the fields of Neptune take a purple dye. The queen herself, amidst the loud alarms, with cymbals tossed warmed her fainting soldiers—fool as she was, who had not yet divined her cruel fate, nor saw the snakes behind. Her country gods, the monsters of the sky, great Neptune, Pallas, and Love's Queen, defy: the dog Anubis barks, but barks in vain, nor any longer dares oppose the ethereal train. Mars in the middle of the shining shield is graved, and strides along the liquid field. The Dirae swoop from heaven with swift descent; and Discord, dyed in blood, with rent garments, divides the press; Bellona treads her steps, and shakes her iron rod above their heads. Seeing this, Apollo, from his Actian height, pours down his arrows; at whose winged flight the trembling Indians and Egyptians yielded, and the soft Sabaeans quit the watery field. The fatal mistress hoists her silken sails, and, shrinking from the fight, invokes the gales. Aghast she looks, and heaves her breast for breath, panting, and pale with fear of future death. The god had figured her as driven along by winds and waves, and scudding through the throng. Just opposite, sad Nilus opened wide his arms and ample bosom to the tide, and spread his mantle over the winding coast, in which he wrapped his queen, and hid the flying host. The victor expressed his thanks to the gods, and blessed Rome, triumphant, with his presence. He placed three hundred temples in the town; he graced every temple with spoils and altars. For three shining nights, and three succeeding days, the fields resounded with shouts, the streets with praise, the domes with songs, the theaters with plays. All altars flame: before each altar lies the destined sacrifice, drenched in his gore. Great Caesar sits sublime upon his throne, before Apollo's porch of Parian stone; accepts the presents vowed for victory, and hangs the monumental crowns on high. Vast crowds of vanquished nations march along, various in arms, in habit, and in tongue. Here, Mulciber assigns the proper place for the Carians, and for the ungirt Numidian race; then he ranks the Thracians in the second row, with the Scythians, expert in the dart and bow. And here the tamed Euphrates humbly glides, and there the Rhine submits her swelling tides, and proud Araxes, whom no bridge could bind; the unconquered offspring of the Danes march behind, and the Morini, the last of humankind.

These figures, divinely wrought on the shield, labored by Vulcan, and brought by Venus, filled the hero's thought with joy and wonder. Unknown the names, he yet admires the grace, and bears aloft the fame and fortune of his race.

chapters.title: Book IX
paragraphs: Turnus takes advantage of Aeneas's absence, fires some of his ships (which are transformed into sea nymphs), and assaults his camp. The Trojans, reduced to the last extremities, send Nisus and Euryalus to recall Aeneas, which furnishes the poet with that admirable episode of their friendship, generosity, and the conclusion of their adventure.

While these affairs passed in distant places, Juno sent the many-colored Iris with haste to find bold Turnus, who, with anxious thought, was seeking the secret shade of his great-grandsire. She found the daring man retired alone, and opened her rosy lips, and began thus: "What none of all the gods could grant to your vows, Turnus, this auspicious day bestows. Aeneas, gone to seek the Arcadian prince, has left the Trojan camp without defense; and, short of succors there, he employs his pains in remote parts to raise the Tuscan swains. Now snatch an hour that favors your designs; unite your forces, and attack their lines." This said, she poised her weight on equal wings, and formed a radiant rainbow in her flight.

The Daunian hero lifted his hands and eyes, and thus invoked the goddess as she flew: "Iris, the grace of heaven, what divine power has sent you down, to shine through dusky clouds? See, they divide; immortal day appears, and glittering planets dancing in their spheres! With joy I obey these happy omens, and follow to the war the god who leads the way." Thus having said, as he stood by the brook, he scooped water from the crystal flood; then with his hands he threw the drops to heaven, and loaded the powers above with offered vows.

Now the bold confederates marched through the plain, well horsed, well clad; a rich and shining train. Messapus led the van; and, in the rear, the sons of Tyrrheus appeared in bright arms. In the main battle, with his flaming crest, mighty Turnus towered above the rest. Silent they moved, majestically slow, like the ebbing Nile, or Ganges in his flow. The Trojans viewed the dusty cloud from afar, and the dark menace of the distant war. Caicus saw it rise from the rampart, blackening the fields, and thickening through the skies. Then he called aloud to his fellows: "What rolling clouds, my friends, approach the walls? Arm! Arm! And man the works! Prepare your spears and pointed darts! The Latian host appears."

Thus warned, they shut their gates; with shouts they ascended the bulwarks, and, secure, awaited their foes. For their wise general, with foreseeing care, had charged them not to tempt the doubtful war, nor, though provoked, to advance in open fields, but to abide their chance close within their lines. Unwilling, yet they kept the strict command, and sourly awaited the hostile band in arms. Fiery Turnus flew before the rest: he pressed a piebald steed of Thracian strain; his helm was of massy gold, and his crest was crimson. With twenty horse to second his designs, an unexpected foe, he faced the lines. "Is there," he said, "any here in arms, who bravely dares to share his leader's honor and his danger?" Then spurring on, he threw his brandished dart, as a sign of war: applauding shouts ensued.

Amazed to find a dastard race, that ran behind the ramparts, and shunned the battle, he rode around the camp, with rolling eyes, and stopped at every post, and tried every passage. So roams the nightly wolf about the fold: wet with descending showers, and stiff with cold, he howls for hunger, and grins with pain (his gnashing teeth are exercised in vain), and, impotent of anger, finds no way in his distended paws to grasp the prey. The mothers listen; but the bleating lambs suck securely at the dug, beneath the dams. Thus ranges eager Turnus over the plain, sharp with desire, and furious with disdain; he surveys each passage with a piercing sight, to force his foes to fight in equal field. Thus while he gazes round, at length he spies where, fenced with strong redoubts, their navy lies, close underneath the walls; the washing tide secures this weaker side from all approach. He takes the wished occasion, fills his hand with ready fires, and shakes a flaming brand. Urged by his presence, every soul was warmed, and every hand was armed with kindled fires. From the fired pines the scattering sparks flew; fat vapors, mixed with flames, involved the sky. What power, O Muses, could avert the flame that threatened the Trojan name in the fleet? Tell; for the fact, obscure through length of time, is hard to faith, yet shall the fame endure.

It is said that, when the chief prepared his flight, and felled his timber from Mount Ida's height, the grandam goddess then approached her son, and with a mother's majesty began: "Grant me," she said, "the sole request I bring, since conquering heaven has owned you for its king. On Ida's brows, for ages past, there stood a shady wood, filled with firs and maples; and on the summit rose a sacred grove, where I was worshiped with religious love. Those woods, that holy grove, my long delight, I gave to the Trojan prince, to speed his flight. Now, filled with fear, I come on their behalf; let neither winds overset, nor waves entomb, the floating forests of the sacred pine; but let their safety be mine." Then thus replied her awful son, who rolls the radiant stars, and controls heaven and earth: "How dare you, mother, demand endless date for vessels molded by a mortal hand? What then is fate? Shall bold Aeneas ride, certain of safety, on the uncertain tide?
